title: Eco-salience Cues and Online Apparel Purchases: A Randomized A/B Field Experiment

detail.title: Eco-salience Cues and Online Apparel Purchases: A Randomized A/B Field Experiment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has an ownership interest in Good Spirit Wear LLC, which operated the online stores used in the experiment.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was reviewed and approved prior to data collection via the ISEF Human Participants Form (4), with full committee review determining that the study was minimal risk.
declarations.funderStatement: No external grant or sponsorship funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Consumers may care about sustainability but overlook products’ environmental attributes when those attributes are not prominent during browsing and product choice. This study tested whether a bundled eco-salience treatment changed what shoppers viewed and purchased in live online spirit wear stores. Storefront visitors were randomized at the browser/device level to a standard storefront (Condition A) or an otherwise identical storefront with a social-norm banner, prominent eco labeling, and eco-first product placement (Condition B). The final sample included 12 organizations, 153 eligible orders, 476 purchased focal-pair items, and 3,813 focal-pair product-detail page views. Eco purchase share was 40.9% in Condition A and 48.1% in Condition B, a 7.3-percentage-point increase (95% CI: +1.6 to +13.0; p = 0.017). Mean eco focal-pair items per eligible order were 1.22 in A and 1.57 in B, a positive but inconclusive difference of 0.35 items (95% CI: −0.04 to +0.74; p = 0.072). Mean organization-level eco view share was 45.9% in A and 52.0% in B, a 6.0-percentage-point increase (95% CI: +2.6 to +9.5; p = 0.003). The results indicate that increasing eco salience shifted both product viewing and purchase composition toward eco-designated alternatives, while evidence for increasing the absolute number of eco items per order remained uncertain.

title: Case Study: How African Fintechs became successful by using Grassroots Product Strategy

detail.title: Case Study: How African Fintechs became successful by using Grassroots Product Strategy
detail.abstract: The financial technology revolution in sub-Saharan Africa has transitioned from isolated microinnovations into a structurally coordinated financial inclusion renaissance. Despite global macroeconomic headwinds and an overall tightening in global venture capital funding, African fintech ecosystems continue to experience exponential growth driven by genuine social needs: affordable credit, seamless transactional rails, and low-cost digital infrastructure. This report evaluates how African and specifically Nigerian fintechs successfully penetrate underserved populations by deploying Grassroots Product Strategies. Anchored on the Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this case study dissects the interplay between public infrastructure (e.g., identity databases, settlement systems) and private enterprise. Additionally, it highlights dedicated strategies used to empower historically marginalized segments, such as women entrepreneurs, rural populations, and informal micro-enterprises.

title: Online Shopping Search: Mobile vs. Non-mobile
affiliations: University of Sydney Business School, University of Texas at Austin and University of Houston - Bauer College of Business

detail.title: Online Shopping Search: Mobile vs. Non-mobile
detail.abstract: In the past decade, smartphones have surpassed desktop computers as the most popular devices for accessing the internet. Consequently, understanding consumers' shopping search behavior on mobile devices has become a crucial focus for marketers. We expect that the distinctive characteristics of mobile devices, vis-à-vis their portability, screen size, shareability, interface, and cost-effectiveness, contribute to differences in shopping search behavior. To investigate this, we analyze daily online shopping search volume data from Google Shopping Insights. Our analysis covers thousands of products across various categories on two types of search devices: mobile (smartphones and phablets) and non-mobile (desktops, laptops, and tablets). Our findings reveal that the share of shopping searches conducted on mobile devices is higher on weekends and holidays, which are typically associated with brick-and-mortar shopping. This trend is particularly pronounced in product categories that involve more impulsive buying decisions or require a greater need for personal privacy. Furthermore, we observe this behavior in market areas with a higher proportion of economically disadvantaged groups. We discuss the managerial and public policy implications stemming from our findings, highlighting the need for marketers to tailor their strategies to accommodate the unique characteristics and behaviors of mobile shoppers. Additionally, our research sheds light on the role of mobile devices in enhancing accessibility and equality in online shopping, particularly for economically disadvantaged groups.

title: Schema Markup Adoption in Top-Ranking Personal Injury Law Firm Websites: A Structured Data Audit of 1,005 Google Page-1 Sites Across 50 US States

detail.title: Schema Markup Adoption in Top-Ranking Personal Injury Law Firm Websites: A Structured Data Audit of 1,005 Google Page-1 Sites Across 50 US States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Founder and CEO of Rank Brilliance, a Semantic SEO agency that provides search engine optimization services to clients across multiple verticals, including legal services. The research was conducted independently and does not involve any client data, proprietary engagements, or commercial partnerships with the 500 personal injury law firm websites included in the study sample. All analyzed websites were selected through publicly available search engine results and directory listings. The author declares no other financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the findings reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or personally identifiable information. The research is based exclusively on publicly accessible website content, including HTML source code and structured data markup, collected through automated crawling in accordance with standard web research practices. No ethics approval was required as the study does not fall under the scope of human subjects research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was self-funded and conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Structured data markup on the open web has moved from a rich-snippet convenience to a load-bearing input for entity extraction, knowledge-graph onboarding, disambiguation, corroboration, and, increasingly, large-language-model context assembly. Personal injury (PI) law firms operate in a legal vertical characterized by high commercial intent and dense local competition. In this context, the practical question is whether the firms already winning Google Page 1 are using schema markup, and how completely they are using it. This study addresses that question through a targeted audit of 1,005 unique PI law firm websites ranking on the first page of Google Search for five core practice-area keywords (personal injury, car accident, truck accident, medical malpractice, and wrongful death) across the largest city in each of the 50 U.S. states plus Washington, D.C. For every domain we crawled the homepage plus up to four ranking practice-area pages, extracted all JSON-LD blocks, scored the implementation against a five-dimension Schema Completeness Index (SCI), and evaluated eligibility for ten Google Rich Results features. We find that 63.7% of top-ranking PI firm websites deploy some schema, yet only 35.3% use the industry-specific LegalService type and only 20.6% emit Person or Attorney schema for their lawyers. Only 4.7% ship an Organization payload complete enough to constitute a brand-quality entity declaration. Spearman rank correlation between SERP position and SCI is a weak but consistent-0.0581, and between rank and Rich Results feature count is-0.084: schema quality is a tiebreaker, not a primary lever, in this sample. We anchor the findings to Google and Microsoft patents and published research that establish structured data as the codified interface into entity recognition, knowledge-graph onboarding, and generative-answer surfaces, and offer a prioritized set of deployment recommendations for firms and their SEO teams.

title: Distributed Redundancy: A New Lens for Resolving the Lean-innovation Paradox

detail.title: Distributed Redundancy: A New Lens for Resolving the Lean-innovation Paradox

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports there are no competing interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication of this article.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-Lean management improves operational efficiency, yet it appears to quietly undermine an organization's capacity to innovate and, in service settings, to serve customers well. This paper asks why, and tests the field's standard remedy, structural ambidexterity, against a genuine alternative.

 Design/methodology/approach-This is a conceptual paper drawing on literature spanning lean operations, organizational slack, exploration-exploitation, ambidexterity, and service quality (SERVQUAL). The argument is developed through five theoretically sampled cases spanning manufacturing, finance, technology, and retail: 3M, Ping An Insurance Group, Google, Haier, and Starbucks, several drawing on peer-reviewed or institutional case material. A future research agenda proposes testable hypotheses.

Findings-Lean practice pushes organizations toward the inefficient tail of the slack-innovation curve, largely by stripping out resource, temporal, and psychological slack. Structural ambidexterity resolves this only partially: walling exploration off in its own unit excludes most resources from innovation, a pattern this paper calls innovation apartheid. The same pressure shows up in services, where it erodes the Responsiveness and Assurance dimensions of service quality during complex customer encounters. Distributed redundancy, built through T-shaped talent, offers a more durable alternative. 

Originality/value-The paper introduces distributed redundancy as a new construct, extends Tshaped capability theory to the organizational level, critiques ambidexterity theory structurally, and connects redundancy structure to customer-perceived service quality through SERVQUAL, a mediation mechanism not previously formalized in this literature.

title: The Location of AI Learning: Employee Teaching, Firm Retention, and Portability

detail.title: The Location of AI Learning: Employee Teaching, Firm Retention, and Portability
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence allows firms to preserve part of employees' task-specific knowledge in systems that remain useful after those employees leave. Prior work studies whether workers contribute knowledge to AI systems that may eventually substitute for them and how rights over training inputs shape that choice. I study a related but distinct question: once employee teaching has created a usable capability, who should be able to keep using it-the firm, the employee, or both? In a two-period incomplete-contracts model, a knowledgeable employee makes a costly, noncontractible teaching investment, and the firm chooses among no independent use, firm retention, employee portability, and concurrent use. Firm retention protects continuity after separation but weakens the employee's incentive to teach; portability strengthens that incentive but may create competitive or confidentiality costs. Retention is therefore selective, and a more effective stand-alone system can leave the firm with less realized capability if employees respond by teaching less. Concurrent use can outperform every exclusive arrangement, including cases in which retention and portability are each unattractive on their own. In those cases, allowing both parties to keep a usable copy preserves the firm's access while bringing the employee's teaching closer to the level that creates the most organizational value. Better measurement and compensation reduce this incentive problem. More broadly, a firm focused only on securing control after an employee leaves may reduce how much useful capability its employees create in the first place.

title: Desire for Perfect Products
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, Red McCombs School of Business, Students, University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business and Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Marketing and Logistics

detail.title: Desire for Perfect Products
detail.abstract: Some consumers evaluate products against demanding, ever-rising ideals of perfection. We introduce the desire for perfect products (DPP), a novel consumer trait capturing the extent to which consumers desire flawless products. Drawing on four qualitative studies, we identify three characteristics that distinguish high (vs. low) DPP consumers: (1) richer and more demanding ideal points, (2) greater susceptibility to upwardly revising those ideals when exposed to superior products, and (3) heightened sensitivity to even minor negative deviations from the ideal. Across scale-development studies reported in the web appendix, we develop an eight-item measure of DPP, establish its discriminant validity, and validate these characteristics. Across eight experiments, we show that high-DPP consumers employ more numerous and stringent search filters, are more attracted to product newness even when quality is unchanged, and are less willing to retain, repair, or donate flawed but usable products. Finally, we identify a managerially relevant intervention: reframing flaws as a source of uniqueness attenuates high-DPP consumers' negative reactions to imperfect products.

title: The Effect of the Wine Critic's 100 Points in the Digital Age: The Case of Spain
affiliations: Unversitat Oberta de Catalunya and

detail.title: The Effect of the Wine Critic's 100 Points in the Digital Age: The Case of Spain
detail.abstract: In any product whose evaluation involves taste factors, subjectivity is a determining factor. For this reason, a rating or evaluation system is sometimes proposed to help potential consumers navigate different decision-making alternatives. In recent decades, the wine sector has been characterized by the use of ratings issued by specialized critics. This access channel serves as a means of knowledge for potential customers who have not physically seen the product and who, upon seeing the ratings received by these critics, see them as an influential factor in their final decision-making. Making a decision based on the numerical rating given by a wine reviewer after tasting a wine, where the wine is awarded the maximum score (100 points), can have a positive influence on the consumer's decision. However, not all critics, and consequently their ratings, have the same relevance to the final buyer. This work designed a methodology and proposed a formulation that objectively assesses the real influence of a wine's highest rating by a critic, based on its increased online visibility, search volume, and references in digital media. Several indicators were designed to compare the influence of different critics' scores over a time horizon of one to four weeks after a wine received its highest rating. The study examined whether the highest rating awarded by a specialized wine reviewer has the same impact in all cases or whether it depends on the critic. It also determined the duration of its influence over time.

title: Employee Productivity and Corporate Debt in the Face of Labor Market Conditions – A European Company-Level Study
affiliations: Instituto Politécnico do Porto - Instituto Superior de Contabiladade e Administracao do Porto (ISCAP), ISCAP - Porto Accounting and Business School, ISCAP and Instituto Politécnico do Porto - Instituto Superior de Contabiladade e Administracao do Porto (ISCAP)

detail.title: Employee Productivity and Corporate Debt in the Face of Labor Market Conditions – A European Company-Level Study
detail.abstract: The main purpose of this research is to test the effectiveness of the debt disciplinary effect, proxied by labor productivity, under differing external conditions in the labor market. Specifically, the study focuses on assessing how the debt disciplinary effect is impacted by changes in employment opportunities in 19 European Union (EU) countries and the United Kingdom between 2010 and 2018, highlighting the effects of heterogeneity in labor policies and the impact of the European and Euro Area sovereign debt crisis on unemployment. The empirical specification is derived from a Cobb-Douglas production function and estimated on firm-level microdata from Orbis Europe, Datastream, Eurostat and the OECD, covering 1,938 listed firms in an unbalanced panel of 10,445 firm-year observations. Static and dynamic panel data methodologies are employed to analyze how the relationship between debt and productivity is affected by labor market conditions. The results suggest that the effectiveness of debt as a disciplinary mechanism is amplified when employees face worse employment alternatives in the labor market, and indicate a non-linear, convex relationship between debt and employee productivity within firms. The institutional and cyclical dimensions are consistent with this channel: employment opportunities are scarcer in the more protective legal regimes, where employee productivity is correspondingly higher, and the effect of the sovereign debt crisis is captured by the deterioration of employment opportunities rather than by the crisis period itself.

title: Attacking a Rival's Communications: A Strategic Marketing Theory of Counter-Competitive Advantage

detail.title: Attacking a Rival's Communications: A Strategic Marketing Theory of Counter-Competitive Advantage

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any people or organizations that could have influenced this study. No funding was received for this research. The cases examined are drawn entirely from publicly available secondary sources, and the author has no affiliation, advisory, consulting, or equity relationship with any of the organizations discussed.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patients, clinical trials, or primary data collection of any kind. The research is a conceptual paper that examines publicly available secondary sources, published case databases, peer-reviewed literature, and archival records. No ethics approval or participant consent is required or applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Strategic marketing theory explains how firms build competitive advantage but says comparatively little about how a firm can weaken a rival’s advantage by attacking the rival’s communications program. This paper develops Counter-Integrated Marketing Communications (C-IMC): a competitive strategy in which a firm coordinates its communications to degrade a rival’s program by targeting its structural elements, rather than building brand equity independently. Bridging competitive dynamics, dynamic capabilities, comparative advertising, and persuasion research, we theorize four attack mechanisms—pre-emptive inoculation, narrative decoupling, journey interception, and asymmetric conformability—each grounded in an established theory and differentiated from its parent theory in distinct, testable predictions. Six theory-based propositions, including two boundary conditions, render the framework falsifiable. Examined against twelve criterion-sampled competitive episodes spanning six industries and three decades, the framework yields a structural theory of counter-competitive advantage and a diagnostic tool for identifying where a rival’s marketing strategy is most exposed to attack.

title: The Help Me Search Era: Do We Choose "Better" with AI?
affiliations: New York University - Stern School of Business, Georgetown University and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Help Me Search Era: Do We Choose "Better" with AI?
detail.abstract: AI-powered search tools are rapidly becoming a primary interface through which consumers discover and evaluate products. This paper asks whether consumer choices improve when they delegate search to AI tools such as ChatGPT, relative to searching on their own via traditional e-retailer websites such as Amazon.com. We proceed in four steps. First, we identify common shopping-related AI prompt types. Second, scraping more than 27,000 responses from ChatGPT (OpenAI's GPT 5.1) and Google AI Mode to these common shopping prompt types, we find that AI consistently adopts a best-for format which emphasizes the features each brand is best suited for while leaving others implicit. As a result, only a fraction of features per brand appear in a response, so full information requires follow-up questions, allowing for inferior choices. Third, we develop a search model formalizing this best-for structure. It predicts that AI typically leads to the same choice as under full information, but can induce errors when the preferred product's highlighted attribute dominates and its non-highlighted attribute is inferior. Finally, we test these predictions in a pre-registered incentivized experiment, comparing traditional e-retailer search with AI search. Our results provide the first direct experimental evidence on the causal effect of AI-formatted information on consumer choice quality.

title: From Logo to Linked Entity: Reframing Corporate Book Sponsorship as a Semantic Knowledge Asset in the Age of Generative Search

detail.title: From Logo to Linked Entity: Reframing Corporate Book Sponsorship as a Semantic Knowledge Asset in the Age of Generative Search

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of EVENTICA Publications and works as an independent researcher and consultant in artificial intelligence, digital growth, and publishing. These professional activities informed the broader research interests but did not influence the design, analysis, interpretation, or conclusions of this study. No financial or commercial support was received for this research, and the author declares no competing financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual study is based solely on publicly available literature and theoretical analysis. It did not involve human participants, human data, animals, or clinical materials. Accordingly, ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently by the author without financial support from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agency.

detail.abstract: Corporate sponsorship of books is still treated, in both practice and theory, as a form of visual brand placement: a logo on a cover, a line of acknowledgement in the front matter. This article argues that in an environment where search and generative systems increasingly mediate discovery, that framing is incomplete. A printed logo carries almost no value for machine reasoning; a sponsorship relationship expressed as structured, interoperable metadata linked to persistent identifiers can, in principle, become a discoverable and machine-readable brand asset. Building on sponsorship-linked marketing, brand-asset theory, semantic publishing, and the emerging study of generative search, we develop a conceptual framework that separates this claim into four distinct conditionsencodability, discoverability, resolution, and brand outcome-and advance seven propositions that make each condition testable and refutable. We deliberately treat the strongest link in the popular version of this claim, that generative systems will reproduce sponsor relationships in their outputs, as unproven rather than assumed. We then identify a consequence the marketing literature has not addressed: because a semantic sponsorship relationship can be visible to machines while remaining invisible to human readers, undisclosed semantic sponsorship at scale is functionally similar to astroturfing and constitutes an information-integrity risk. Paired human-readable disclosure is the mitigating condition. The article distinguishes the proposed construct from native advertising, branded content, and content marketing, closes with a matched-pair research agenda, and draws out theoretical, managerial, and ethical implications for sponsors, publishers, and communications practitioners.

title: Relating Cognitive Skills and Personality Traits to Economic Preferences: Decision-making under Cognitive Shocks and Guessing
affiliations: , Jinan University, University of Chicago - Department of Economics and Liaoning University

detail.title: Relating Cognitive Skills and Personality Traits to Economic Preferences: Decision-making under Cognitive Shocks and Guessing
detail.abstract: Using rich data on Chinese schoolchildren, we study the relationships of IQ and personality traits with children's risk preferences and how they affect the precision with which those preferences are measured. Our structural model separates preferences from deliberation noise and guessing, and relates guessing to deliberation noise. Psychological measures have weak direct influences on preferences but strongly affect deliberation noise and guessing behavior. Shocks to choice have persistent individual-specific components and are not independent. Socioeconomic background has little direct influence on preferences or deliberation noise once traits are accounted for. Background variables affect psychological traits, however. Risk preferences differ across and within genders. For small gambles, girls are less risk averse than boys, but the opposite holds for larger gambles.

title:
Artificial Intelligence as Input-Biased Technical Change: Labor Productivity, TFP, and KLEM Substitution in a Translog Framework 

A Professional Journal Article on the Production-Theoretic Nexus of Capital, Labor, Energy, and Materials
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Artificial Intelligence as Input-Biased Technical Change: Labor Productivity, TFP, and KLEM Substitution in a Translog Framework 

A Professional Journal Article on the Production-Theoretic Nexus of Capital, Labor, Energy, and Materials
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is best understood not merely as software capital but as a generalpurpose technological system that can change the organization, direction, and measurement of production. This article examines AI's effects on technological change, technical change, labor productivity, and total factor productivity (TFP) within a Translog production framework using capital, labor, energy, and materials inputs. The central argument is that AI affects productivity through multiple channels: digital capital deepening, labor augmentation and task reallocation, energy and materials optimization, organizational redesign, and shifts in the bias of technical change across KLEM inputs. A Translog specification is appropriate because it permits non-neutral technical change, variable substitution elasticities, and second-order interaction effects among inputs. The article develops a conceptual and empirical framework for estimating AI-related productivity effects and highlights measurement challenges related to intangible capital, delayed organizational adjustment, AI-specific input classification, and the residual nature of TFP.

title: Recession and Resilience: Long-Term Labor Market Outcomes of Starting College in a Bad Economy
affiliations: Hanyang University, Yonsei University - Department of Economics, Hanyang University and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Recession and Resilience: Long-Term Labor Market Outcomes of Starting College in a Bad Economy
detail.abstract: This study examines how economic conditions at the beginning of college affect postgraduation labor market outcomes, with particular attention to behavioral responses related to job market preparation. Exploiting variation in regional unemployment rates within college entry cohorts, we utilize the historically large and unexpected recession triggered by the Asian financial crisis in South Korea as a natural experiment. Using data from the Korean Labor and Income Panel Study, we find that individuals who began college under more adverse economic conditions have higher employment probabilities and earnings during the first decade after graduation. Analyses of activities during college and the transition to work suggest that these gains are driven by greater effort devoted to education, training, and job search aimed at improving employment prospects. We develop a theoretical framework based on ambiguity aversion to explain these behavioral responses.

title: International Experience of Digital Transformation in Public Administration
affiliations: MGIMO University

detail.title: International Experience of Digital Transformation in Public Administration
detail.abstract: International practice increasingly treats digital transformation in public administration as a comprehensive institutional reconfiguration in which technological solutions are integrated into regulation, interagency coordination, data governance, and digital infrastructure. This paper compares the methodological approaches of the OECD and the World Bank and examines the models of the United States, China, and Brazil. The US model combines a single point of entry with distributed service delivery; China relies on a centralized government-data architecture; and Brazil is building a unified platform environment. The common trend is a transition from fragmented digitalization to digital public infrastructure.

title: The Effects of Ads on Beliefs and Implications for Consumer Search
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Northwestern University,  and Northwestern - Kellogg

detail.title: The Effects of Ads on Beliefs and Implications for Consumer Search
detail.abstract: We study how in-store display ads communicate information about a product's price and quality, both directly through ad content and indirectly through inferences consumers draw from the presence and content of the ad. We run an incentivized experiment in a simulated online store, randomizing ad exposure, ad content, and the advertised product's price, while also eliciting participants' beliefs and choices. Display ads shift beliefs about price and quality, even when the ad copy does not directly reveal either attribute. We provide evidence that these belief shifts have a causal effect on searches and purchases of the advertised product. Using a stylized search model, we show that while visibility explains most of the ad effects, belief updating explains a statistically and economically significant share. Casting ad content choice as an information design problem, we show that advertisers may find it optimal to conceal product information even when it exceeds consumers' expectations.

title: Energy Uncertainty, Product Market Competition, and Corporate Investment
affiliations: University of Otago, Lincoln University (NZ) and Auckland University of Technology (AUT)

detail.title: Energy Uncertainty, Product Market Competition, and Corporate Investment
detail.abstract: A firm's investment depends on uncertainty it does not fully control. We show that corporate investment responds not only to a firm's own energy uncertainty but, more strongly, to the energy uncertainty facing its product market rivals. We build firm-level measures of energy uncertainty from the text of 10-K filings for 5,317 US firms over 2001 through 2023. A one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's own energy uncertainty is associated with a decline in capital expenditure of about 6.0 percent of mean investment. Rival energy uncertainty is measured through the text-based product market network of Hoberg and Phillips (2016). It is associated with a further decline of about 20 percent of mean investment per standard deviation, and the two channels reinforce one another. The rival effect is horizontal rather than vertical, which rules out a shared input cost explanation. Both effects concentrate among firms in oil and gas producing states, operate in part through elevated idiosyncratic return volatility, and strengthen with financial constraints, product market fluidity, and CEO energy-sector experience. They survive a quasi-natural experiment around the 2014 OPEC oil-price collapse and Lewbel (2012) instrumental-variable estimation. Energy uncertainty delays investment through a real options channel that operates both within the firm and across the competitive network in which it is embedded.

title: Scale-Selected Consolidation: A Multilevel Selection Theory of Innovation and the Means of Production

detail.title: Scale-Selected Consolidation: A Multilevel Selection Theory of Innovation and the Means of Production

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare I have no personal gain from this publication.
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: Major productivity-transforming innovations are often followed by concentration of control over the relevant means of production, as in the transition from cottage industry to the factory system. Taken naively, this suggests a rule-sufficiently important innovations consolidate production-but the rule fails: personal computing and open-source software are transformative innovations that were followed by mass deconsolidation of production capacity. We propose a refined thesis: an innovation consolidates production if and only if it raises the returns to coordinated scale by enough to exceed the cost of coordinating that scale. We formalize this with a Price-equation decomposition of the change in aggregate coordination scale into a between-unit selection term and a within-unit term, derive an explicit threshold condition together with a closed-form critical scale, and extend the statics to a replicator dynamics that generates logistic consolidation trajectories of the same functional form long documented in the technology-diffusion literature. Decomposing a technology into an infrastructure layer (which builds a capability) and a use layer (which deploys it) lets a single innovation consolidate one layer while deconsolidating the other. We apply the framework, with order-of-magnitude quantification disciplined against external data wherever available, to the Industrial Revolution and the parallel case of automobile manufacturing, to railroads, electrical utilities, and chip fabrication, to personal computers and open-source software, and to artificial intelligence, whose training layer is consolidating at what may be the fastest rate yet observed even as its use layer deconsolidates. We situate the model against the cross-industry evidence on rising concentration and markups, against Zipf's-law regularities in the firm-size distribution, and against the transaction-cost, business-history, and network-effects literatures, and we state the model's testable predictions and scope limitations explicitly. The framework is explicitly non-normative: it assigns no praise or blame to consolidation, and it predicts that command economies-despite explicit anti-concentration ideology-consolidate production more completely than market economies, a prediction consistent with comparative evidence on pre-Soviet and Soviet enterprise concentration. This specializes the result of Scalar Naturalism (n.d.), that capitalism and communism are scale-dependent, observer-dependent expressions of one allocation principle, to the dynamics of innovation specifically.

title: Separating Original Tenement Value and Earn-in Spend in Joint Venture Terms Valuation

detail.title: Separating Original Tenement Value and Earn-in Spend in Joint Venture Terms Valuation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed as a Principal Consultant at SRK Consulting and works in the Project Evaluation Team valuing mineral assets. The views expressed in this paper are the author's own and do not necessarily represent the position of SRK Consulting.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper contains no human participants, patient data, or clinical research.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research. This paper was prepared independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Joint venture (JV) terms are widely used as market indicators of exploration tenement value, particularly at early stages where income-based valuation is not possible. In the standard "Case 2" earn-in formulation, the expression

V100% = $E(1-I%)/I%

is stated to be the correct formula for calculating value where a farminor spends E to earn an interest I% under the simplifying assumption that expenditure is "instantaneous and with certainty" (Rudenno, 2014). In practice this leads to inconsistency when compared with the simple "cash-for-equity" Case 1 expression

V100% = $E/I%

If these formulas are both interpreted as total post-spend value, they return implausible return-on-investment (ROI) patterns across realistic JV terms.

This paper clarifies what the Case 2 expression is measuring and proposes a simple reformulation of the JV terms formulae. The Case 2 expression after notational correction is re-interpreted as the implied pre-spend tenement value, Vpre. The total un-risked value at completion is then

V100% = E + Vpre

or

V100% = E + E(1-I%)/I%

which reconciles exactly with the Case 1 "cash-for-equity" result (noting that 1 is a unitary constant), under the same limiting setting "instantaneous and with certainty". Building on this decomposition, a risked form is proposed:

VR,100% = (E × R%) + E(1-i%)/i%

where R% is a deal-completion/timing factor applied only to the expenditure. This placement of risk is consistent with Lawrence's (2001) treatment of option-like and contingent interests and with the requirement to distinguish fully vested interests from those subject to conditions.

The paper concludes with guidance on when this simplified formulation is appropriate to use.

AI Disclosure Statement
The author used AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) during the preparation of this paper for peer review support, structural feedback, and editorial suggestions such as formatting and grammar. All intellectual content, mathematical derivations, findings, outcomes and conclusions are the author's own. AI was not used to generate data, results, or conclusions. The author takes full responsibility for all content of the published paper.

title: Market Participation Decisions, Commercialization Intensity, and Structural Transformation in Maryland's Goat Sector: An Empirical Analysis
affiliations: Tribhuvan University, University of Maryland Eastern Shore, University of Maryland Eastern Shore and University of Maryland Eastern Shore

detail.title: Market Participation Decisions, Commercialization Intensity, and Structural Transformation in Maryland's Goat Sector: An Empirical Analysis
detail.abstract: Although goat production accounts for a small share of the total U.S. livestock output, it plays a crucial role in diversified and small-scale farming systems. Despite representing less than 1% of the U.S. goat inventory and sales, Maryland provides valuable insights into the commercialization of small-scale livestock systems. However, limited empirical evidence exists on the drivers of goat commercialization at the state level, particularly in distinguishing between market growth driven by expansion within existing farms and that driven by the entry of new producers. This study examines the determinants of goat market participation and commercialization intensity using county-level panel data from the USDA Census of Agriculture for 2002-2022 (92 county-year observations). A Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) and Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) frameworks are employed to isolate within-county variation over time. Results show that increases in herd size are positively and significantly associated with goat sales (TWFE: β = 0.844, p < 0.05; PPML: β = 1.204, p < 0.01), while changes in the number of farms are not statistically significant. Although market participation increased until 2017 and declined by 2022, the overall pattern indicates emerging structural constraints in commercialization. These findings demonstrate that commercialization in small-scale goat production systems is primarily driven by intensification among existing producers rather than by new farm entry. By focusing on within-county variation, this study provides a clearer understanding of scale effects in smallscale livestock systems and contributes to the literature on structural transformation. The results suggest that policies focusing on improving market access, processing infrastructure, and support for herd expansion among existing farmers are more effective than policies aimed at increasing the number of producers.

title: Astrocytic-Modulated Regional Plasticity in Noise-Tolerant Memristive Neuromorphic Crossbar Arrays: A Hardware-Parameterised In-Silico Framework

detail.title: Astrocytic-Modulated Regional Plasticity in Noise-Tolerant Memristive Neuromorphic Crossbar Arrays: A Hardware-Parameterised In-Silico Framework
detail.abstract: Non-volatile memory (NVM) crossbar arrays are increasingly deployed as synaptic substrates in edge neuromorphic devices, where write-cycle endurance is the primary hardware bottleneck. Standard spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) issues weight updates unconditionally, saturating memristive devices with spurious writes under noise. Biological cortex addresses this through tripartite synapses, in which perisynaptic astrocytes monitor regional activity and suppress plasticity during chaotic epochs. This work derives and validates the Astrocytic-Modulated Regional Plasticity (AMRP) rule, governed by ∆w ij = H R (t) • f STDP (∆t ij), where H R (t) ∈ [0, 1] is a sigmoid gate driven by a leaky-integrated regional spike density ρ R (t). Across Brian2 experiments (n = 10 seeds, 1-20 Hz background noise), AMRP achieves: (i) 6.0 ± 2.2× lower weight entropy at 5 Hz; (ii) 191.2 ± 17.4× lower NVM write-operations Σ|∆w| at 20 Hz (CV 9.1%); (iii) elimination of a representation-inversion failure in which unconstrained STDP potentiates noise synapses above signal synapses (∆ w =-0.128 ± 0.022 vs. AMRP's-0.001 ± 0.002); and (iv) τ astro as the dominant metaplasticity parameter, with 16× lower NVM wear across a fourfold τ astro increase, motivating τ astro /τ m ≈ 10-30 consistent with astrocytic calcium timescales. At low noise the gate stays mostly open (H R ≈ 0.8-0.9), so AMRP costs little relative to STDP. A structural ablation shows AMRP's multiplicative gate outperforms an additive astrocytic control, modelled on prior hardware-resident astrocyte implementations, across all noise levels and 16 of 20 parameter-grid cells, without the per-regime re-tuning the additive formulation requires. These results establish a physically grounded, empirically validated framework for astrocyte-inspired write-cycle management, with explicit design mappings for mixed-signal ASIC and FPGA implementations.

title: AI-Enabled Credit Assessment for MSMEs: A Framework for Transparency and Inclusion

detail.title: AI-Enabled Credit Assessment for MSMEs: A Framework for Transparency and Inclusion
detail.abstract: Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) are a critical component of the Indian economy, contributing 30% to GDP and 60% to employment. Yet, a severe credit gap persists, with the sector receiving only ~16% of total bank credit. This financing constraint stifles growth and reflects a fundamental market failure. This research directly responds to the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) mandate for efficient, transparent credit by building FinTech a proof-of-concept prototype that operationalizes India's digital public infrastructure (IndiaStack). Our system automates credit assessment by integrating consented data flows from GSTN, bank transactions, and metadata. A rule-based engine executes a multi-faceted financial analysis (liquidity, DSCR, cash flow stability, sectoral NPA exposure), while an integrated Large Language Model (LLM) generates narrative, explainable AI (XAI) rationales for full transparency. The pivotal achievement is a reduction in credit decision time to under 15-20 seconds. This demonstrates a viable model for banks to drastically reduce operational costs and, critically, has the potential to mitigate NPAs through a more dynamic, forward-looking risk assessment that surpasses static collateral evaluation. By providing a tangible blueprint to bridge the gap between IndiaStack's potential and banking practice, this work offers a strategic tool for policymakers, financial institutions and fintech developers. It enables a shift towards a resilient, inclusive lending ecosystem that unlocks the full potential of MSMEs, directly fueling India's broader digitalization vision and sustainable macroeconomic health.

title: Judicial Roulette: The Political Economy of Doctrinal Uncertainty in the Recent Jurisprudence of The Supreme Court of Nigeria
affiliations: University of Nigeria

detail.title: Judicial Roulette: The Political Economy of Doctrinal Uncertainty in the Recent Jurisprudence of The Supreme Court of Nigeria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None needed
declarations.funderStatement: Personally funded

detail.abstract: Public confidence in the Supreme Court of Nigeria is presently strained by a pattern this article calls doctrinal somersaulting: the tendency of coordinate or near-identical panels of the Court to hand down, within a short interval and often without express acknowledgment, decisions that point in opposite normative directions on the same point of law. Using three recurring and representative fault lines: locus standi in public interest litigation, dismissal from employment and the admissibility of unregistered registrable land instrument; this article traces the doctrinal history of each principle through the Supreme Court's jurisprudence, with particular attention to the last decade, and interrogates the most recent cases in each line for what they reveal about the health of stare decisis in Nigeria. It integrates and engages directly with four recent contributions to this debate: Ubani, Odunaike and Ekundayo's account of an oscillating locus standi jurisprudence; a rejoinder to that account, which recharacterised Okonjo-Iweala v Fawehinmi as a calibrating rather than a regressive decision; Idigbe and Ogunbadewa's case note on the Supreme Court's "unsettled verdicts" on employment rights; and Professor Osita Nnamani Ogbu's lecture on the crisis in the application of the doctrine of judicial precedent. The article shows that the Supreme Court's decision in Chief Nduka Edede v Attorney-General of the Federation, delivered three months after Okonjo-Iweala, complicates the taxonomy the rejoinder proposed, by denying standing even in what was clearly a facial challenge to the constitutionality of section 84(12) of the Electoral Act 2022-precisely the category of case the rejoinder's taxonomy had assumed remained open to every citizen. The article then turns to the economic consequences of this pattern of doctrinal instability, drawing on the new institutional economics of Douglass North and its progeny to argue that unpredictability at the apex of the judicial hierarchy is not merely a professional irritant but a measurable drag on investment, contracting and capital formation; compounded in Nigeria's case by the long lag between the commencement of litigation and its resolution at the Supreme Court, which means litigants and firms frequently plan and act on legal positions that have silently changed by the time their own matters are decided. The article concludes by adopting Ubani, Odunaike and Ekundayo's call for doctrinal consistency, endorsing Professor Ogbu's proposal that the Supreme Court should sit as a full panel before overruling itself and should renounce the practice of implied overruling. It finally proposes a concrete institutional mechanism-a standing Certainty Protocol; by which the Court might discipline its own departures from precedent.

title: A Competitive-Fuel-Indexed Pricing and Margin-Recovery Framework for India's City Gas Distribution Sector

detail.title: A Competitive-Fuel-Indexed Pricing and Margin-Recovery Framework for India's City Gas Distribution Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based entirely on publicly available data from company reports, investor presentations, and government publications. No human participants, patient data, personal data, or animal subjects were involved. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: India's city gas distribution (CGD) companies price industrial gas from their own cost base, while industrial customers decide on the delivered cost of the next-best fuel-propane and furnace oil. This paper shows the resulting tension is a structural, sector-wide margin squeeze whose severity is governed by a company's industrial exposure. Rebuilding the audited economics of the five largest listed operators-Gujarat Gas, IGL, MGL, MNGL and Adani Total Gason a common per-unit basis reveals a monotonic gradient: profitability per unit of gas falls sharply as industrial (propane-contestable) exposure rises, from CNG-and household-dominated networks down to industrial-heavy Gujarat Gas. The driver is not the cost of gas but the customer-Adani Total Gas carries almost identical gas cost to Gujarat Gas yet earns roughly double the margin by selling to captive users rather than propane-exposed industry. Taking Gujarat Gas as the sharpest case, and converting all fuels to a common thermal basis, the analysis showscorroborated by bootstrap, leave-one-out and Monte-Carlo tests-that its industrial cost floor has risen to meet the competing-fuel ceiling, erasing margin and coinciding with a near-halving of its industrial volume. The paper proposes a decision framework any CGD can apply: price industrial gas by a formula indexed to the competing fuel, read that ceiling backwards into a per-cluster procurement budget, segment and diversify the customer base, and index procurement to the same benchmark to keep the corridor open. Benchmarked against China, Japan, Korea, Europe and Indonesia, industrial gas prices are anchored to cost, subsidy, or service quality-but nowhere to competing-fuel parity, the mechanism that actually governs fuel switching. The framework therefore delivers the protective effect of Indonesia's HGBT scheme without its fiscal subsidy: a self-funding, cluster-specific route to margin recovery.

reference: American University Business Law Review, Vol. 16, No. 2, 2026 (forthcoming)
title: The Failed Neo-Brandeisian Section 5 Experiment: Speed Bump or Time for a Major Course Correction?
affiliations: William & Mary Law School

detail.title: The Failed Neo-Brandeisian Section 5 Experiment: Speed Bump or Time for a Major Course Correction?

publicationDetails.detailsText: American University Business Law Review, Vol. 16, No. 2, 2026 (forthcoming)

detail.abstract:
Led by Neo-Brandeisian Lina Khan, President Biden’s Federal Trade Commission launched an ambitious effort to revitalize Section 5 of the FTC Act, which prohibits “unfair methods of competition.”  Rejecting a consumer-focused Rule of Reason, the Commission announced in 2022 that Section 5 condemns any conduct that “goes beyond competition on the merits,” subject to a stingy business justification defense.  Drawing on this new standard, the Commission issued a 2024 legislative rule banning nearly all employee non-compete agreements (“NCAs”) as unfair methods of competition.  However, President Trump’s FTC acceded to vacatur of the Rule, agreeing with two federal courts that the Commission lacks authority to promulgate such regulations.

This article critiques the Biden Commission’s Section 5 experiment and offers a pessimistic prognosis for any future efforts to revitalize the Neo-Brandseisian Section 5 agenda.  Taken together, the 2022 Statement and 2024 NCA Rule reflect two fundamental weaknesses in the Section 5 project, one legal and one scientific.  Legally, neither pronouncement described any valid intelligible principle to replace the consumer-driven Rule of Reason.  While both documents condemned conduct that “goes beyond competition on the merits,” neither defined the term or engaged modern definitions. 

Moreover, the Rule presumptively condemned as “restrictive” any agreement reducing competitive rivalry and presumptively banned as “exclusionary” conduct that slightly disadvantages rivals.  Both definitions would presumptively condemn numerous garden-variety agreements that courts usually enforce despite incidental impacts on competition or rivals.  While some such agreements produce net harm, the Commission cited no authority suggesting that all such agreements are presumptively unlawful. 

Scientifically, the Final Rule ignored key economic concepts, particularly teachings of transaction cost economics (“TCE”) regarding the formation, function and impact of nonstandard contracts such as NCAs.  For instance, comments described how an exit-driven process of contract formation could, without negotiation, ensure that NCAs are voluntary and result in compensation.  Recognition of such a voluntary formation process undermined the Rule’s finding that 99 percent of NCAs are “coercive” as well as the Rule’s claim that mandatory disclosure would not impact the number or content of such agreements. 

The Rule also assumed that benefits of NCAs necessarily coexist with harms that establish a prima facie case, echoing the 2022 Statement’s description of business justifications.  This coexistence assumption ignored comments contending that proof that a fully-disclosed NCA produces benefits undermines the prima facie case of harm, obviating any requirement of justification.  The Commission also incorrectly found that certain less restrictive alternatives would achieve the same benefits as NCAs, ignoring comments that invoked the teachings of TCE to refute this finding.  Finally, the Rule ignored Raising Rivals’ Costs theory, which undermines the claim that exclusionary agreements necessarily result from coercion and suggests that most markets are not susceptible to the use of NCAs to injure consumers or rivals.

These weaknesses would hinder future efforts to advance the Neo-Brandeisian Section 5 agenda vis a vis NCAs and other non-standard contracts the Biden Commission sought to address.  Claims that reducing competition or disadvantaging rivals is presumptively unfair and thus unlawful will likely fall on deaf ears of judges reviewing legislative rules under the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”), particularly after the demise of Chevron deference to agency interpretations.  A future Neo-Brandeisian Commission would thus have to identify some less expansive Section 5 principle, something Neo-Brandeisians have shown no inclination to do.

Moreover, refusal to recognize modern economic theory regarding the formation, function and impact of nonstandard contracts will render expansive rules vulnerable to judicial determinations that such pronouncements are arbitrary and capricious under the APA.  Such rules will be particularly vulnerable when the Commission ignores public comments that highlight how such theory and record evidence undermines the basis for a proposed rule.  In a society governed by law, electoral success is no substitute for doing the work required to develop well-grounded legal standards and understand the economic theory and evidence necessary to apply such standards when formulating legislative rules.

title: Exploring Customer Perception Towards Fintech Services in Karimnagar District Central Cooperative Bank: A Study on Usage and Adoption
affiliations: Osmania University and Osmania University

detail.title: Exploring Customer Perception Towards Fintech Services in Karimnagar District Central Cooperative Bank: A Study on Usage and Adoption
detail.abstract: The study investigates customers' perceptions of the usability of FinTech services in the context of Karimnagar District Central Cooperative Bank and the qualitative and exploratory research approach identified the elements that drive customer adoption and usage of FinTech services. The study collected the primary data through a questionnaire with convenient sampling method and applied the neural network and exploratory factor analysis statistical methods. The findings of the study emphasised the significance of prioritising customer wants and expectations in the development and delivery of FinTech services and concluded that to meet the client needs, financial institutions must prioritise improving the speed and effectiveness of their FinTech offerings. Furthermore, when designing FinTech services, financial institutions must consider clear instructions and ease of learning. The study highlighted the potential benefits of financial institutions engaging in FinTech services as, the FinTech services can be used to save money while earning revenues.

title: The Chirality Bound
affiliations: MYRA School of Business, ETH Zurich and MIT

detail.title: The Chirality Bound
detail.abstract: Ambarish, Kreuser, and Seigel (AKS 2026a) introduced market chirality as the measurable handedness of the implied-volatility surface and proposed a local slope-to-curvature index to quantify that asymmetry. This paper develops a probabilistic restriction associated with that geometric object. We identify two centred second-order innovations that enter finite-horizon option profit and loss: an unexpected spotvolatility product shock and an unexpected volatility-squared shock. Under conditional joint Gaussianity, their correlation is available in closed form and is governed by the spot-volatility correlation. We then use a local stochastic-volatility skew relation to connect that dynamic correlation to the chirality index introduced in the earlier AKS paper. The resulting theory yields a simple chirality frontier and, crucially, an exact condition under which that frontier is a lower envelope for the magnitude of the correlation between the two quadratic innovations. We call this the chirality dominance condition. The paper therefore moves chirality from a geometric characterization to a falsifiable restriction on the dependence of option-risk innovations. We also correct the exact SVI representation of the local chirality index and distinguish it from its commonly used first-order approximation. Preliminary SPX surface evidence reproduces the negative chirality, hump-shaped maturity structure, and stress amplification documented in AKS-I, but these surface facts are treated only as motivation. The decisive empirical test must construct the quadratic innovations independently, estimate the surface-to-dynamics conversion, and test the lower envelope only in the dominance region.

title: Cutting AI Datacenter Energy with Reinforcement Learning: Measured Power Control of LLM Training from One GPU to the Fleet

detail.title: Cutting AI Datacenter Energy with Reinforcement Learning: Measured Power Control of LLM Training from One GPU to the Fleet
detail.abstract: Reinforcement-learning post-training dominates modern language-model development, yet its power behavior on GPU hardware has not been characterized, and datacenters manage GPU power only with workload-blind mechanisms, static caps and reactive throttling, that slow the hardware indiscriminately. We instrument GRPO training with half-second power telemetry at 7B, 14B, and 72B scales on one to four A100s, over 380,000 samples, and train a PPO meta-controller that adapts the workload's own generation parameters to measured power. Evaluated against the full 500-step 7B trace, the controller cuts power-limit violations by 89.8% while increasing token output by 18.1% and energy efficiency by 26.2% in tokens per megawatt-hour. Deployed live at 72B, the same controller family yields replicated null results, diagnosed as the group-size actuator losing authority under model sharding. An actuator-authority sweep shows the same parameters applied as generation concurrency retain 17 to 22% power authority, isolating an occupancyversus-volume principle; a controller rebuilt on that actuator controls a live 72B rollout-generation workload across three hardware replications: 35.7% more output than a static safe baseline at 2.27 ± 1.08% budget violations, 87.2% fewer violations than uncontrolled operation, and the highest mean throughput and lowest mean energy per token among the constrained controllers, with an adaptive threshold rule matching it in one of three operating conditions. Under realistic measurement windows the original 72B transients collapse from 23.6% at half-second resolution to 1.6% at thirty seconds and zero at five minutes; a composed sixteen-GPU fleet shows zero violations at thirty seconds and longer, with peak demand at 50 to 56% of nameplate. For this fleet mix, approximately twofold oversubscription of nameplate appears feasible for similar workloads, subject to operator validation. We quantify the economic and carbon consequences and specify a low-cost operator pilot to verify the estimate.

title: Generative AI as a Limited Equalizer: Experimental Evidence on Gender Gaps in Competition
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou),  and

detail.title: Generative AI as a Limited Equalizer: Experimental Evidence on Gender Gaps in Competition
detail.abstract: We study whether access to generative AI (GenAI) changes gender gaps in willingness to compete. In a laboratory experiment, 360 university students solve numerical and logic questions that are highly suitable for ChatGPT assistance in a Niederle and Vesterlund (2007) piece rate versus tournament paradigm. In the main experiment (n = 240), sessions are randomly assigned either to a baseline condition without Chat-GPT or to a condition with ChatGPT available for optional use. ChatGPT access substantially increases performance for both women and men and largely eliminates baseline gender differences in scores, yet it does not significantly reduce the gender gap in tournament entry. Additional analyses reveal a dual-channel mechanism where ChatGPT access raises performance but lowers confidence. The gender gap in tournament entry disappears among participants with a stronger intention to use GenAI. In a follow-up information provision treatment (n = 120), participants receive credible information that men and women perform similarly in prior ChatGPT-assisted tournaments. The gender gap in tournament entry persists, suggesting that correcting social-comparative beliefs alone is insufficient when uncertainty about tool reliability remains salient.
