publicationDetails.journalName: Ohio State University, Fisher College of Business Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Charles A. Dice Center Working Paper No. 2026-14

detail.abstract: Following the global financial crisis (GFC), regulators made it harder for banks to retain leveraged loan exposure. We conjecture their actions increased the share of leveraged loan issuances with no maintenance covenants (cov-lite loans) because such loans are easier to sell. We find that, post-GFC, the share of cov-lite loan issuance increased more for banks facing stricter regulation, failing to pass a stress test outright, or exhibiting greater vulnerability to the severely adverse stress test scenario. We show that, as expected from theory, cov-lite loans have a liquidity advantage that lowers their credit spread and is higher for private firms.

title: Early-warning Volatility Regime Detection in Equity Markets: A Combined Markov Switching and Persistent Homology Approach
affiliations: Universitas Tanjungpura

detail.title: Early-warning Volatility Regime Detection in Equity Markets: A Combined Markov Switching and Persistent Homology Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve any human participants or animals. It utilizes entirely public financial market datasets, and ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Standard Markov regime-switching filters suffer from inherent latency because they rely exclusively on second-moment variance to identify structural breaks. This paper introduces Topological Markov Regime Switching (T-MRS), a framework that embeds persistent homology within the Hamilton filter to detect volatility regimes through phase-space geometry rather than return magnitude. Empirical testing across the 2020-2024 period demonstrates that T-MRS identifies crisis onset an average of 18 days earlier than classical benchmarks while maintaining statistical orthogonality to VIX and realized volatility. Although this anticipatory capacity increases false-positive turnover, simulation results confirm the strategy remains economically viable when paired with algorithmic transaction-cost filters. The findings establish topological complexity as a distinct leading indicator for financial risk management that bypasses the structural inertia of traditional variance-based inference.

title: Pricing Network Trust: Attack Cost, Hash-Rate, and the Illusion of Stability in Bitcoin Markets

detail.title: Pricing Network Trust: Attack Cost, Hash-Rate, and the Illusion of Stability in Bitcoin Markets
detail.abstract: This study reexamines the relationship between the cryptographic security of a blockchain network and the volatility of the cryptocurrency market that operates on top of it. Much of the prior literature has proxied network security with a simple normalization of hash-rate, St = Ht/Hmax, a measure that is by construction a linear transformation of hash-rate itself (Corr(St, Ht) = 1) and therefore carries no independent economic information. This paper instead constructs an attack cost index that combines hash-rate with mining hardware efficiency and electricity price, Ct = Ht • Jt • 24 • P elec t , and tests its relationship with GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility using a full sequence of unit root tests, cointegration analysis, trend-controlled regressions, and first-differenced (growth-rate) regressions on daily data from January 2019 to March 2026 (n = 2,630). A levels regression reproduces the negative relationship reported in prior work (λ = 0.117, p < 0.001, R 2 = 0.121), but the coefficient loses all statistical significance once a linear time trend is added (p = 0.420), and the relationship disappears almost entirely in first differences (R 2 ≈ 0.000). The price-hash-rate correlation that prior work treated as its most robust finding is reproduced here in levels (r = 0.850, consistent with the 0.781-0.865 range reported previously) but likewise collapses in growth rates (0.0009) and at every lag from 7 to 90 days. The paper argues that these results are consistent with spurious regression between non-stationary trending series (Granger and Newbold, 1974), and shows that introducing a more economically grounded security index does not, by itself, resolve this problem unless the non-stationarity of the underlying series is explicitly addressed.

title: Evolutionary Economic Development: Singapore and Japan's Experience

detail.title: Evolutionary Economic Development: Singapore and Japan's Experience
detail.abstract: Evolutionary economics, in contrast to the neoclassical approach, does not reduce the concept of economic growth solely to an increase in the total output of goods and services but implies that economic growth consists in increasing the overall potential of the economy by expanding the "routines" and "skills" of firms, which in the future will allow them to use these acquired abilities to further expand production. This research examines the role of the evolutionary approach in describing economic growth using the example of the economies of Singapore and Japan. The article shows that the introduction of innovations, the development of new technologies, and the implementation of R&D allow firms to significantly increase their economic potential and enhance their competitiveness, which corresponds to the theory of evolutionary economic growth developed by J. Schumpeter, R. Nelson, and S. Winter.

title: Financing Cooperation: Establishing A Syr Darya Basin Trust Fund for Water-Energy Stability
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Financing Cooperation: Establishing A Syr Darya Basin Trust Fund for Water-Energy Stability
detail.abstract:
This policy brief examines the financing gap in transboundary water-energy cooperation in the Syr Darya River Basin and proposes the establishment of a Syr Darya Basin Trust Fund as a practical mechanism for strengthening regional stability. The basin is shared by Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan and plays a critical role in agriculture, energy production, food security, and economic development. However, cooperation remains constrained by a structural imbalance between upstream and downstream countries: upstream countries bear the costs of water storage and flow regulation, while downstream countries capture much of the economic benefit from stable irrigation flows.

The brief argues that the main challenge is not the absence of agreements, but the lack of a coherent financial architecture that aligns incentives, shares costs, compensates services, and supports joint investment. Existing arrangements remain fragmented, sector-specific, and often ad hoc, limiting their ability to address the basin as an integrated water-energy system.

Drawing on international experience, the paper proposes the Syr Darya Basin Trust Fund as a centralized financial platform to pool resources, structure financial flows, and support incentive-based cooperation. The fund could finance compensation mechanisms, joint infrastructure investment, risk management, climate adaptation, and performance-linked cooperation across the basin. By linking financial flows to water, energy, and climate outcomes, the proposed mechanism can help transform coordination-based arrangements into a more predictable, incentive-driven model of regional cooperation.

The brief concludes that a dedicated basin-level financial mechanism can improve resource efficiency, reduce coordination failures, strengthen regional trust, and support long-term sustainability in the Syr Darya Basin.

title: Time Commodification: How Capitalism Justifies Enslavement and Organ Harvesting

detail.title: Time Commodification: How Capitalism Justifies Enslavement and Organ Harvesting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this paper is a conceptual thought experiment and does not involve human participants, patient data, interviews, surveys, experiments, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a reductio ad absurdum of an imagined complete capitalist market where morals and ethics are disregarded. It begins with two premises: (i) everything is allowed to be transacted under a complete capitalist market, including the claim of one’s time, and (ii) every human being is subject to their own time because every action requires and consumes parts of a finite lifespan. From the two premises above, the paper argues that the selling of one’s remainder of the lifespan would effectively transfer the control over the seller’s future actions, bodily autonomy, and practical volition to another party, which would lead to a condition described as a Corpse Puppet. A state in which a biologically living person loses all autonomous control over their own body, and is considered functionally dead. After establishing the absurd conclusion, the paper continued to price the time through minimum wage, current earnings, potential lifetime earnings, and buyer surplus. The conclusion implied that the Corpse Puppet condition is unacceptable, so the universal tradability premise should be morally limited or restricted. As a result, human time, bodily autonomy, and practical volition must remain protected from complete commodification to prevent the worst-case scenario of a complete capitalist market.

title: From Tax Cliff to a Growth Path: Modernizing E-Commerce Taxation in Uzbekistan
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Tax Cliff to a Growth Path: Modernizing E-Commerce Taxation in Uzbekistan
detail.abstract:
This policy brief examines the taxation and regulatory challenges affecting the formal development of e-commerce in Uzbekistan. Although the sector is growing rapidly, the current tax framework creates structural disincentives for firms to scale transparently within the formal economy. The brief argues that the main policy challenge is not the headline level of taxation, but the design of incentives and transition rules that shape firm behavior, business formalization, and digital transaction visibility.

The analysis focuses on the simplified tax regime for e-commerce, the abrupt transition from the 3 percent turnover-based regime to the general tax regime at the UZS 1 billion threshold, and the treatment of hybrid online-offline business models. It highlights that the existing framework may encourage fragmentation, informal practices, and limited scaling among firms that would otherwise have the potential to grow within the formal economy.

The brief proposes a reform package centered on raising the simplified-regime threshold from UZS 1 billion to UZS 5 billion while maintaining the 3 percent rate, reconsidering the 90 percent e-commerce income requirement, strengthening digital compliance infrastructure, and improving integration between tax administration, digital payments, platforms, logistics, and customs systems. It also links e-commerce tax reform to broader developments in bonded warehouse-based cross-border logistics, where deferred duty payments and controlled supply chains can reduce liquidity pressures and improve transparency.

The brief concludes that e-commerce tax reform should be treated as part of a broader modernization agenda for Uzbekistan’s digital economy. A well-designed reform pathway can reduce barriers to formal scaling, improve fiscal visibility, support fair competition, and strengthen the long-term competitiveness of Uzbekistan’s formal e-commerce ecosystem.

title: Coherent Shocks: External Identification and Internal Validation with an Application to Geopolitical Risk
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank, Heidelberg University, Deutsche Bundesbank, Research Centre and

detail.title: Coherent Shocks: External Identification and Internal Validation with an Application to Geopolitical Risk
detail.abstract: We propose the concept of coherent shocks: externally identified shocks whose structural interpretation is independently validated within the empirical model. Using textual data, we classify articles by economic mechanism and construct mechanismspecific shock proxies. Our coherence criterion measures the posterior share of impulse-response draws matching the assigned signature, benchmarked against its prior share. Applied to geopolitical risk (GPR), we use a large language model to construct supply-type and demand-type GPR series. Shocks identified from both series are strongly coherent with their assigned signatures. Innovations in the overall GPR index blend the two, and neither recursive nor sign-restriction identification separates them. The criterion applies to any externally identified shock for which theory implies a response signature.

title: Legitimacy-Sensitive Technological Competition
affiliations: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley and University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) (Formerly University of Texas-Pan American) - Economics and Finance

detail.title: Legitimacy-Sensitive Technological Competition
detail.abstract: We investigate how consumer perceptions of the social acceptability of technological implementation and organizational governance practices shape firms' incentives to adopt advanced technologies. Consumers care about prices, productive efficiency, and whether technological transition is implemented through transparent, accountable, and worker-inclusive organizational arrangements. Firms pursue innovation to escape competition, but socially contested technologies may face legitimacy discounts that reduce innovation rents. Acting as complements under mild conditions, governance and competition jointly determine innovation incentives, market outcomes, and welfare. We illustrate the theory using firm-level data on AI-related disclosure, organizational legitimacy, and financial performance for publicly traded U.S. firms. Consistent with the model's predictions, firms with stronger legitimacypreserving organizational arrangements exhibit more favorable economic outcomes during AI-related technological transformation, particularly along labor-relational dimensions. The empirical patterns suggest that stronger governance and organizational legitimacy may substantially increase the economic value of technological innovation.

title: Motivation Crowding in Audit Market Regulation: A Conceptual Framework

detail.title: Motivation Crowding in Audit Market Regulation: A Conceptual Framework
detail.abstract: This study challenges the standard assumption that extrinsic regulatory interventions in the audit market generally enhance audit quality. Drawing on Motivation Crowding Theory and evidence of auditor intrinsic motivation, it develops a framework analyzing how regulation perceived as controlling may crowd out the intrinsic motivation sustaining discretionary audit effort through impaired self-determination and self-esteem, subject to a proposed tolerance threshold arising from professional socialization. Mandatory rotation, restrictions on non-audit services, joint audits, and liability tightening are mapped to these channels. The framework yields the following analytical claims. First, crowding out affects discretionary effort beyond the regulatory minimum, so tightening may reduce total effort while raising the legal minimum. Second, regulation affects the two quality components, effort and independence, asymmetrically: structural instruments primarily target independence but offer little motivational counterweight on effort, whereas liability-based regulation targets effort directly. Third, under controlling-perceived regulation, adverse effects are expected to be more pronounced for auditors with high than with low professional identification, implying a selection effect opposite to that intended. Fourth, the effect on audit effort is expected to be non-linear, accelerating beyond the tolerance threshold and decelerating as effort converges toward its extrinsically sustained lower bound. The theoretical argument translates into four empirically testable propositions for future research.

title: Large Cycles of Solar Activity Maxima and K-Waves of the Global GDP Deflator (1962–2025): R=0.925, Forecast Until 2035
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Large Cycles of Solar Activity Maxima and K-Waves of the Global GDP Deflator (1962–2025): R=0.925, Forecast Until 2035
detail.abstract: This preprint uses a methodological approach developed by W. S. Jevons and A. L. Chizhevsky. For the period 1962-2025, Wolf numbers in years of solar maximum were compared with global GDP deflator values. The correlation coefficient was found to be 0.925. That is, large waves of solar activity maxima (a concept proposed by the author) are synchronized with large Kondratiev conjuncture cycles. The mechanism of this connection is explained by the fact that the production of the hormone serotonin, and, consequently, the mood of optimism, is directly proportional to solar activity and the ultraviolet index. With a predicted Wolf number of 156.02 for 2035 (the year of the next solar maximum), the global GDP deflator for 2035 will be 4.42%. This makes it possible to forecast Kwaves in the global economic situation based on the solar activity forecast.

title: Natural Disasters and Migration Patterns: A Case Study of the L'Aquila Earthquake in Italy

detail.title: Natural Disasters and Migration Patterns: A Case Study of the L'Aquila Earthquake in Italy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares to have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: In this study, I analyze the migration responses to natural disasters by focusing on one of the most devastating earthquakes occurred in Italy during the last decades. Using municipality-level data for the years 2002-2023 and adopting a propensity score-based method for continuous treatments (dose-response analysis), I evaluate the causal effect of the event of L'Aquila earthquake (2009) on internal and international immigration and emigration of both Italian and foreign citizens. I take into account the possible heterogeneous effects of the treatment on the affected spatial units using data on the intensity of the quake at municipality level. Indeed, in the large earthquake zone of L'Aquila the affected municipalities presented an heterogeneity in the level of damages and in the disbursements of post-quake financial and fiscal aids. The results corroborate just in part the narrative that emigration acts as an adjustment mechanism, providing relief to the shock. I found, instead, strong evidence of an attraction effect, probably due to the opportunities of the reconstruction process.

title: From Residues to Revenue ? Local Spillovers of Biogas Plants on Neighbouring Farms *
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Residues to Revenue ? Local Spillovers of Biogas Plants on Neighbouring Farms *
detail.abstract: We estimate the local spillovers of biogas plant installation on neighbouring farms in France over 2010-2023, combining three administrative sources on farm tax filings, crop allocation, and plant location. Exploiting the staggered roll-out, we compare newly treated areas to notyet-treated ones, an approach that addresses the non-random siting of plants and is robust to heterogeneous treatment effects; we find no differential pre-trends. Effects differ sharply with the residue a farm supplies. For neighbouring crop farmers, revenue and value added fall by about 2% across the buffer, as land shifts toward short-cycle, highly methanogenic crops such as silage maize and away from long-cycle crops. One reason farmers accept this loss is that income risk also declines, offering greater stability in bad years following installation. Input expenditure falls among the nearest farms, fertiliser by roughly 3% and pesticides by up to 4%, through two channels, digestate substituting for mineral fertiliser and a reallocation toward low-input crops. For neighbouring livestock farmers the same reallocation lowers feed costs by around 2%, while effluent valorisation raises the return to holding livestock; plant owners gain throughout. A scheme aimed at energy and climate goals thus reshapes the economic resilience and environmental footprint of the farms around each plant, in a sector where both are constantly under strain. * We are grateful to Fabien Candau, Isabelle Chort, Carole Haritchabalet, Anant Sudarshan, and the participants of the 23rd IOEA Conference for their helpful comments and valuable suggestions.

detail.abstract: This brief exposes how schools criminalize disability, especially for students of color, by responding to disability and trauma with punishment, surveillance, and law enforcement instead of support, tracing how these practices feed the school-prison nexus and arguing for transformative, justice-centered approaches to education.

title: Production Networks, Directed Technical Change, and Structural Transformation
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) and Shanghai Jiao Tong University

detail.title: Production Networks, Directed Technical Change, and Structural Transformation
detail.abstract: Production networks shape not only how technological change propagates across sectors but also where it originates. We develop a multisector model of endogenous innovation and structural transformation. Downstream linkages expand a sector's appropriable market beyond final demand, while upstream linkages transmit innovation-induced cost reductions through the production network. These channels interact: network-transformed expenditure determines private innovation incentives, while cost propagation generates sector-specific price dynamics that reallocate final demand. We characterize a regular asymptotic growth path along which aggregate growth converges to a stable rate, even as sectoral reallocation and uneven technical progress persist. Along this path, sectors with greater network-adjusted market size innovate faster. Under gross complementarity, uneven innovation shifts final demand toward sectors with slower price declines and, generically, concentrates it in a single asymptotically dominant sector. Intermediate-input linkages nevertheless propagate this demand upstream and sustain innovation throughout the production network. Finally, private returns reflect expenditure propagation, whereas social returns reflect cost propagation, creating sector-specific innovation wedges. We derive the Ramsey-optimal schedule of differentiated R&D taxes and subsidies that corrects these wedges.

title: Returns and Volatility Around FOMC Announcements: A High-Frequency Analysis of Policy Tone and Novelty
affiliations: Université Laval - Faculté d'Administration, Université Laval - Faculté d'Administration and Université Laval - Département de Finance et Assurance

detail.title: Returns and Volatility Around FOMC Announcements: A High-Frequency Analysis of Policy Tone and Novelty
detail.abstract: We decompose FOMC statements into policy tone (hawkish/dovish) and informational novelty (departure from previous messaging) and estimate their effects on high-frequency asset returns and volatility. Using 1-minute data for 7 futures contracts across 148 FOMC events (2008-2025), we find that tone predicts directional returns (a one-standard-deviation dovish shift is associated with equity gains that build to about 12 basis points within two hours) while novelty predicts volatility changes (the stance-novelty interaction on VIX persists from 5 to 120 minutes, t =-5.06). Policy stance is associated with realized volatility changes in 6 of 7 contracts (p < 0.01). Pre-announcement placebo tests and five independent inference methods validate these results. To construct our measures, we train a dual-model ensemble (MiniLM and BERT) on FOMC communications with data-driven PCA-based reference selection.

title: Credible High-for-Longer Guidance after Inflationary Supply Shocks

detail.title: Credible High-for-Longer Guidance after Inflationary Supply Shocks

keywords: and Ramsey Performance Proposed running head: High-for-Longer Guidance

detail.abstract: This paper studies adoption, intensity, duration, and credibility of high-forlonger policy after temporary cost-push shocks. With fixed policy amplitudes, the model yields separate shock-depth thresholds for adopting post-shock restraint and extending it beyond one period. When the current peak and announced future gap are chosen endogenously, the policy mix is unique for each duration and scales with shock size while bounds remain slack, so a positive adoption threshold requires a minimum policy step, fixed implementation cost, or another non-scalable commitment. Under discretion, effective post-shock tightening is zero. A Markov-perfect reputational mechanism delivers only a fraction of the announcement, and a minimum-delivery requirement implies a finite maximum credible duration. Ramsey and numerical comparisons quantify the costs of restricted intensity, duration, and credibility.

title: Central Bank Language and Long-Run Volatility: A Harmonized Four-Bank Test of Measurement and Regime Dependence

detail.title: Central Bank Language and Long-Run Volatility: A Harmonized Four-Bank Test of Measurement and Regime Dependence
detail.abstract: Does the volatility relevance of central-bank language travel across institutions, measures, and policy regimes? Using a harmonized text-scoring and GARCH-MIDAS pipeline, we study 362 scheduled statements from the Federal Reserve, ECB, Bank of England, and Bank of Japan during 2015-2026. Only ECB uncertainty remains significant after Holm correction, and that loading disappears after the ECB's 2021 strategy redesign. Formal interactions also identify loading shifts around the 2024 Bernanke Review and the Bank of Japan's exit from negative rates and yield-curve control. A Federal Reserve reconciliation shows strong sensitivity to lexicon choice. Textual volatility channels are measurementand regime-contingent.

title: Reserves and the Buyer of Last Resort
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: Reserves and the Buyer of Last Resort
detail.abstract: We examine the role of central bank reserves and public liquidity when secondary markets may freeze. Central bank reserves help intermediaries purchase assets during stress but crowd out investment. Under laissez-faire, intermediaries hold insufficient reserves, overlooking how aggregate liquidity reduces freeze risk. We propose a "market-backstop principle", akin to Bagehot's principle for intermediaries. It combines state-contingent buyer-of-last-resort interventions to restore trading with modest liquidity requirements to limit moral hazard. The welfare benefits of restoring market functioning exceed the fiscal costs of interventions. We explore implications for the size and composition of central bank balance sheets.

title: The 2024 Valencia DANA Floods, Business Fabric, and Territorial Resilience: A Comparative Analysis of SMEs in the Province of Valencia
affiliations: Universitat Jaume I de Castelló, , Universitat Jaume I de Castelló and Universitat Jaume I de Castelló

detail.title: The 2024 Valencia DANA Floods, Business Fabric, and Territorial Resilience: A Comparative Analysis of SMEs in the Province of Valencia

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by MCIN/AEI/10.13039/501100011033/FEDER, EU, through project PID2021-126516NB-I00.

detail.abstract: This working paper analyses the structural differences in the business fabric between municipalities affected and not affected by the 2024 Valencia DANA floods. Drawing on data from the Central Business Register (DIRCE, 2024), it compares firm size, sectoral specialisation, and the degree of economic diversification using descriptive statistics, weighted means, and the Herfindahl index. The results show that the affected municipalities concentrate a significant share of the provincial business fabric, display greater specialisation in trade, construction, and industry, and have lower economic diversification. These findings provide a baseline for future assessments of the economic impact and business resilience after the disaster.

title: The European Green Deal and the Climate Debate: A Marxian Critique of Financialisation, Crisis Management, and Imperial Continuity
affiliations: University of Algarve and

detail.title: The European Green Deal and the Climate Debate: A Marxian Critique of Financialisation, Crisis Management, and Imperial Continuity
detail.abstract: We read the European Green Deal (EGD) as a policy shaped less by climate goals than by the financial imperatives of the European Union. Launched after decades of neoliberal restructuring and in the wake of the 2008 crisis, the EGD promises “green growth” without touching the structural weaknesses of European production, labour markets, or industrial capacity. From a Marxian angle, we place it within the wider turn toward financialisation and permanent crisis management. Climate governance, in our reading, leans heavily on technocratic modelling, expert authority, and moral framing. This is a combination that permits aggressive intervention despite deep scientific and economic uncertainty. The “climate crisis” label, mobilised in this way, depoliticises major economic decisions and opens fresh channels for capital accumulation. We also argue that the EGD carries an imperial dimension: environmental conditions attached to trade, finance, and technology transfer deepen the dependency of peripheral economies, while inside the EU the same policies push deindustrialisation, higher energy costs, and rising inequality.

title: Skill or Sustainability? Deconstructing The Stock-Selection Timing Abilities of European ESG Fund Managers Within the European Context
affiliations: , National and Kapodistrian University of Athens - Faculty of Economics, School of Economics & Political Science and National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

detail.title: Skill or Sustainability? Deconstructing The Stock-Selection Timing Abilities of European ESG Fund Managers Within the European Context
detail.abstract: Purpose-Driven by the rapid expansion of ESG investing and the heightened volatility recently observed in the financial landscape, we investigate the stock-selection timing abilities of ESG fund managers. Design/methodology/approach-We employ a novel holdings-based stock-selection timing test targeting funds operating within the leading European markets for sustainable investing-the UK, France, and Germanyspanning the period from January 1, 2012, to December 31, 2024. Findings-Bootstrap analysis reveals that 25.76% of UK funds exhibit timing abilities that cannot be attributed to luck, though positive timers remain fewer than among conventional peers. Conversely, French and German managers generally fail to time active trades successfully. Nonetheless, strategy efficacy is weakened during turbulent periods. Notably, positive timers generate significantly higher Fama-French-six-factor abnormal returns than negative timers at the short-term six-month horizon, with return spreads ranging from 2.72% to 4.68% across all regions. Timing skills correlate positively with active trading but negatively with ESG ratings. Finally, UK and German fund investors recognize adept timers, whereas French ones do not. Practical implications-Our results provide crucial insights for market participants, highlighting that France's strong ESG integration and government incentives may create an environment that disincentivizes active timing, leading investors to prioritize social impact over financial performance. Originality/value-To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first empirical attempt to evaluate the stock-selection timing abilities of ESG fund managers within the European context.

title: mWAR: A Mesoscale, Skill-Based Alternative Estimate of WAR

detail.title: mWAR: A Mesoscale, Skill-Based Alternative Estimate of WAR

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No relevant interests
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: WAR is conventionally estimated by valuing the outcomes of a player's plate appearances against fixed conventions: a replacement level applied identically to every season since 1871, a fixed batter/pitcher split, and payment for realized production at every age. Retrosheet's nearly complete record of plate appearances from 1910 through 2025, 15,374,332 of them, permits a different construction. mWAR estimates each player's career skill from a fixed-effects regression on every plate appearance, adjusting for season, park, opponent, catcher, team defense, lineup regularity and age to the day, then prices each season at age-expected quality against a replacement pool measured from the players who actually replace. The measured quantities disagree with the conventions. The pitcher share of above-replacement value is about 43% in the dead ball era and has never reached either fixed convention since 1930. The measured replacement pool wins 57-64 games per 162, nine to fifteen more than the .294 fiat floor implies. Career relievers are closer in skill to career starters than to replacement pitchers. Validated against actual team wins using no current-season statistics, the projection correlates 0.84 with the standings across 2,562 team-seasons since 1910. Skill and value leaderboards, and the largest career movers against bWAR and fWAR, are presented.

title: Minimum Wage Policy and Youth Employment in Canada: A Machine Learning Approach
affiliations: Strathcona Tweedsmuir School and University of Calgary

detail.title: Minimum Wage Policy and Youth Employment in Canada: A Machine Learning Approach
detail.abstract: It was the common consensus among economists that price floors would inevitably result in a surplus of supply, and lead to a lower rate of demand of whatever goods are supplied. As a result, minimum wage policy, a form of price floors in the labour market, has often been viewed as a detriment towards employment rate. The revolutionary, Nobel prize-winning, paper published in 1994 by David Card and Alan B. Krueger offered unique perspectives that contradicted the proposed model of traditional economics. The study concluded that there is no indication that a rise in minimum wage reduced employment. This paper will explore the causal effect between minimum wage policies on youth employment rate by using the public data available at the government of Canada. This paper aims to demonstrate a more quantified trend regarding the relationship between minimum wage and youth employment rate. By using machine learning techniques including neural networks and random forests, this study investigates the in-depth mechanisms of how minimum wage affects different variables that further contributes to the variations in employment rates. This machine-learning based approach allows for a more quantified and generalized data trend between minimum wage and youth employment and allows for an optimal minimum wage policy for future government decisions.

title: The Verification Gap

detail.title: The Verification Gap
detail.abstract:
We argue that capital allocation to managed futures and hedge fund strategies is distorted by a
"verification gap": emerging managers with strong underlying performance are systematically
filtered out of the allocation process because their track records are costly to verify and structurally
biased. Building on prior findings that managed-futures databases exhibit upward-biased
performance (Malkiel and Saha 2005; Fung and Hsieh 2000; Liang 2000; Gregoriou 2002; Bhardwaj,
Gorton, and Rouwenhorst 2014), we synthesize three literatures: (1) emerging-manager
performance persistence (Aggarwal and Jorion 2010), (2) operational due diligence (ODD)
economics (Brown, Fraser, and Liang 2008; Brown, Goetzmann, Liang, and Schwarz 2009), and (3)
reporting bias in performance databases. We show that ODD is expensive and scale-biased, leading
allocators to concentrate diligence on larger, more established managers. At the same time, emerging
managers exhibit superior early-stage performance on average, so excluding them pre-diligence is a
costly filter, not a prudent one. Even when an emerging manager completes the diligence process, the
underlying track record data carries structural upward bias, contaminating the process itself. Taken
together, these forces imply that capital allocation to systematic strategies may be systematically
misallocated away from skilled emerging managers due to verification failures, with implications for
allocator behavior, regulatory design, and future research.

title: What Does the 2025 FMTI Observe Relative to the EU GPAI Code? A Requirement-Level Content-Validity Audit
affiliations: Fundação Getulio Vargas

detail.title: What Does the 2025 FMTI Observe Relative to the EU GPAI Code? A Requirement-Level Content-Validity Audit

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research received no specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available regulatory documents, benchmark data, and secondary research materials. It did not involve human participants, personal data, clinical information, or intervention. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI) is increasingly relevant to policy debates about artificial-intelligence disclosure, but its 100 indicators were not designed as a compliance instrument for the European Union's General-Purpose AI (GPAI) Code of Practice. This paper evaluates the content validity of using the FMTI to observe the final Code. The analysis reverses the usual indicator-first comparison: 53 grouped legal requirements from the Transparency Chapter, Model Documentation Form, Copyright Chapter, and Safety and Security Chapter are the primary units, and each is mapped to FMTI indicators using a transparent single-author directed content analysis. Content overlap is coded separately from legal audience, disclosure mode, evidence type, applicability, and benchmark observability. The FMTI has direct content overlap with 30 requirements, partial overlap with 16, and no overlap with seven. Yet only 16 requirements are fully observable through the FMTI process; 29 are only partially observable and eight are not observable. Copyright is the clearest blind spot: only one of five requirements has direct content overlap, and none is fully observable. Safety and Security shows broad topical overlap, but all 31 requirements apply only to systemic-risk GPAI models and many require implementation, confidential regulator-facing evidence, or reporting processes that a transparency benchmark cannot verify. At the indicator level, 66 FMTI indicators have direct overlap with at least one Code requirement, nine are partial-only, and 25 are unmapped. These counts do not constitute compliance coverage because repeated indicators can represent the same requirement and because disclosure to the public differs from evidence supplied to authorities or downstream providers. The paper contributes a reproducible requirement-to-indicator matrix, identifies legal blind spots and redundancy, and clarifies the evidentiary boundary between transparency benchmarking and regulatory compliance. Company-level score differences are retained only as a descriptive appendix and are not used to infer a regulatory effect or Brussels Effect.

title: The Degeneration of Relational Asymmetry: A Taxonomy of Coldness and Arrogance by Dimension of Degradation

detail.title: The Degeneration of Relational Asymmetry: A Taxonomy of Coldness and Arrogance by Dimension of Degradation
detail.abstract: Among those most invested with the expectation of help, the physician being the recurring instance, one sometimes meets two postures easily confused: coldness, a withdrawal, and arrogance, a settling into height. This paper asks whether the two are the same thing wearing different faces, or two degenerations with distinct mechanisms, and it approaches the question by classification. Working within a framework that takes being to be at once generative and relational, it treats relationality as holding a transcendental priority: as the condition under which difference and constraint can be posited at all, upon which the possibility of structural evolution, which is generativity, emerges. That priority is itself offered as a questionable premise, held open and not settled. On this footing degeneration is defined as the contraction of that possibility, and the two dimensions, the generative and the relational, serve as the axes of a taxonomy. Coldness and arrogance are then found to fall on different axes: arrogance appearing where the relational dimension degrades, a position ceasing to have its direction returned and ossifying into a supposed property of its occupant; one class of coldness appearing where the generative dimension degrades, the relation still holding while it no longer produces. Because the two dimensions mutually constitute one another in occurrence, a single posture is reachable by more than one path, so that the mechanisms are plural. The paper does not assert that this structure is the truth of arrogance. It proposes the structure as a candidate and asks whether the established accounts, from recognition, from disposition, from internalized oppression, from the psychoanalysis of the gaze and of narcissism, from the political economy of extraction, can be recovered as its projections, each such mapping being a place at which the structure, should the mapping fail, would be shown to be wrong.

detail.abstract:
Background: Digital transformation in healthcare relies on professional’s digital literacy, yet evidence remains scarce for older professionals, despite Europe's ageing workforce. This study aimed to characterise digital skill levels and their sociodemographic, occupational and health-related determinants among healthcare professionals aged 50 years and older and identify digital competency development priorities.

Methods: This cross-sectional study used self-reported secondary data from Wave 9 (2021-2022) of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Employed healthcare professionals aged 50–65 years were included. Digital literacy was operationalised through a composite Self-Reported Digital Skills Index (computer skills, computer use, and internet use), analysed against sociodemographic, occupational, and health-related variables using multivariate ordinal logistic regression.

Findings: Of 69 448 participants, 616 professionals were included (85·1% female; median age 55 years, IQR 52–57). Digital skills were intermediate in 69·0% of participants, high in 24·8%, and low in 6·2%. After adjustment, tertiary education (vs basic education; aOR = 15·35, 95% CI 5·37-43·90) was the strongest predictor of higher digital skills, followed by medical doctors (vs personal care workers; aOR = 3·73, 95% CI 1·65-8·42), very good self-perceived health (vs poor/fair; aOR = 2·94, 95% CI 1·58-5·47), and holding more than one job (vs single employment; aOR = 1·93, 95% CI 1·02-3·64). Increasing age was associated with lower digital skills (aOR = 0·93, 95% CI 0·88-0·98). Sex, income, European region and working hours were not significant predictors.

Interpretation: Digital skills in older healthcare professionals are shaped by educational, occupational, health- and age-related factors. Personal Care Workers and less-educated professionals should be prioritised for targeted and age-sensitive interventions to strengthen digital competency and promote equitable digital transformation.

title: Ownership Versus Access: A Comparative Case Study of Urban Mobility Costs in Sri Lanka
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title: Ownership Versus Access: A Comparative Case Study of Urban Mobility Costs in Sri Lanka
detail.abstract: This paper examines the financial and non-financial trade-offs between private car ownership and ride-hailing services (Uber and PickMe) for urban commuters in Sri Lanka, a developing economy characterized by severely distorted vehicle prices due to import restrictions and taxation. Using a comparative case study design grounded in Multivism, the study analyzes two vehicle categories, moderate cars (LKR 10 million, e.g., Toyota Raize) and lower-grade cars (LKR 6 million, e.g., Suzuki Wagon R), against ride-hailing alternatives for a typical 40 km daily round trip (880 km monthly). Financial analysis incorporating lease payments, fuel, insurance, maintenance, and opportunity cost of down payment reveals that ride-hailing services (LKR 150/km for moderate segment; LKR 125/km for lower-grade) are cheaper than owning a moderate car (LKR 213/km) by LKR 63/km (LKR 55,500 monthly). However, the gap narrows substantially for lower-grade ownership (LKR 136/km), creating a marginal difference of LKR 14/km (LKR 9,500 monthly) against comparable ride-hailing options. The paper concludes that financial irrationality lies not in car ownership per se but in owning vehicles inappropriately expensive for one's actual mobility needs. Non-financial considerations, privacy, availability, family utility, and autonomy versus driving stress, coordination friction, and asset management burden, become decisive at narrow cost differentials.

title: The Opportunity Access Gap in Egypt: Mapping How Secondary Students Discover, Navigate, and Access Educational Opportunities

detail.title: The Opportunity Access Gap in Egypt: Mapping How Secondary Students Discover, Navigate, and Access Educational Opportunities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests or conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on publicly available literature and secondary sources. No human participants were involved, and ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency, commercial organization, or not-for-profit organization.

detail.abstract: This report examines how secondary school students in Egypt discover, navigate, and access educational opportunities beyond the formal curriculum, and how institutional, informational, and socioeconomic factors shape this process. Rather than asking whether such opportunities exist, the report investigates whether students have equitable pathways to reach them. Drawing on academic literature and policy documents, it finds that Egypt hosts a rich and active ecosystem of opportunity providers, but that the mechanisms through which students discover and act on these opportunities are unevenly distributed. Access is shaped less by opportunity scarcity than by institutional capacity, digital literacy, English-language proficiency, personal networks, and students' ability to navigate complex application processes. International, private, and specialized STEM schools tend to offer structured guidance and institutional support, while many public secondary schools operate under constraints—high student-to-teacher ratios, examination pressures, and limited counseling capacity—that leave students to rely on informal channels. To explain how these inequalities emerge, the report introduces an Access Pathway Model, which frames opportunity access as a sequential process spanning existence, discovery, comprehension, eligibility alignment, application capacity, participation, and completion, rather than a binary outcome. The report concludes that closing Egypt's opportunity access gap requires strengthening the infrastructure connecting students to opportunities, not merely expanding the opportunities themselves.

title: Bringing Data Autonomy, Digital Sovereignty to the European Health Data Space

detail.title: Bringing Data Autonomy, Digital Sovereignty to the European Health Data Space

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The European Health Data Space (EHDS), established by Regulation (EU) 2025/327, represents the EU’s most ambitious attempt to enable secondary use of health data across Member States while safeguarding individual rights. Yet the EHDS is fundamentally a data access framework: it enables institutional intermediaries to govern the flow of health data to researchers and policymakers, without by itself satisfying the more demanding standard of data autonomy and digital sovereignty as developed in recent scholarship. This article develops a normative framework for evaluating the governance conditions under which the EHDS can be said to deliver genuine data autonomy rather than formal compliance with it. Drawing on theories of data autonomy (Gstrein, 2023), cybernetic governance (Zwitter, 2024), and digital identity infrastructure (Zwitter, Gstrein & Yap, 2020), the article argues that data autonomy at individual, regional, and European levels requires four governance conditions: layered data sensitivity assessment, institutional locality, controlled data mobility, and substantive democratic accountability. It then derives from these conditions a concrete institutional proposal‚ the enhanced Health Data Access Body (HDAB)‚ that can be implemented under existing EHDS law through the sub-national designation mechanism of Article 55 of the Regulation, requiring no primary legislative change. The enhanced-HDAB architecture, combined with a 3-tiered data governance framework constitutes the minimum institutional design for a genuinely data autonomous and digitally sovereign European health data space, including for nonanonymisable data categories such as genomic data and human digital twins.

title: Decision Flow: The Missing Fourth Dimension of Enterprise Architecture Why the Enterprise's Only Living Flow Remains Ungovernedand What Its Governance Requires

detail.title: Decision Flow: The Missing Fourth Dimension of Enterprise Architecture Why the Enterprise's Only Living Flow Remains Ungovernedand What Its Governance Requires
detail.abstract: Enterprise architecture recognises and governs three organisational flows: the material-process flowone solid flow in which decided sequences of action execute as physical movementthe information flow, and the fund flow, each instrumented and measured by dedicated systems. This paper identifies a structural inversion: these flows are dependent variables of a single independent variable, the decision, yet the enterprise instruments its dependent variables with precision while the variable that generates them remains unobserved, unmeasured, and ungoverned. What separates decision flow from every other architectural dimension is that it is the only living flow among the enterprise's recognised flows. The solid flows are inertthey never change, never interact, never judge, executing the frozen output of past decisions. Decision flow is real-life interaction: deliberation within the individual, interaction dynamics and feedback among humans, engagement with the actual ecosystem, and increasingly exchange with AInot a simulation running on assumptions and supposed situations. As a living flow, it accommodates the enterprise's situationcompressing in crisis, expanding in prosperityand it matures as the company matures. The relations genuinely connecting organisational functions are decision relations, horizontal and vertical, and the most consequential dependencies in the enterprise are those between decisions themselves: a change in an upper-level decision entrains derivations in every decision that depends on it, so that where this entrainment is ungoverned, superseded premises persist silently downstream, undetectable at the level of the flows. AI's entry into this ungoverned living layer accelerates rather than corrects its failures. The paper derives the minimum requirements any decision flow architecture must satisfy: capture of reasoning at the moment of commitment, validation of premises rather than data correctness alone, governed learning that matures with the enterprise, and named accountability spanning the decision dependency graph. The paper identifies the Decision-Making Driven Design (DMDD) architecture as one existing response to these requirements, offered as an existence proof rather than a unique solution.

title: Hybridizing Investors: Designing Investment Organizations for Social Impact
affiliations: and ECOLE POLYTECHNIQUE

detail.title: Hybridizing Investors: Designing Investment Organizations for Social Impact
detail.abstract: Sustainable investors seek to align capital markets with sustainability goals, but are often criticized for their limited social impact. Understanding this paradox requires shifting the focus from investors' interactions with firms to the organizational design of institutional investors-the intermediaries that manage financial capital. We examine how asset owners and asset managers jointly design these investment organizations to pursue financial and social objectives. Based on an 18-month ethnography in a private equity fund, we trace how these actors negotiate and stabilize the fund's organizational architecture (its objectives, resources, and control structures) before it becomes active on the market. We identify two interrelated mechanisms. First, locking in the organizational architecture early reduces agency issues and shapes subsequent investment behavior. Second, integrating financial and social logics coherently throughout this architecture creates a hybrid organization capable of pursuing dual objectives. These design choices generate a framing effect that directs attention and decision-making toward the pre-locked goals. By theorizing these mechanisms, we offer an organizational perspective on financial intermediation, showing how early design choices influence investment behavior. We finally conceptualize sustainable finance as an organizational design problem in which social impact potential is built through the design of investment organizations.

title: Did Voter Roll Deletions Help the BJP? Constituency-Level Evidence from West Bengal Special Intensive Revision of 2025-2026

detail.title: Did Voter Roll Deletions Help the BJP? Constituency-Level Evidence from West Bengal Special Intensive Revision of 2025-2026
detail.abstract: This paper tests whether voter roll deletions as a result of the Special Intensive Revision helped the BJP win West Bengal's 2026 assembly elections using constituency-level electoral data. Using a panel of 294 constituencies, two deletion measures are constructed: a stage-1 ASDD rate (from a booth-level scrape of ECI documents) and the draft-to-final adjudication rate during stages 2-3. Across 16 specifications, stage-1 deletion intensity is positively associated with BJP vote share swing (+40.27 pp, p = 0.008), but this disappears under district fixed effects (p = 0.231) and is explained by roll staleness. Placebo regression on 2021 turnout yields R² = 0.796, suggesting that deletions track low-turnout constituencies rather than being targeted political action. The stage-1 variable is null for binary seat outcomes, and negative associations for the draft-to-final rate of latter stages reflect confounding in Muslim-majority areas. A within-district positive flip coefficient (p = 0.031) is consistent with BJP mobilization in former AITC strongholds. Power calculations rule out underpowered nulls. The data demonstrate little evidence in favor of the suppression hypothesis at the aggregate level.

title: Making Institutional Claims Auditable in Research and Innovation Systems Systemic Evaluability as a Governance Capability

detail.title: Making Institutional Claims Auditable in Research and Innovation Systems Systemic Evaluability as a Governance Capability
detail.abstract: Public organisations produce unprecedented volumes of indicators, impact assessments, evaluation reports, and audit documents, yet institutional claims about research performance, innovation contribution, and public value remain persistently contested. This article argues that the problem is not simply a shortage of evidence but a failure to organise evidence around claims whose boundaries, assumptions, actor dependencies, and evaluative criteria are sufficiently explicit for independent scrutiny. It introduces the institutional claim as the missing conceptual bridge between evaluability assessment and performance auditing: a formally articulated assertion through which an organisation attributes causal contribution, public value, effectiveness, efficiency, economy, or societal impact to its actions under conditions of distributed governance. Drawing on evaluation, research evaluation, performance auditing, systems thinking, innovation systems, and public governance, the article develops systemic evaluability as a relational property of a claim system, produced through a governance capability and assessed through a diagnostic framework. The article shifts the unit of analysis from bounded programmes to claim systems, distinguishes reportability from auditability, specifies the anatomy of an institutional claim, and advances four analytical propositions concerning interdependence, traceability, information abundance, and governance learning. A real, anonymised illustrative case and an explicit comparison of candidate process notations are used to make the framework's diagnostic logic and processual architecture transparent and reproducible. For Research Evaluation, the framework provides a theory-building basis for assessing when claims about distributed research and innovation contribution are sufficiently formed to support credible evaluation, performance audit, and policy learning.

title: Went With Another Offer: The Fallout of the Nar Settlement and Its Potential to Cut First-Time Homebuyers Out of the Housing Market
affiliations: Bentley University - Department of Law

detail.title: Went With Another Offer: The Fallout of the Nar Settlement and Its Potential to Cut First-Time Homebuyers Out of the Housing Market
detail.abstract: The recent National Association of Realtors (NAR) settlement and its resulting policy changes made it even harder for potential first time homebuyers to realize the American dream and purchase their first home. Although the settlement and changes were seen as a major consumer victory, this Article argues that their effects could be disastrous for certain groups of first-time homebuyers who were already struggling to compete. By no longer requiring sellers to pay the buyer’s broker’s commission out of their proceeds and installing new rules meant to restrict commission transparency, it will be harder for homebuyers to secure independent real estate agent representation, get financing approvals, and compete when sellers are comparing their offers to other offers from wealthier competitors—only furthering wealth gaps in this country. This Article also sheds new light on how these new policies will disproportionately impact Black first-time homebuyers and offers three potential solutions for scholarly debate. First, the Article suggests changes in transparency and appraisal procedures. This suggestion is followed by an examination of the viability of an antitrust exception to the buyers’ brokers’ commission structure through state-mandated seller rebates. The Article offers a thoughtful and wide-ranging approach to redressing the inequities in the entry-level home buying market that the NAR settlement exacerbated, while recognizing the issues sellers had with NAR’s prior procedures.
