detail.abstract:
Paper 2.5 established Attributable Resolution Authority (ARA) as the strongest
candidate diagnostic variable for fragmented sovereign governance environments and
classified it as moderately supported on theoretical and secondary evidence. That
status carried one explicit condition: empirical testing was required before stronger
support could be justified. Three validation conditions were identified but not
completed: inter-rater reliability, discriminant validity, and predictive validity. This
paper initiates that programme. It also states one substantive proposition, derived from
the three-case evidence and declared before the case sections are examined: in
fragmented sovereign governance systems, ARA primarily operates by identifying
unresolved veto-capable authority — the specific actor class whose effective veto
prevents binding closure from attaching at system scope. Ghana (China comparable
treatment), Zambia (OCC veto over bondholder terms), and Sri Lanka (ISB bondholders
until December 2024) all exhibit the same structural mechanism. Whether this
proposition generalises is a question Paper 4 will test.
Three sovereign debt restructuring cases are examined using publicly available
institutional documentation: Ghana (2022–2025), Zambia (2020–2024), and Sri Lanka
(2022–2024). Seventeen governance moments are classified using the ARA four-class
diagnostic and the closure trigger criteria established in Paper 2.5. The cases are
selected because they involve comparable governance architecture — IMF programme
track, official bilateral creditor committee, and commercial bondholder track — but
different ARA trajectories and closure outcomes.
The Sovereign False Confidence Signal is observed across all three cases at comparable
governance moments, with SFCS scoring 3/3 at each. Preliminary evidence consistent
with predictive validity is produced: the ordering of ARA achievement at system scope
correlates with closure speed across the three cases. ARA remains a candidate variable.
This paper initiates, rather than completes, the validation programme.

title: Relative Deprivation in Social-Ecological Exposure, Private Shielding, and the Divergence between Economic Activity and Societal Well-being
affiliations: DTU Management

detail.title: Relative Deprivation in Social-Ecological Exposure, Private Shielding, and the Divergence between Economic Activity and Societal Well-being
detail.abstract: Modern economies can expand material throughput without corresponding gains in societal wellbeing. We introduce relative deprivation in social and ecological exposure: individuals experience disutility not only from absolute harm, but from exposure above the mean. Decentralized activity lowers welfare through two channels, aggregate harm and unequal harm incidence, so that even holding private behavior fixed, a more unequal distribution of harm reduces societal well-being. A heterogeneous-groups extension shows that structural differences in exposure magnify the welfare cost of excessive activity, bringing environmental injustice into the welfare analysis. When shielding from harm is available but access to it is unequal, decentralized adaptation can widen welfare losses through unequal insulation. We characterize the corrective instrument that implements the socially optimal allocation under relative deprivation and show that, unlike the analogous correction for heterogeneous vulnerability, it must be explicitly sized to the incidence gap across groups. These results survive when individuals partially internalize harm and when shielding is only partially effective. The welfare cost of economic activity depends not only on the level of harm it generates, but on its distribution and on the distribution of protective capacity.

title: The Organizational Intelligence Framework for High-Uncertainty Event Management

detail.title: The Organizational Intelligence Framework for High-Uncertainty Event Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The illustrative case presented in Section 11 involves an organisation associated with the author and is explicitly included for conceptual demonstration rather than empirical validation. This relationship is fully disclosed in the manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual and theoretical research paper. It does not involve human participants, animals, clinical data, or identifiable personal information. Therefore, ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required. The illustrative organisational case is presented solely for conceptual demonstration and does not report confidential or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: For four decades, event management theory has borrowed its vocabulary from construction and engineering project management: a bounded planning phase, a bounded execution phase, a terminal evaluation phase. That inheritance is not wrong so much as increasingly incomplete. It struggles to explain how festivals, concerts, exhibitions, conferences, sporting fixtures and mega-events actually survive weather volatility, crowd unpredictability, sponsor churn, cybersecurity exposure, algorithmically amplified reputational attack and AI-generated misinformation, conditions that a plan, however carefully drawn, cannot fully anticipate. This paper argues that the linear paradigm has reached its explanatory limit and proposes a replacement: Intelligence-Driven Event Ecosystems (IDEE), socio-technical adaptive systems that continuously sense, interpret, predict, coordinate and learn from multidimensional information before, during and after an event. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory, complex adaptive systems, cybernetics, organisational learning and information processing theory, the paper develops a companion construct, Defensive Hybrid Event Intelligence (DHEI), which reframes event resilience as continuous defence against fourteen classes of operational, informational and reputational uncertainty rather than as fourteen separate specialisms. A further move follows from this reframing: we introduce Event Decision Intelligence as the organisation’s true output, arguing that the marketable “event” is the visible residue of a more valuable, underlying decision-production process. The structural skeleton proposed for IDEE is a seven-layer Organisational Intelligence Architecture (Environmental, Stakeholder, Operational, Risk, Digital, Learning and Strategic Intelligence), coupled to a recursive Decision Intelligence Loop (Information → Intelligence → Prediction → Decision → Action → Feedback → Learning → Updated Intelligence) and a formal capability function, OI = f(K, D, A, R, L), from which we derive an Organisational Intelligence Maturity Index. Twenty-two research propositions link organisational intelligence to resilience, decision quality, stakeholder trust and innovation. We illustrate (deliberately not validate in the statistical sense) the framework through a single-organisation conceptual case, an independent event management company operating in Türkiye (Eventica), used to examine the constructs’ descriptive traction against lived practice rather than to confirm the propositions themselves. The paper closes with theoretical, managerial and research-agenda contributions and a central claim worth stating plainly: the durable competitive advantage of twenty-first-century event organisations will come not from the resources they own but from their capacity to manufacture superior decisions under uncertainty.

title: The Megawatt Wall: Utility Demand Charges and the Cost of Electric Freight Relative to Diesel Across United States Utility Territories

detail.title: The Megawatt Wall: Utility Demand Charges and the Cost of Electric Freight Relative to Diesel Across United States Utility Territories

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares the following financial interests/personal relationships which may be considered as potential competing interests: James Lightfoot is the founder and operator of RightSite, a commercial EV-charging site-selection service that uses the tariff library and pricing methodology described in this manuscript. This constitutes a competing financial interest in the subject matter of the article.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was self-funded by RightSite.

detail.abstract: Electric trucks are expected to undercut diesel on fuel, yet that expectation can invert at the charging site. Using 241 United States commercial electricity tariffs priced with a demand-aware engine, we compute the cost of heavy-duty charging as a function of station utilization and convert it to cents per mile against diesel (about 80 cents per mile at $4.80 per gallon). At the near-zero utilization of a new megawatt corridor site (a 3% load factor), the median territory's electricity costs 102 cents per mile, exceeding diesel in 63% of territories before any margin, because the demand charge is spread over almost no throughput. Utilization erases most of the gap, and managed depot charging escapes it almost entirely (2% of territories). The finding holds across diesel prices from $3.76 to $5.36 per gallon. The early barrier to electric freight is utility rate design, not the vehicle.

title: Enterprise Redefinition: Toward an Enterprise Evolution Theory for the Age of AI

detail.title: Enterprise Redefinition: Toward an Enterprise Evolution Theory for the Age of AI
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming not only business operations but also the fundamental assumptions of enterprise management. As knowledge, analytical capability, and execution become increasingly democratized through AI, traditional sources of competitive advantage-including scale, information asymmetry, and operational efficiency-are becoming less sustainable. This paper proposes Enterprise Redefinition, a management framework describing how organizations continuously redesign themselves to create sustainable Future Value in the Age of AI. Unlike conventional transformation approaches that focus on optimizing existing organizations, Enterprise Redefinition conceptualizes transformation as a continuous organizational capability involving the coordinated re-examination and redesign of five interdependent dimensions: Purpose, Business, Organization, Capital, and Leadership. Importantly, these dimensions do not change at the same frequency: enduring elements of organizational purpose may remain stable, while the expression and realization of that purpose evolve in response to technological and societal change. The paper introduces the Enterprise Redefinition Framework, the Enterprise Redefinition Process, and the Enterprise Redefinition Capability Model as integrated approaches to continuous enterprise evolution, together with a maturity model and eleven research propositions intended to establish a foundation for future empirical studies. The central argument is that the primary source of competitive advantage in the Age of AI is no longer superior execution of existing business models but the capability to repeatedly redefine the enterprise itself.

title:
Navigational Intelligence:
An Information-theoretic Limit on what AI can Learn from Published Research

detail.title:
Navigational Intelligence:
An Information-theoretic Limit on what AI can Learn from Published Research

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable — this work involves no human or animal participants, patient data, or case studies. It is a theoretical/mathematical paper in information theory.

detail.abstract: Every contemporary AI system learns from the published outcomes of research — papers, preprints, finished text — and therefore learns what researchers concluded, not how they got there. We prove that this omission is a limit, not an engineering gap. Under a single explicit assumption — that the publication map taking research trajectories γ to outcome documents E_T is non-degenerate (distinct trajectories can produce the same outcome with positive probability) — Shannon's data processing inequality yields I(γ) > I(E_T): the conditional information ΔI = I(γ | E_T), which we call the navigational intelligence, is strictly positive and irreducible by any algorithm operating on outcomes alone, at any scale, with any architecture. We identify three observable categories of this gap — dead ends, corrections, and breakthroughs — and prove an exact chain-rule decomposition of ΔI into these categories plus a completeness term, with non-negative conditional-dependence residuals. We further prove an information hierarchy over a proposed preservation infrastructure, the Living Research Graph: papers, trajectories, connected trajectory pairs, and the full graph each strictly exceed the level below. The framework's central open problem is geometric: construct a metric on epistemic states under which the counterfactual reference trajectory is a geodesic. We state three candidate constructions (Fisher–Rao, embedding pullback, Nielsen-type), two correctness conditions any candidate must satisfy, and a falsifiable empirical test. The limit is not a data-quantity problem but a memory-architecture problem: current AI encodes declarative knowledge (what was found) and discards evolutionary knowledge (how the finding was reached). AI should remember how knowledge was created, not only what was created.

title: Hospital Bed Expansion, Regional Heterogeneity, and the Limits of Supply-Demand Explanations: Evidence from China's hospitalisation Surge, 2011–2024
affiliations: Fudan University - Key Laboratory of Health Technology Assessment, Fudan University - Key Laboratory of Health Technology Assessment, Fudan University, Fudan University - Key Laboratory of Health Technology Assessment and Fudan University - Key Laboratory of Health Technology Assessment

detail.title: Hospital Bed Expansion, Regional Heterogeneity, and the Limits of Supply-Demand Explanations: Evidence from China's hospitalisation Surge, 2011–2024
detail.abstract:
Background: China experienced a rapid increase in hospitalisation over the past decade, yet the relative associations of healthcare demand and supply remain unclear. We examined long-term trends in hospitalisation and quantified the model-based contribution of hospital bed expansion to hospitalisation growth across provinces in China.
Methods: We conducted a provincial panel study of 31 mainland Chinese provinces, 2011–2024. Hospitalisation rate was the primary outcome. Demand-side and supply-side factors were analysed using two-way fixed-effects models. Regression-based decomposition quantified model-based contributions. Subgroup analyses assessed heterogeneity by region, economic development, and bed density.
Findings: The hospitalisation rate increased from 11.37% in 2011 to 22.62% in 2024, with persistent regional disparities. Hospital bed density was positively associated with hospitalisation after adjustment for demand-side factors and physician density (β=0.992, p<0.01). Bed density had the largest model-based contribution to this growth (3.44 percentage points, 30.6%), exceeding economic development (22.8%) and population ageing (7.2%). This association was stronger in central (β=1.505, p<0.01) and western provinces (β=2.453, p<0.01) but was not statistically significant in eastern provinces. Measured demand-side and supply-side factors together explained 38.6% of the total increase; the remaining 61.4% was unexplained.
Interpretation: Long-term hospitalisation growth in China is associated with both rising healthcare needs and supply expansion, yet a substantial proportion remains unexplained by conventional frameworks. Hospital bed expansion showed the largest model-based contribution, but this association was context-dependent. Future reforms should prioritise resource optimisation over capacity expansion.
Funding :  None

title: The Impact of Mindfulness on Financial Decision-making: A Systematic Review of Behavioural and Cognitive Perspectives

detail.title: The Impact of Mindfulness on Financial Decision-making: A Systematic Review of Behavioural and Cognitive Perspectives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial, personal, or professional conflicts of interest that could have influenced the work reported in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on secondary data obtained from publicly available scholarly literature. No human participants, personal data, or animal subjects were involved. Therefore, ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant or funding from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit organization.

detail.abstract: Mindfulness is becoming more prominent as a psychological intervention in favour of enhancing the quality of human judgment and reducing systematic behavioural biases. Prior empirical research from the fields of neuroscience, psychology, behavioural economics, and organizational studies indicates that mindfulness promotes stability of attention, regulation of emotion, and metacognitive awareness-elements closely associated with less impulsive and more intentional decision-making. Experimental studies from diverse fields indicate that both brief state-based mindfulness inductions and more extended mindfulness training programs can affect risk-taking behaviours, time discounting, maximization tendencies, and susceptibility of cognitive biases. In the financial decision-making literature, several scholars have argued that mindfulness reduces overconfidence, better promotes attention to relevant information, and dampens emotional reactivity to gains and losses-constructs of human behaviour of which account for irrational economic behaviours. However, existing studies also reveal substantial variation in effect sizes, differences in intervention duration, and incomplete understanding of the underlying mechanisms. Using information found in the literature reviewed here, we analyse the effects of both short-term and long-term mindfulness practices on specific types of behaviour in making financial decisions, including loss aversion, over-confidence and present bias. Therefore, the goal of this research is to provide new knowledge regarding whether/how mindfulness will be an effective means of enhancing the quality of real-world financial decision-making.

title: Investment, Saving, and Envy
affiliations: St John's University and

detail.title: Investment, Saving, and Envy
detail.abstract: Beginning with a critical review of Hayek's "Atavism of social justice" thesis, this paper suggests an alternative explanation of the widespread and increasing demands for social justice in contemporary society. While Choi (1993a) explores the nature of entrepreneurship and its tendency to incite envy, we focus here on the likelihood of saving and investment activities in a market economy to incite envy. Our analysis reinforces Choi's earlier understanding of the persistent hostility against commerce and the market system, adding to a systematic exploration of the factors that make the demand for social justice stronger or weaker.

title: Optimal Processing and Trading for a Commodity in the Presence of Inventory Conversion Flexibility and Random Supply
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore - Indian Institute of Management (IIMB), Bangalore, Students, Indian Institute of Management (IIMB), Bangalore, University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign and Indian Institute of Management, Bangalore

detail.title: Optimal Processing and Trading for a Commodity in the Presence of Inventory Conversion Flexibility and Random Supply
detail.abstract: In this paper, we present a decision support system used by an agricultural cooperative in the Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana to purchase, blend, sell, and store groundnut to maximize profits. The cooperative purchases raw groundnuts (input commodity) from its member-farmers, which is then processed to obtain multiple grades of groundnut seeds (output commodity). After the processing, two grades may be blended to obtain an intermediate grade to take advantage of arbitrage opportunities. The cooperative then sells some or all the output commodity in the spot market and carries the remaining inventory to the following period. It faces the problem of determining the quantity of input commodity to process and the quantity of different grades of output commodity to blend and, subsequently, sell in every period. The novel features of the problem are that the supply of input commodity is random every period, which is caused by the obligation of the cooperative to purchase all the supply that its members bring, and the option to blend grades to create intermediate ones. The possibility of blending over a multiperiod planning horizon has not been examined yet in the operations management literature on commodities. We formulate the problem as a dynamic program over a harvest season and use the associated framework to identify structural properties of the optimal value function and optimal decisions. We show that the optimal value function is not separable in the input inventory and the output inventory vector. This makes the identification of the optimal solution challenging. In special cases, the value function may have a simpler form, for example, when blending is not permitted. We develop an efficient procedure to compute the optimal decisions in the general case. We illustrate the benefits of blending and using a multi-period model, employing data obtained from a cooperative: the net profit of the cooperative could improve by 100-900% depending upon the model parameters, which translates to Indian National Rupees 1.94-17.46 million per annum.

title: Independent Judgment, Theatrical Distribution, and Competition An Economic and Legal Analysis of the Proposed Acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount under Section 7 of the Clayton Act

detail.title: Independent Judgment, Theatrical Distribution, and Competition An Economic and Legal Analysis of the Proposed Acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount under Section 7 of the Clayton Act
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount under Section 7 of the Clayton Act. Its thesis is that competition in the motion picture industry is competition among independent centers of creative and commercial judgment, exercised across the entire commercial life cycle of a film — from acquiring intellectual property and greenlighting production to marketing, nationwide theatrical distribution, and decades of downstream licensing. On that view, the transaction's competitive significance lies not in market share but in eliminating one of the few remaining independently owned studios capable of exercising that judgment.

The analysis grounds a structural Section 7 argument in the business's operating mechanics: greenlight economics, print-and-advertising commitments, the windowing sequence, slate co-financing and risk allocation, exhibitor bargaining, and the downstream licensing cascade that theatrical performance sets in motion. It explains why theatrical distribution remains the industry's principal value-creation platform and why streaming complements rather than displaces it. It then evaluates the defendants' anticipated arguments on entry, efficiencies, financial structure, technological change, and remedies, and addresses the two challenges to the transaction filed in the Northern District of California in July 2026. The article concludes that the acquisition may substantially lessen competition and merits scrutiny at its incipiency, before the combination becomes practically irreversible.

title: Do Shoot-the-Moon Executive Compensation Contracts Create Shareholder Value?
affiliations: Sabanci University - School of Management and University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: Do Shoot-the-Moon Executive Compensation Contracts Create Shareholder Value?
detail.abstract: Do the large, high-hurdle equity awards boards now hand star chief executives help shareholders? Tesla's "shoot-the-moon" packages for Elon Musk are the leading case. We study more than five million insider option grants from 1996 to 2024. The ordinary grant does not reliably create value: the median grantee underperforms its matched peers by about a sixth over four years, and the risk-adjusted average is indistinguishable from zero. The grants built to look most demanding are the worst, losing value on both the mean and the median by 24 to 32 percent, consistent with wealth destruction from misaligned risk incentives.

title: Conservation Planning at Scale: Efficient Design of Connected Reserve Networks via Random Spanning Trees
affiliations: , Yale School of Management and Yale University

detail.title: Conservation Planning at Scale: Efficient Design of Connected Reserve Networks via Random Spanning Trees
detail.abstract: To combat accelerating biodiversity loss, governments around the world have committed to large-scale conservation planning. Realizing these ambitions requires decision-support tools that can guide the design of reserve networks, enabling planners and policymakers to allocate limited land resources effectively. A critical operational challenge underlying these efforts is the design of reserve networks that achieve biodiversity representation goals at minimum cost. Geographic connectivity is also a key consideration in conservation planning, as fragmented reserves can impede species dispersal, reduce ecological resilience, and compromise long-term persistence. Yet designing large-scale connected reserve networks remains computationally challenging because of the combinatorial nature of the problem. Existing exact methods, which largely rely on mixed-integer programming, often struggle to scale because they encode connectivity through large numbers of auxiliary variables and constraints. In this paper, we propose a new graph-theoretic approach for developing scalable and theoretically grounded methods for designing connected reserve networks. Our method enforces connectivity by optimizing over connected subtrees of spanning trees. By leveraging the geometry of the underlying linear relaxation, we develop a linear-time rounding algorithm whose approximation ratio matches the integrality gap. Repeated sampling of spanning trees generates a diverse collection of feasible connected solutions. To provide theoretical justification for searching over sampled spanning trees, we show that under certain spatial regularity assumptions and on sufficiently fine grids, a random spanning tree contains a low-cost solution with a nonvanishing probability. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our method on benchmark conservation landscapes. For medium-sized problems, our computational experiments show that the proposed framework often matches the cost of exact mixed-integer solutions while requiring substantially less time. In a large-scale case study on Salt Spring Island with nearly 20,000 planning units, we show that our method produces a high-quality solution at the original spatial resolution, whereas existing methods struggle to scale and can only produce inferior solutions after coarsening the landscape. Together, these results suggest that structured search over sampled tree representations provides a scalable and theoretically grounded alternative for connectivity-aware spatial optimization.

title: Tractable Relaxations of Multivariate Stochastic Dominance via Optimal Transport and CVaR
affiliations: Business School, National University of Singapore

detail.title: Tractable Relaxations of Multivariate Stochastic Dominance via Optimal Transport and CVaR
detail.abstract: Many operational decisions involve alternatives with several uncertain attributes. Stochastic dominance avoids committing to a single multivariate utility function, but one lower-set or utility comparison with the opposite ranking can rule out exact dominance, and multivariate dominance is often difficult to verify. We develop two tractable relaxations, each tied to a standard representation of stochastic orders. First, compensated stochastic dominance (CSD) relaxes Strassen's coupling characterization. First-order dominance requires a coupling in which the draw from Q is at least the draw from P in every coordinate almost surely. CSD instead allows selected monotone scores of the draw from Q to be lower on some coupled pairs, provided that the expected weighted amount by which they are lower does not exceed a prescribed fraction of the expected weighted amount by which they are higher. We show that one optimal-transport problem computes the entire CSD tolerance path and, through transport duality, characterize exactly the utility functions whose expected values generate the order. The framework contains substitution multivariate almost stochastic dominance (Müller et al., 2025), and a multivariate extension of the orders between first-and second-order dominance (Müller et al., 2016). Second, reference-weighted stochastic dominance (RWSD) retains the generating functions of an integral stochastic order but restricts the probability measures used to combine their expected-utility differences. We show that checking RWSD reduces to a conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) problem and construct RWSD versions of first-order, lower-orthant, and increasing-concave dominance. We use the transport and CVaR characterizations to obtain finite-sample statistical guarantees for CSD and RWSD. Conditional on fixed score or basis systems and deterministic sensitivity or range bounds, the margins add no covering-number or explicit ambient-dimension term.

title: Structured Cross-Domain Calibration (SCC): A Diagnostic Reasoning Framework for Initial Judgment Under Domain Knowledge Absence
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Structured Cross-Domain Calibration (SCC): A Diagnostic Reasoning Framework for Initial Judgment Under Domain Knowledge Absence
detail.abstract:
(1) Purpose: This study explores why cross-domain judgments may still produce systematic biases under conditions of information asymmetry and the absence of target-domain knowledge, and analyzes how institutional frameworks influence cross-domain calibration. To this end, it proposes an operational analytical framework termed Structured Cross-Domain Calibration (SCC).

(2) Design/Methodology/Approach: Adopting a conceptual analysis and theory-building approach, this study integrates insights from analogical reasoning, ecological rationality, case-based decision theory, and naturalistic decision making to develop the Structured Cross-Domain Calibration analytical framework, in order to analyze institutional framework contamination in cross-domain judgment.

(3) Findings: The study indicates that judgments of structural similarity in cross-domain contexts may be systematically influenced by the decision-maker’s existing institutional framework, giving rise to Institutional Framework Contamination (IFC). To analyze this mechanism, the paper proposes the Structured Cross-Domain Calibration analytical framework, which comprises four operational steps—information retrieval, filtering, weighting, and output—as well as a three-dimensional calibration matrix, thereby enabling the systematic identification and analysis of institutional framework contamination.

(4) Research Limitations/Implications: As a conceptual study, the proposed theoretical propositions require further empirical validation. Future research may examine the applicability of the SCC framework, the three-dimensional calibration matrix, and institutional framework contamination across different cross-domain decision-making contexts.

(5) Theoretical/Practical Implications: This study addresses the insufficient discussion of institutional framework contamination in cross-domain judgment within existing decision theories, and proposes the Structured Cross-Domain Calibration analytical framework, which allows for the systematic analysis of this theoretical phenomenon. It also provides analytical tools for managerial practices such as supplier evaluation, due diligence, and cross-border investment.

(6) Originality/Value: This study introduces the concept of Institutional Framework Contamination (IFC), pointing out that cross-domain experience can serve as a calibration resource but may also lead to systematic biases due to differences in institutional frameworks. It further proposes the Structured Cross-Domain Calibration (SCC) analytical framework, enabling the operational analysis and subsequent empirical testing of this theoretical phenomenon.

title: After The Closure Scenarios for the Strait of Hormuz
affiliations: Szymon Zephan Capital (SZC Group)

detail.title: After The Closure Scenarios for the Strait of Hormuz

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: SZC Group

detail.abstract:
This paper evaluates the 12–18-month outlook for the Strait of Hormuz following the 2026 closure and incomplete reopening
process. Its central proposition is that the relevant test is not whether the Strait is nominally open, but whether passage is lawful,
non-discriminatory, physically safe, insurable and commercially dependable. The analysis assigns equal 35 per cent probabilities
to managed but militarized normalization and to selective or Iranian-influenced passage, a 20 per cent probability to recurrent
near-closure and a 10 per cent probability to broader multi-chokepoint conflict. It traces each scenario through energy supply,
inflation, monetary policy, trade balances, sovereign risk and financial markets, and then through firm-level effects on freight,
insurance, working capital, hedging, sanctions exposure and contract performance. Particular attention is given to Canada and to
the nonlinear consequences of simultaneous disruption or coercive tolling at Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. The paper concludes
that the modal risk is neither peace nor total closure, but a partially functioning and politically conditioned waterway that sustains
a persistent risk premium. Governments and firms should therefore plan against operational indicators rather than a single oil-
price assumption, diversify routes and counterparties, test liquidity and insurance contingencies, and preserve legal and naval
opposition to coercive private toll regimes in international straits.

title: Auditable Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting: Leakage Control, Conditional Failure Maps, and Walk-Forward Evidence from Germany-Luxembourg
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Auditable Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting: Leakage Control, Conditional Failure Maps, and Walk-Forward Evidence from Germany-Luxembourg
detail.abstract: Day-ahead electricity-price models are unusually easy to overstate. Prices are spiky and can be negative; twenty-four hourly products clear jointly; forecast errors are strongly dependent within a delivery day; and public archives do not always preserve the information vintage that would have been available before gate closure. This paper presents a deliberately compact, fully executable forecasting study for the Germany-Luxembourg (DE-LU) day-ahead market. The artifact combines 15,576 hourly observations from 2024-08-31 to 2026-06-11 with day-ahead wind and solar forecasts, lagged prices, and calendar variables. Its primary claim excludes weather covariates whose public historical archive does not preserve a fixed D-1 lead time. Four point forecasts are evaluated on a strict expanding-window experiment covering 365 delivery days and 8,760 hourly prices. Models are refitted every seven days, and all observations from a local delivery day remain in the same train or test block. The weekly naive forecast obtains an MAE of 32.89 EUR/MWh, pooled Ridge obtains 17.11, a 24-model hourly Ridge obtains 15.73, and deterministic LightGBM obtains 13.59 with a seven-day moving-block bootstrap 95% interval of [12.39, 14.86]. The corresponding improvement is 13.6% relative to the strongest linear baseline. Daily absolute-loss differentials remain significant under a seven-lag heteroskedasticity-and autocorrelation-consistent variance estimate with a Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold finite-sample correction. Feature-family ablations show that removing day-ahead renewables raises MAE by 84.9%, whereas adding the ambiguous-vintage weather proxy changes MAE by only-0.81%. Uncertainty is reported rather than inferred from point accuracy. A strictly prequential, rolling-residual interval achieves 90.07% empirical coverage against a 90% nominal target, with mean width 59.03 EUR/MWh. This marginal result masks a formal hour-conditional failure: 18 of 24 hours differ from nominal coverage under an unadjusted normal test and 16 remain significant after Holm correction. Tail diagnostics show that MAE reaches 21.59 on negativeprice hours and 61.12 above 200 EUR/MWh. A separate prompt-proxy experiment is explicitly bounded by no-signal, naive, linear-model, and infeasible perfect-day references. It carries direction beyond weekly persistence, but much of its raw 74.3% hit rate is mechanical. It is not presented as tradable P&L. The contribution is methodological rather than a claim of market dominance: the repository binds every table and figure to frozen CSV evidence, exposes data-vintage limitations, includes executable tests, and builds an arXiv source archive without private data or credentials.

title: Analyzing Inflation Dynamics in Pakistan: The New Keynesian Phillips Curve Perspective

detail.title: Analyzing Inflation Dynamics in Pakistan: The New Keynesian Phillips Curve Perspective
detail.abstract: Inflation in Pakistan has been an area of great debate and policy makers are striving hard to control it by adopting different fiscal and monetary tools. Inflation in Pakistan is either demandpull or cost-push but an unseen factor which plays significant role in a sharp increase in its rate are expectations about future. The present study investigates the role of expectations in determining inflation dynamics for a small open economy of Pakistan. The study analyzes the New Keynesian Phillips Curve (NKPC) in both standard and hybrid forms for the period of 1980-2022. Output gap and labor income share are being used proxies for real economic activity. To check the stationarity of variables, the Dicky Fuller test has been applied while Generalized Method of Moments has been employed to estimate the long run parameters of the model. Results of the study show that NKPC explains well inflation dynamics in Pakistan and fits with the data well. The output gap has been observed as an inappropriate proxy for measuring economic activity while the income shares of labor appeared significantly positive. Results also showed that inflation in Pakistan is dominated by forward-looking behavior rather than backward-looking. Structural estimates of parameters of the model show that the degree of nominal rigidity in Pakistan is very high and prices remain rigid up to nine quarters.

title: Volatility Spillovers in Frontier Financial Markets: Evidence from the Algiers Stock Exchange
affiliations: , University of Bejaia and University of Bejaia

detail.title: Volatility Spillovers in Frontier Financial Markets: Evidence from the Algiers Stock Exchange
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the volatility transmission within the Algiers Stock Exchange which is an extreme frontier market characterized by severe structural illiquidity and zero-volume trading days exceeding 90%. Applying the Diebold-Yilmaz connectivity framework to adjusted weekly returns of key listed equities from 2016 to 2025, a Total Connectivity Index (TCI) of merely 0.99% is observed. The research demonstrates that the near-absence of spillovers is not a sign of market resilience, but rather a microstructural symptom of extreme fragmentation where price discovery is dominated by isolated, mechanical corporate actions and idiosyncratic noise rather than genuine information transmission. Methodologically, the study proposes a novel dual-track data treatment template to disentangle corporate adjustments from economic shocks in thinly traded markets. These findings contribute to the conceptualization of extreme frontier markets as distinct microstructural regimes requiring customized analytical tools.

title: The Rodrigo Duterte Case at The International Criminal Court: Towards The Erosion Of States’ Right To Withdraw From The Rome Statute?
affiliations: Alfaisal University

detail.title: The Rodrigo Duterte Case at The International Criminal Court: Towards The Erosion Of States’ Right To Withdraw From The Rome Statute?
detail.abstract: The Rodrigo Duterte case raises complex questions concerning the interpretation of Article 127 of the Rome Statute (RS), particularly regarding its statutory limits relating to the one-year window governing the effects of withdrawal, as well as the interpretation of the procedural identity of the preliminary examination. This paper is divided into two parts: the first briefly outlines the procedural history of the war on drugs case from 2016 to 2024; the second analyses the dissenting opinion concerning the interpretation of Article 127 RS and explores the key developments from 2025 to 2026, focusing on the main issues raised by the defence challenge to jurisdiction, culminating in the Appeals Chamber’s decision of 22 April 2026. What emerges is that the majority of the judges adopted a broader interpretation of the nature of the preliminary examination, moving beyond its traditional character as an internal prosecutorial assessment and recognising it as a mechanism capable of preserving ICC jurisdiction beyond the temporal limits established by the Rome Statute for the withdrawal of a State Party. This interpretation raises fundamental questions as to whether Article 127 RS protects a meaningful right of withdrawal or instead reflects a judicial interpretation that has transformed withdrawal into a largely symbolic act, given the relative ease with which a preliminary examination may be opened by the Prosecutor without judicial control, thereby potentially circumventing the statutory one-year limit and eroding a State's effective right to withdraw.

title: Coarse Q-learning: Indifference, Indeterminacy, and Instability
affiliations: University College London - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Coarse Q-learning: Indifference, Indeterminacy, and Instability
detail.abstract: We introduce Coarse Q-learning (CQL), a reinforcement-learning model for bandit problems with stochastically varying menus. Alternatives are exogenously partitioned into similarity classes, and feedback from sampled alternatives is pooled within classes into class-level valuations. Choices follow multinomial logit over class valuations, and valuations update toward realized payoffs as in Q-learning. Using stochastic approximation, we derive the mean-field dynamics and characterize the steady states as smooth analogues of Valuation Equilibria. The model yields novel long-run phenomena in the high payoff-sensitivity limit: depending on the environment, CQL may exhibit multiple stable strict equilibria, a unique globally stable mixed equilibrium with indifference across classes, or no stable equilibrium at all, with valuations and choice probabilities converging instead to a stable limit cycle. These outcomes are driven by coarse aggregation and do not arise in the standard alternative-level benchmark.

title: Is National Security the First Step for the Development of a Nation? A Comparative Analysis of India (2014-2026), El Salvador under Bukele, and Pakistan as a Negative Mirror, with Cross-national Evidence

detail.title: Is National Security the First Step for the Development of a Nation? A Comparative Analysis of India (2014-2026), El Salvador under Bukele, and Pakistan as a Negative Mirror, with Cross-national Evidence
detail.abstract:
Is national security the first step for the development of a nation? This paper tests the proposition-that a credible state monopoly on violence is the precondition on which growth, investment, and human development are built-through a structured, focused comparison. Two "treatment" cases show a datable security improvement preceding a development response: India (2014-2026), across the Left-Wing Extremism (LWE) "Red Corridor" and Jammu & Kashmir theatres, and El Salvador (2022-2026) under President Nayib Bukele's gang crackdown. Pakistan serves as a negative mirror: born at parity with India in 1947 and ahead in per-capita income for decades, it saw that lead erased during its first terrorism wave (2007-2014) and, amid the post-2021 resurgence compounded by chronic fiscal mismanagement, slid into macroeconomic crisis. Five shadow cases (Colombia, Rwanda, Sri Lanka, Georgia, Singapore) extend the comparison. 

The evidence supports a conditional, weak-form thesis: in the cases examined, security improvements preceded, and plausibly enabled, gains in investment, tourism, and fiscal stability. India's internal-security metrics fell by 67-85% across both theatres while nominal GDP nearly doubled, annual FDI more than doubled, and foreign-exchange reserves rose from ~US$304 bn to a peak of ~US$728 bn. El Salvador's homicide rate collapsed from ~103-106 to ~1.3 per 100,000, accompanied by tourism and sovereign-bond recoveries and a 2025 IMF programme. Pakistan ran the logic in reverse: by 2026 it was the world's most terrorism-impacted country, after reserves fell below three weeks of import cover (2023), inflation peaked near 38%, and it entered its latest IMF programme. 

The strong-form thesis-security as the singular, strictly sequential first step-is not supported: reverse causation (education pacifies violence), security-without-development (North Korea, Myanmar), brittle repression-based "stability" (Sri Lanka's 2022 default after winning its civil war; the Arab Spring), and guns-versus-butter trade-offs all point to joint determination. El Salvador's gains, moreover, came at the cost of mass arbitrary detention and documented custodial deaths. We conclude that security is a necessary but not sufficient enabling condition for development-"security-first" is defensible; "security-only" is not.

title: "Profitability Performance of State-Owned Commercial Banks in Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Key Metrics"
affiliations: University of Dhaka

detail.title: "Profitability Performance of State-Owned Commercial Banks in Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Key Metrics"
detail.abstract:
This study explores the factors influencing the profitability (ROA) of state-owned commercial banks in Bangladesh over a ten-year period (2014–2023). In the context of rising non-performing loans (NPLs), operational inefficiencies, and varying levels of capitalization, the research aims to identify key internal and external determinants of bank profitability. Using a combination of descriptive analysis, correlation, and multiple regression, the study examines the impact of financial indicators such as capital adequacy ratio (CAR), NPL, net interest margin (NIM), loan-to-deposit ratio, return on loans and advances, cost-to-income ratio, and macroeconomic variables like GDP growth and inflation.

The findings reveal that internal factors such as CAR and return on loans and advances significantly influence ROA, with CAR showing a positive impact (p = 0.012) and NPL negatively affecting profitability (r = -0.358, p = 0.005). Macroeconomic variables, including GDP and inflation, showed no significant relationship with ROA, emphasizing the dominance of internal bank-specific factors.

The study highlights the need for improved capitalization, effective credit risk management, and operational efficiency to enhance profitability. The findings provide actionable insights for policymakers and bank managers to address systemic challenges and optimize financial performance in the state-owned banking sector.

title:
The Decision Evidence Divide: Why the Power to Prove a Decision, Not the Power to Make One,
will Decide who Gets Into the Machine-speed Economy

detail.title:
The Decision Evidence Divide: Why the Power to Prove a Decision, Not the Power to Make One,
will Decide who Gets Into the Machine-speed Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a Senior Fellow at the Verida Charter Foundation, a United States 501(c)(6) nonprofit research foundation whose stated remit covers the category of infrastructure this paper argues should exist. To test the concepts described in the underlying research, the author has built prototype implementations; these are his own work and his personal intellectual property, and a successor commercial entity may operate an implementation in future. Readers should weigh the argument with that interest in view. The paper's central recommendation runs against that interest. It argues that no private party, including any the author might be associated with, should own the format it describes, and that any standard arising from this research should remain openly licensed and freely implementable by any party. No party funded, commissioned, or directed this work, and no party reviewed it prior to publication. Findings are published in full whether or not they favour any particular approach.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The research draws on semi-structured interviews with senior practitioners conducted between October 2025 and July 2026. The author is an independent researcher without institutional affiliation, so no institutional review board oversight was available. The following safeguards were applied. Participation was voluntary and by invitation. Each participant was informed of the purpose of the research and of how their contribution would be used before the conversation began. All participants were professionals speaking about professional practice in their own field. No vulnerable groups were involved, and no personal, health, financial, or otherwise sensitive personal data was collected. Quotations are anonymised at role and tenure level by default. Participants are named only where they gave explicit consent, and named participants reviewed and approved how they appear. Participants who preferred not to be identified are described at a level of generality they approved. Authors of published sources are cited normally and are not treated as research participants.
