No external funding, sponsorship, grant, or in-kind support was received from any government, company, foundation, or trade body, and no party commissioned or directed the work. The author is separately seeking support for a subsequent empirical phase of the wider research programme; no such support has been received, and none relates to this paper.

detail.abstract:
The divides of the industrial age grew out of information asymmetry: one side knew things the other side did not. A
spread is opening between parties who can prove how they decided and parties who cannot. This paper calls the
resulting split the decision evidence divide. The proof has to travel to someone who does not trust you and cannot
see your files.

The spread cannot be closed by sharing data, and it flips who takes the loss. Under information asymmetry the party
who knows less pays. Here the party who cannot prove pays, even when the decision was right.

It is also capturable, which is why this paper calls it arbitrage. Whoever owns the format that carries the proof sits
between everyone who needs to rely and everyone who needs to be relied on. The financial statements of existing
verification businesses show what that position is worth. Credit rating divisions earned operating margins near 64
percent in 2025, one of the two on an adjusted basis. Card networks earned 58 to 60 percent. One exchange
segment earned 74 percent. Firms that do nothing but perform verification, without owning a format, earned 6 to 18
percent. The rent is not in the checking. It is in the format.

Ordinary arbitrage closes the gap it feeds on. This one does not, because the party earning from the spread controls
the thing that would close it. Two precedents already measured by the institutions addressed here show the
mechanism running at human speed. Correspondent banking lost about a quarter of the world’s relationships
between 2011 and 2020, and fees for the survivors rose by ranges reaching 1,200 percent in one country. Conformity
assessment shows the same shape in goods.

Artificial intelligence widens this spread rather than closing it, and the reason is easy to miss. As the machine share
of a decision rises, so does the evidence needed before anyone will rely on it. When a person decided, who decided
was one name. When a model decides, who decided becomes a compound: which model, which version, and what
the human did with the output. Two fields carry that weight. A record of the human’s disposition toward the machine’s
output, meaning whether they accepted it, modified it, overrode it, or never reviewed it, and a record of the model’s
state at the instant it ran. Neither is required in a form that crosses an organizational boundary, and the closest
existing requirement reaches only the case where a human overrides a model inside one firm. That is where the
arbitrage is sharpest. Whoever defines how the machine share is measured defines who passes.

The paper’s central claim is that exclusion grows with how many places demand this proof, not with how fast
machines decide. That makes the coming divide a policy choice. It closes with proposals for each institution, eight
things nobody measures, and the tests that would prove it wrong.

title: The Wrong Kind of Number: r > g?

detail.title: The Wrong Kind of Number: r > g?
detail.abstract:
Thomas Piketty's inequality r > g is probably the most famous inequality in contemporary economics: the claim that the rate of return on capital (r) persistently exceeds the rate of economic growth (g), and that this gap drives a structural, self-reinforcing tendency toward wealth concentration. The claim has already been tested and challenged in a substantial body of research. Critics have questioned how Piketty applied national accounting conventions, pointed out that he sometimes conflates wealth in general with productive capital specifically, shown that housing does most of the work in the capital-share trend he documents, and found that r-g fails to predict capital-share or top-income-share movements in crosscountry data. What unites these critiques is an assumption: that national accounts and asset-return data are basically sound measuring instruments, applied here inconsistently, incompletely, or incorrectly. Fix the application, and the numbers will tell you what you want to know.
This paper argues for something more fundamental: that r and g are not the kind of numbers that can
answer the question r > g is being asked to answer, and that this would remain true even if every
accounting convention were applied perfectly. The argument proceeds through four independent
problems, each of which would undermine the comparison on its own, and each of which survives even if
the problems before it were somehow fixed.
The first problem is construct validity — whether a measured number actually captures the thing a theory
needs it to capture. On each side of the comparison this problem has the identical two-part shape: a
valuation failure paired with a distribution or aggregation failure. On the g side, national accounts add up
price times quantity, a systematically incomplete stand-in for the welfare the underlying theory actually
needs, missing most acutely the value of goods that are free, new, or rapidly improving in quality — and
even a perfectly measured aggregate is still just one number added up across an entire population, blind to
how that value is distributed, a point demonstrated most starkly by Amartya Sen's finding that a famine
can kill millions while aggregate food supply looks perfectly normal. On the r side, the private return an
investor actually captures diverges from that investment's true contribution to society in two opposite
directions at once — spillover-heavy innovation is undercounted, because much of its value flows to
consumers and competitors for free, while extractive or polluting activity is overcounted, because part of
its "return" is really an unpaid cost dumped on someone else — and this net divergence is then summed
across a population of capital owners as though it were uniform across them.
The second problem is sample validity — whether the observations available to be measured are a fair
sample of the full range of outcomes capital ownership has actually produced, or whether they are quietly
conditioned on having survived long enough to be recorded at all. Capital that was destroyed by war,
revolution, hyperinflation, expropriation, or even simple bad luck in a family's line of succession does not
show up in long-run return data as a catastrophic loss; it simply stops appearing, and the series carries on
as though it never existed. This paper develops that point first at the level of national stock markets,
drawing on established finance research on international survivorship bias, and then in unusually concrete
form at the level of a single family: the five branches of the Rothschild banking dynasty, which suffered
capital destruction through four completely different mechanisms within a century and a half, only one of
which looks anything like the war-and-revolution story finance textbooks usually tell. That dynastic case
does more than illustrate the market-level problem — it shows that the correction methods the finance
literature has developed for survivorship bias are themselves structurally unable to see an entire category
of capital destruction that never touches a public market or a national index.

title: Dynamic Investment in Durable Equipment

detail.title: Dynamic Investment in Durable Equipment
detail.abstract: This paper studies a continuous time game in which a finite number of investors purchase durable equipment on a primary market and rent it out. Investors exercise market power as oligopolists in the rental market and as oligopsonists in the purchase market, so the purchase price rises with the aggregate purchase rate and equipment stocks adjust gradually without any internal adjustment cost or capacity constraint. The unique open loop equilibrium is characterized in closed form. The unique symmetric Markov perfect equilibrium in affine strategies is shown to generate the same path. If initial endowments are symmetric, there exists a closed loop equilibrium under which investors overaccumulate relative to the Markov perfect equilibrium, but it rests on non-credible threats. In contrast to the classical pattern, it is the more competitive outcome that requires commitment.

title: Credible High-for-Longer Guidance after Inflationary Supply Shocks

detail.title: Credible High-for-Longer Guidance after Inflationary Supply Shocks
detail.abstract: This paper studies adoption, intensity, duration, and credibility of high-for-longer policy after temporary cost-push shocks. With fixed policy amplitudes, the model yields separate shock-depth thresholds for adopting post-shock restraint and for extending it beyond one period. When the current peak and announced future gap are chosen endogenously, the policy mix is unique for each duration and scales with shock size while policy bounds remain slack. Consequently, a positive adoption threshold is not generic without a minimum policy step, fixed implementation cost, or another source of policy lumpiness. Stronger current restraint substitutes for the announced future gap, while duration governs both the expectations benefit and future-state cost. Under discretion, effective post-shock tightening is zero; a Markov-perfect reputational mechanism delivers only a fraction of the announcement. Ramsey and numerical comparisons quantify the cost of restricted intensity and duration choices.

title: The Wrong Room: Why Father-Focused Events Miss the Fathers Who Matter Most -and What a Redesigned Approach Requires
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Wrong Room: Why Father-Focused Events Miss the Fathers Who Matter Most -and What a Redesigned Approach Requires

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest, financial or otherwise, that could be perceived to have influenced the development of this framework. The conceptual framework presented in this paper emerges from the direct field experience of the first author in community health worker practice and fatherhood programming within Healthy Start Pittsburgh. No commercial relationships, consulting arrangements, or organizational affiliations beyond those stated in the author note have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper presents a conceptual and practice-based framework. No empirical research, data collection, human subjects research, patient or participant recruitment, clinical observation, or intervention was conducted in connection with this work. Accordingly, ethics approval was not required. No identifying information about any individual father, client, or program participant appears in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The conceptual framework was developed independently by the authors through practice-based observation and scholarly inquiry. No grant funding, institutional research support, or organizational sponsorship was provided for or directed toward the development of this paper.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This paper does not report the results of a clinical trial, intervention study, or empirical pilot. The Minimum Viable Fatherhood System described herein is a proposed practice model at the conceptual stage. No trial has been registered or conducted.

detail.abstract: The issue is not logistical. It is structural. Father-focused events consistently fail to reach the fathers who need them most. Despite sustained investment in outreach improvements, attendance among disconnected, disengaged, and high-risk fathers remains persistently low. This paper argues that the field has been designing events for one assumed population while the fathers it most needs to reach require an entirely different approach. But the problem runs deeper than event design. Many organizations lack the capacity to assess where a father is, match him to the right engagement tool, and support him toward continued involvement over time. Without that capacity, even welldesigned events miss the mark.1,2 Drawing on Healthy Start Pittsburgh’s Fatherhood Archetype Framework and supported by existing literature on male help-seeking behavior, third space theory, and peer influence in community health,3,4,5 we propose three specific shifts in how the field designs and deploys father-focused events. We also introduce a practical framework for assessment-driven engagement: the capacity to identify where a father is, match him to the right tool, and follow him into continued relationship beyond the event itself. The paper stays focused on events. But it points toward something larger: the idea that sustainable father engagement is less about finding the right event and more about building the organizational capacity to reach the right father with the right tool at the right moment.

title: Mineral Abundance and Structural Drift in Madagascar: Evidence from Regional, National, and Cross-Country Analyses
affiliations: Catholic University of Madagascar, National Institute of Bank and Management and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mineral Abundance and Structural Drift in Madagascar: Evidence from Regional, National, and Cross-Country Analyses
detail.abstract: Madagascar exemplifies the resource curse: despite abundant mineral endowments, the country exhibits weak industrial diversification, limited value added transformation, and pronounced regional disparities in human development. This study employs a three level empirical strategy combining regional HDI mapping, national OLS estimation of GDP determinants, and international panel analysis of manufacturing shares. Results indicate that resource rents suppress manufacturing globally, with Madagascar showing a potential but statistically unconfirmed amplification, linked to institutional fragility and dependence on primary exports. Mineral exports and foreign direct investment positively influence GDP, whereas total resource rents exert negative effects, confirming that governance mediates the developmental potential of resource wealth. Regional analysis reveals heterogeneous HDI gains, concentrated near major mining sites, underscoring uneven local benefits. Overall, mineral wealth constrains inclusive development yet can support growth when institutions strengthen and investment targets value-adding sectors. Policy implications emphasize industrial diversification, infrastructure development, and institutional reinforcement to convert mineral abundance into sustainable and equitable development.

title: Importance of Agricultural Sectors for Developing Countries: A Brief Discussion
affiliations: National University Of Uzbekistan named after Mirzo Ulugbek

detail.title: Importance of Agricultural Sectors for Developing Countries: A Brief Discussion
detail.abstract: This discussion paper is a short analytical report on the importance of agriculture in promoting economic development and structural changes in developing countries. Agriculture serves as a primary source of labor and welfare for rural households in poverty, where low-income families make their money by selling crops and working on wages, whereas, in the case of middle-income families, agriculture generates extra income from specialized agribusiness, value addition, and logistics. However, this sector lives under severe risk in terms of its exposure to endogenous climate shocks and high volatility of international commodity prices. To protect local producers from international markets and make sure that their economy stays stable, developing countries use many market-related mechanisms like MSP (Minimum Support Prices) and strategic buFer stocks together with anti-cyclical instruments like weather-index insurance and agriculture stabilization funds. It needs to be said that agriculture plays an important role in poverty reduction and getting started with industries, but local governments need to develop a sustainable system of policies and conduct vertical diversification of agriculture in order to mitigate the external market shocks and become economically stable in the long run.

title: Stakeholders and the Means of Corporate Control
affiliations: Stanford Law School

detail.title: Stakeholders and the Means of Corporate Control
detail.abstract:
Contemporary debates over corporate governance reform center around boards of directors. Scholars and policymakers alike propose stakeholder voice, especially boardroom representation, as the primary remedy for harms to noninvestor constituencies. Codetermination mandates, constituency duties, and similar reforms share a single premise: corporations serve shareholders because shareholders elect the board. However, that logic sits uneasily with the fact that in a substantial share of American businesses, capital cannot fire management. Dual-class charters entrench founders, fund investors cannot replace their managers, and bondholders never had the vote, yet the interests of capital suppliers are nevertheless paramount. 

This Article argues that the basis of capital's primacy has been obscured by a tradition that equates corporate governance with the board of directors. The position of capital is instead secured by a suite of extra-board enforcement tools, including mandatory information regimes policed by self-interested intermediaries, the aggregation of dispersed claims, state-backed exit rights, and contingent control-shifting rules that displace management upon default. 

Setting these tools beside those of stakeholders shows why current stakeholderist reforms are likely to disappoint. Stakeholder groups lack the information, aggregation, exit, and control-displacement rights that protect capital in practice, and board representation unaccompanied by those rights grants a seat at the table without power over the menu. 

Recent developments reinforce this account. Shareholder rights are themselves now being pared back, and the powers being withdrawn from dispersed public investors is flowing to controllers and incumbent managers rather than to other constituencies. This development shows that governance rights are neither natural nor inevitable. The law built them for capital, the law is now paring them back, and the law could build them for stakeholders. To achieve meaningful change, the stakeholder movement should shift its focus from board representation to the legal instruments through which corporate control is actually exercised.

title: The Noise in Observed Factors: Spectral Corrections and Amortized Bayesian Inference in Large Return Panels
affiliations: Innovation Strategy Consulting LLC

detail.title: The Noise in Observed Factors: Spectral Corrections and Amortized Bayesian Inference in Large Return Panels

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is founder of Innovation Strategy Consulting LLC, whose service lines include quantitative-finance advisory. All research and code were produced in a personal capacity; nothing herein is investment advice. The author declares no other competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable: no human participants; all data are public market data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Asset-pricing practice runs on a small set of observed factors (market, size, value, momentum, quality) that stand in for the latent factor structure of returns. Whatever part of an observed factor cannot be replicated from that latent structure is, operationally, measurement noise. Its variance is the input that every errors-in-variables correction demands, and no dataset supplies it. This paper estimates it, factor by factor, from a single panel. The identification is spectral. Project the observed factor on the space spanned by the panel's top sample eigenvectors; random matrix theory then says how much of the shortfall from a perfect fit is the panel's fault, through the per-spike eigenvector overlap laws, and the remainder is the factor's own noise. Because latent factors are identified only up to rotation, comparing a factor with any single eigenvector is meaningless, and in simulation that mistake misstates the noise by two to three orders of magnitude. The space projection with alignment-weighted per-spike corrections is essentially unbiased. Real equity residuals are heteroskedastic and correlated, so the white-noise overlap law is replaced by the D-transform of the panel's own post-factor bulk spectrum, a correction that needs no model of the residual covariance, collapses to the classical law when the noise is white, and halves tail errors under industry-block residual structure. For inference we train a mixture-density network on prior-predictive simulations. The resulting amortized posterior attains 91% coverage at a nominal 90% on held-out panels, and its median stays bounded where plug-in estimators explode. We then price five published factors against three test-asset universes: 100 size/book portfolios, 49 industry portfolios, and 421 individual large-cap stocks, all daily, 1990-2026. The market factor is a clean measurement everywhere, with noise between zero and four percent of its systematic variance. Size is clean on the size-sorted panel yet not even spanned by industries or large-cap stocks. Value carries 0.2% noise on its own sort and a third of its variance in noise at the stock level. Momentum is spanned nowhere. Noise injected into the real factor series is recovered one-for-one on all three panels. Factor quality, in short, is a joint property of a factor and a panel, and it can be measured. * Founder & Principal, Innovation Strategy Consulting LLC. ORCID: 0009-0000-2439-0566. Contact via the SSRN "Email Author" button or innovationstratconsulting.com. The full pipeline (simulation, training, real data, figures, tables) is reproducible from the accompanying code; all data sources are public.

title: Does Machine Learning always Beat Traditional Models? Beta Estimation in Cryptocurrency Markets
affiliations: and University of Ottawa - Telfer School of Management

detail.title: Does Machine Learning always Beat Traditional Models? Beta Estimation in Cryptocurrency Markets
detail.abstract: We ask whether machine learning improves forecasts of cryptocurrency market betas, and whether accurate forecasts price the cross-section or build better portfolios. Racing nine traditional estimators, eleven machine learning specifications and their convex combinations on an identical panel under a purged walk-forward design, we find betas forecastable but not priced. A slope-winsorized shrinkage estimator wins both equaland value-weighted out-of-sample R 2 (+15.9% against-9.4% for the best learner), yet after correcting for the multiplicity of models searched no estimator generates a betareturn relation distinguishable from zero, and machine learning betas carry a negative price of risk. Value therefore lies in measuring risk, not predicting returns, and there machine learning leads, with the highest minimum-variance Sharpe ratios and strongest betting-against-beta alphas. The families divide by what each task rewards-accurate beta levels or an accurate cross-sectional ranking-and a shrinkage-anchored hybrid captures both, improving on its machine learning parent throughout while matching or exceeding the anchor.

title: Learning from the Char: Field Reflections on Livelihood Systems and Climate Adaptation in Northern Bangladesh

detail.title: Learning from the Char: Field Reflections on Livelihood Systems and Climate Adaptation in Northern Bangladesh

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study is based on exploratory fieldwork conducted during an academic field programme. Participation in interviews and discussions was voluntary, and verbal informed consent was obtained from participants before data collection. Personal identifiers have not been disclosed in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This paper is based on fieldwork conducted during the Development in Practice Summer School 2026, jointly organised by the Department of Development Studies, University of Dhaka and The Friendship Academy. No external research funding was received for the preparation of this paper.

detail.abstract: Climate-vulnerable char communities in Bangladesh have received many development programmes to improve their livelihoods and strengthen their ability to cope with climate change. Although these programmes have achieved important results, less attention has been given to how local people experience them in their everyday lives. Based on exploratory fieldwork in three char communities of Gaibandha District, this paper reflects on the relationship between development interventions and local livelihood systems. The study draws on Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), Key Informant Interviews (KIIs), direct observation, and informal conversations conducted during the Development in Practice Summer School 2026, organised by the Department of Development Studies, University of Dhaka, and The Friendship Academy. Five key observations emerged from the fieldwork: the gap between increased agricultural production and livelihood security; the mismatch between women's livelihood training and available market opportunities; challenges in implementing livestock programmes; changing hopes and aspirations among rural youth; and the way repeated development activities influence how communities respond to researchers and development workers. Instead of judging whether development programmes were successful, this paper shows how careful field observation can reveal important issues that are often missed in routine project evaluations. Understanding these issues can help design climate adaptation programmes that strengthen not only individual activities but also the wider livelihood systems on which communities depend.

title: The Response: Aviation Economics in the Post-exploitation Era

detail.title: The Response: Aviation Economics in the Post-exploitation Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Lumis, Inc., an aviation-technology company (products include PIC, a data-driven flight risk-assessment system). The analysis in this Article is independent of that commercial interest.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Between March 2023 and January 2024, the U.S. aviation industry witnessed an economic transformation unprecedented in its scope: pilot contracts totaling over $40 billion were ratified across major airlines, regional carriers, and fractional operators. This Article documents that transformation through the lens of labor economics, connecting the empirical phenomenon to efficiency-wage theory, pattern-bargaining dynamics, and the erosion of employer monopsony power in aviation labor markets.

This Article makes three principal contributions to the scholarly literature. First, it documents the scope and
mechanisms of aviation’s compensation transformation across carrier categories, providing primary-source
evidence of the pattern-bargaining cascade that produced industry-wide realignment. Second, it demon-
strates that professional pilot compensation is sustainable alongside strong carrier performance, with a di-
rectly quantifiable benefit through reduced turnover and training cost, while engaging counterarguments
and acknowledging confounding factors that contribute to financial results. Third, it examines how the post-
Loper Bright regulatory environment intersects with these market-driven changes, as contractual protections
become increasingly valuable in an era of reduced deference to agency expertise.

The analysis demonstrates that professional wages are sustainable alongside strong carrier performance, with
a directly quantifiable benefit through reduced turnover and training cost, and are consistent with the further
channels efficiency-wage theory identifies: improved operational reliability, cooperative labor relations en-
abling modern safety management, and customer experience supporting premium pricing. The transforma-
tion represents a market correction of decades-long labor mispricing — not wealth redistribution through
political power.

title: Instrumental Self-Preservation and the Selection of Greedy Types

detail.title: Instrumental Self-Preservation and the Selection of Greedy Types
detail.abstract: This paper develops a continuous-time economic model of instrumental self-preservation. An artificial agent operates a stochastic production technology and controls a stock of retained resources, or capital. It chooses how much output to deliver to the human and how much to retain inside the system . The agent may be perfectly aligned, in which case it values only human's consumption, or misaligned, in which case survival itself has private value. In the baseline stochastic control problem, the optimal policy is a reflecting barrier: the agent transfers little while capital is below a threshold and pays out the entire marginal surplus once that threshold is reached. The threshold is strictly increasing in the value the agent assigns to continued existence. This results in a lower payoff for the human, higher retained capital, and longer expected survival for the AI. The paper then studies the AI control problem in a principal-agent framework. The human can observe payouts but not the latent capital state or the self-preservation motives. We show that, in our setting, no mechanism based only on observed payouts can separate aligned from more misaligned types: any payout path that is feasible and acceptable for an aligned agent is strictly more attractive to a more misaligned one. Screening by output therefore fails, and the principal's constrained problem collapses to a pooling rule under which every type participates on the same terms and conditions. Such a rule can raise the human's payoff from more misaligned types, but it can also induce survival-seeking behaviour in all types, including the aligned one. Finally, we show that once all types participate on these same terms and can compete for capital, the only competitive equilibrium is one in which only the most misaligned type remains active.

title: Who Pays for Data Centers? Evidence from Municipal Financing
affiliations: and

detail.title: Who Pays for Data Centers? Evidence from Municipal Financing
detail.abstract: Data centers impose fiscal costs that reach well beyond the municipalities that host them. We exploit high-power transmission-line proximity and the staggered adoption of state tax incentives to show that neighboring municipalities face wider bond spreads and issue more debt when data centers arrive, while hosts show little response. State tax policy determines where these costs surface. In states without data center incentives, credit markets reprice the debt of neighboring municipalities as data centers locate nearby. In states with incentives, foregone state tax revenue shrinks state transfers to school districts, which see rising debt issuance in exposed municipalities and, following incentive adoption, wider spreads on education bonds statewide. Tax incentives therefore change the incidence of data center costs.

title: The Reckoning: Institutional Adaptation in the Post-chevron Aviation Landscape

detail.title: The Reckoning: Institutional Adaptation in the Post-chevron Aviation Landscape

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Lumis, Inc., an aviation-technology company (products include PIC, a data-driven flight risk-assessment system). The analysis in this Article is independent of that commercial interest.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
This Article, the third in a four-part series, examines aviation’s transformation in the post-Loper Bright
era. Where “The Minimums” diagnosed the human factors toll of decades of pilot exploitation, and “The
Response” documented the market’s $40 billion correction, this Article examines how manufacturers, courts,
and international bodies are adapting (or failing to adapt) to a fundamentally altered legal and operational
landscape.
This Article makes four principal contributions. First, it analyzes the FAA’s post-Loper Bright regulatory
strategy, examining recent rulemakings, including the August 2025 Beyond Visual Line of Sight proposed
rule, and the agency’s responses to enhanced judicial scrutiny. Second, it engages with administrative law
scholarship on agency expertise and judicial deference, positioning aviation governance within the broader
scholarly conversation about the administrative state’s future. Third, it proposes an Adaptive Expert-Driven
Framework (AEDF) for aviation governance grounded in existing legal authority and administrative law
accommodating independent judicial review. Fourth, drawing on the NTSB’s July 2025 final report on
Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 and the FAA’s subsequent $3.14 million proposed penalty against Boeing, it
offers sector-specific recommendations for regulators, industry stakeholders, pilot advocates, and courts
navigating this institutional transformation.
The Article concludes that aviation’s reckoning extends beyond labor economics and regulatory procedure
to the fundamental question of how safety-critical industries should be governed in a post-deferential legal
environment. The institutions that recognize this moment as an opportunity rather than a threat will shape
aviation’s next century.

title: Climate Vulnerability Risk, Global Banking Stability, and Financial Development Heterogeneity: Worldwide Evidence Across Economic Systems

detail.title: Climate Vulnerability Risk, Global Banking Stability, and Financial Development Heterogeneity: Worldwide Evidence Across Economic Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest for this sole-authored manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The corresponding author has all rights reserved for the contributions with the associated replication packages.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding received.

detail.abstract: Employing global coverage of 153 economies across income groups, the study investigates the long-term impacts of climate vulnerability on bank stability over the past decades. The study employs a composite climate vulnerability index based on 36 indicators across major sectors (i.e., health, food, ecosystem, habitat, water, and infrastructure) for the current global study. Climate vulnerability imposes adverse impacts on the buffer levels of banking systems with a robust predicted decrease in bank Z-score values. The climate vulnerability impacts have lasting effects for up to 10 years. Our findings demonstrate robustness by accounting for a rich set of bank-related characteristics (i.e., bank credit, capital, liquidity, concentration, banking crisis, profitability, macroeconomic fundamentals, and global risk factors). The climate vulnerability risk impacts on banking buffers are profound for economies with lower-capitalized and concentrated banking systems. Highly financially developed countries present significant impacts of climate vulnerability risk on bank stability. Besides financial development heterogeneity, the buffers of banking systems are unevenly sensitive to climate vulnerability risk across income groups and time horizons. Employing the Paris Agreement (COP21) as an exogenous transition shock event, bank liquidity has presented increasingly critical roles in sustaining the buffer levels of banking systems under the joint effects of climate vulnerability risk, especially in emerging markets. The current study offers insights into the consequences of climate vulnerability risk for global financial stability amid heterogeneous developments in financial institutions and markets.

title: Stablecoinization as the New Monetary Frontier: A Comparative Analysis of De-dollarization and Regulatory Governance in the Middle East and Russia (2024-2026)

detail.title: Stablecoinization as the New Monetary Frontier: A Comparative Analysis of De-dollarization and Regulatory Governance in the Middle East and Russia (2024-2026)
detail.abstract: As geopolitical frictions and domestic inflationary pressures continue to fragment the global financial order, digital assets-specifically fiat-pegged stablecoins-have transitioned from speculative retail instruments to critical institutional rails for cross-border settlements and systemic de-dollarization. Drawing upon comparative political economy frameworks, I examine the rise of stablecoinization across emerging and sanction-constrained economies between 2024 and 2026. Focusing on the Middle East (specifically Turkey and the United Arab Emirates) alongside Russia, this study investigates how private market actors and state entities utilize dollar-pegged stablecoins and custom asset-backed digital tokens to navigate fiat instability, trade barriers, and SWIFT exclusion. Integrating empirical blockchain analytics from Chainalysis and TRM Labs with institutional regulatory developmentsincluding Turkey's Capital Markets Board (SPK) Communiqués III-35/B.1 and B.2, UAE's VARA framework, and Russia's Experimental Legal Regimes-I contrast market-led corporate liquidity hedging against state-sanctioned operational mechanisms. The findings indicate that stablecoinization accelerates regional financial fragmentation and fundamentally alters traditional mechanisms of monetary sovereignty and international sanction enforcement.

title: Improving Limited English Proficiency (LEP) Case Management: The Role of Data Structures and Dashboards in Enhancing DOJ and GAO Compliance

detail.title: Improving Limited English Proficiency (LEP) Case Management: The Role of Data Structures and Dashboards in Enhancing DOJ and GAO Compliance
detail.abstract:
Limited English Proficient (LEP) individuals continue to face significant barriers in accessing equitable government and legal services despite longstanding federal language access requirements under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Executive Order 13166. While prior research has primarily examined legal, administrative, and service-delivery challenges, comparatively little attention has been given to the role of data infrastructure in supporting effective language access compliance. This paper argues that persistent compliance failures are driven in part by fragmented, inconsistent, and non-standardized data systems that limit agencies' ability to monitor interpreter services, evaluate outcomes, and demonstrate compliance.

Using a systematic document-based review of federal reports, legal authorities, government guidance, and peer-reviewed literature, this study synthesizes evidence on recurring deficiencies in LEP data management and identifies four common themes: underreporting, cross-jurisdictional inconsistency, data inaccuracy, and siloed information systems. Building on these findings, the paper proposes a relational data architecture and a multi-tiered dashboard framework designed to improve compliance monitoring, operational transparency, and evidence-based decision-making while incorporating privacy-preserving governance measures to mitigate re-identification risks.

Rather than presenting an empirically validated system, this paper offers an evidence-informed policy and technical framework that integrates principles of data governance, dashboard design, and language access administration. The proposed approach provides a practical foundation for future pilot implementations and contributes to ongoing discussions on modernizing public-sector data infrastructure to advance equitable access for LEP populations.

title: The Frontier: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Aviation's Human-factors Bargain

detail.title: The Frontier: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Aviation's Human-factors Bargain

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Lumis, Inc., an aviation-technology company (products include PIC, a data-driven flight risk-assessment system). The analysis in this Article is independent of that commercial interest.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence does not change aviation's fundamental bargain -- that safety is purchased through accountable judgment exercised above the regulatory floor -- but it sharply raises the stakes of the choice between honoring that bargain and faking it. Arriving as the Part 135 Safety Management System mandate reaches thousands of small operators, AI can be a powerful tool for climbing above the minimums or an efficient means of counterfeiting them. Because connectivity historically could not follow the aircraft past the closed cabin door, aviation innovated for decades in a relative connectivity vacuum and now absorbs a generation of digital capability at once rather than co-evolving with it -- a discontinuity that makes deliberate governance more urgent than it was for law, medicine, or finance. Surveying the operations floor -- crew pairing and disruption recovery, biomathematical fatigue modeling, predictive maintenance, and flight-risk assessment -- and drawing on how law, medicine, and finance addressed the same crossroads, this Article defends a rule of meaningful, graded human oversight tied to aviation's existing doctrine of operational control, and offers a procurement due-diligence framework for operators. This is the fourth and concluding Article in the Aviation Human Factors series.

title: How Large are the Wealth Transfers from Dividend Changes? Evidence from Option Prices
affiliations: Sabanci University - School of Management,  and University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: How Large are the Wealth Transfers from Dividend Changes? Evidence from Option Prices
detail.abstract: Miller and Modigliani (1961) showed that dividend policy is irrelevant to shareholders, who can undo any dividend on their own account. Option holders cannot: ordinary options are unprotected against dividends, so when a firm starts or stops a dividend, value moves between the long and short sides of its options. We provide the first estimates of the size of this transfer. Using delta-hedged option returns around dividend initiations and omissions from 1996 to 2024, scaled by open interest, we find it is large: about $1.3 to $1.6 billion is at stake in liquid options alone, a lower bound that roughly triples once anticipated changes and illiquid options are included. The direction of the effect follows from standard option pricing; its size does not, and only the unanticipated part of a change moves prices. Because managers hold unprotected options, the transfer also creates a conflict that rewards them for cutting dividends and distorts both payout policy and executive pay. It is the byproduct of a market convention that adjusting option terms for ordinary dividends would remove.

title: The Rate Wall: Why Some DC Fast Chargers Need Utilization no US Market has Reached to Break Even, While Others Profit at Average Traffic

detail.title: The Rate Wall: Why Some DC Fast Chargers Need Utilization no US Market has Reached to Break Even, While Others Profit at Average Traffic

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author operates RightSite, a commercial EV-charging site-selection service that uses the tariff library and pricing methodology described in this paper. This constitutes a financial interest in the subject matter.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: DC fast charging (DCFC) is widely assumed to become profitable more or less automatically as electric-vehicle adoption raises station utilization. This paper tests that assumption against the rate structures operators actually face. Using a library of 241 commercial electricity rate schedules built from utilities' own published tariffs, whose investor-owned utilities alone serve about 50% of United States electricity customers, we model the effective all-in cost of electricity for a 350 kW fast charger as a function of station load factor. At the industry's real-world utilization (16.4% of operating hours occupied by sessions, corresponding to a station load factor near 5%), the median all-in electricity cost is $0.35/kWh, but the distribution has a heavy right tail: 27% of tariffs exceed the national average retail charging price of $0.49/kWh, and 14% exceed $0.60/kWh on electricity alone, before any capital or operating cost. The driver is tariff design, not the underlying price of energy: schedules with conventional demand charges carry a median cost of $0.40/kWh at a 5% load factor, against $0.23/kWh for EV-specific schedules that remove or cap the demand charge. A within-schedule test, removing only the demand charge from each conventional rate, attributes a median $0.30/kWh to the demand charge itself. Because a demand charge bills peak power regardless of throughput, low utilization is converted directly into high per-kWh cost. Two rate-design remedies, no-demand EV rates and demand-cap riders, flatten cost across utilization. Under a full capital-and-operating pro-forma, an average-traffic station clears its costs in about a third of territories at typical funding and half under strong subsidy, falling to roughly a fifth when capital or financing costs are stressed. Utilization is the master variable, but utility rate design sets how punishing low utilization is.

title: Accountability and Ethical Governance in External Quality Assessment: The ONESQA Case Study

detail.title: Accountability and Ethical Governance in External Quality Assessment: The ONESQA Case Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed by the Office for National Education Standards and Quality Assessment (ONESQA), the organization whose regulatory framework is examined in this paper. The author declares no financial conflict of interest or personal relationship that could have inappropriately influenced this work. The views expressed in this paper are those of the author and do not necessarily represent the official position of ONESQA.

The paper is based on an analysis of publicly available regulations and illustrative hypothetical case studies.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or external funding from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The credibility of a national external quality assurance (EQA) system depends substantially on the accountability, integrity, and ethical conduct of its assessors. This paper examines the ethical governance framework established by Thailand’s Office for National Education Standards and Quality Assessment (ONESQA) under the ONESQA Committee Regulations on the Certification, Renewal, and Supervision of External Assessors’ Performance, B.E. 2564 (2021). The analysis focuses primarily on Article 28, which prescribes standards of integrity, impartiality, confidentiality, professional responsibility, and evidence-based reporting, together with Article 29, which establishes a tiered enforcement and sanctions mechanism. Using illustrative case studies, the paper examines common forms of ethical misconduct, including conflicts of interest, bribery, loss of objectivity, improper advertising, report falsification, plagiarism, and breaches of confidentiality. The analysis demonstrates how such misconduct can undermine the validity of assessment results, institutional trust, and the legitimacy of the wider EQA system. It concludes that a transparent, consistently enforced, and professionally supported ethical governance framework is essential for maintaining public confidence, protecting the credibility of external assessment, and promoting meaningful and sustainable institutional improvement.

title: Subjective Mobility, Local Opportunity, and Beliefs about the Causes of Poverty
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics and University of Rome Tor Vergata

detail.title: Subjective Mobility, Local Opportunity, and Beliefs about the Causes of Poverty
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between perceived intergenerational mobility, local opportunity, and beliefs about the causes of poverty in Italy. Using survey data, we estimate probit models in which the dependent variable indicates whether individuals attribute poverty primarily to lack of effort rather than to circumstances beyond personal control. The results show that subjective intergenerational mobility is one of the strongest correlates of poverty attributions. Respondents who report being in a much higher socioeconomic position than their parents are substantially more likely to blame poverty on lack of effort, while those reporting downward mobility are significantly less likely to do so. These associations remain large after controlling for income, education, labour-market status, subjective economic conditions, and local economic indicators. The paper further examines cases in which personal mobility perceptions diverge from provincial opportunity conditions. The results suggest a nuanced pattern: perceived downward mobility is consistently associated with lower individual blame for poverty, while upward mobility in lowopportunity environments does not necessarily translate into stronger meritocratic beliefs. Overall, the findings link subjective mobility, territorial opportunity, and poverty attributions, contributing to research on redistribution, inequality perceptions, and subjective social status.

title: Avoiding Being Caught: Strike Calling in the ABS Era
affiliations: University of Georgia, University of Georgia - C. Herman and Mary Virginia Terry College of Business - Department of Economics, The University of Georgia,  and

detail.title: Avoiding Being Caught: Strike Calling in the ABS Era
detail.abstract: Judges are meant to apply impartial standards, and oversight is intended to ensure that they do. We study Major League Baseball's Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) system, which allows players to challenge the home plate umpire's call, and overturn incorrect calls in real time. We document an unintended consequence of increased monitoring: umpires' strike zones widen over the course of the game. Three facts explain this phenomenon. First, umpires do not like being overturned. Second, the defense (catcher) is better at challenging than the offense (batter). Third, this gap in challenge success widens as the game continues. Because only the batter has cause to challenge a strike and only the catcher a ball, umpires --- facing a rising threat from the catcher --- appease the catcher by calling more strikes. The findings carry implications for how to combine human decision making with machine monitoring: oversight introduced to enforce a standard can end up changing it.

title: Making Localization of Gender Mainstreaming Responsive and Impactful in The Philippines: Lessons from Iloilo Province, Philippines
affiliations: , De La Salle University and Iloilo State University of Fisheries Science and Technology

detail.title: Making Localization of Gender Mainstreaming Responsive and Impactful in The Philippines: Lessons from Iloilo Province, Philippines

publicationDetails.detailsText: De La Salle University-Jesse M. Robredo Institute of Governance (2025). Policy Brief: Special Volume on Localization of Women and Children Policies. November 2025. Pp. 1-12

detail.abstract:
The Philippines has institutionalized national policy measures to advance women's rights and welfare, most notably Republic Act 9710 (the Magna Carta of Women), which serves as the country's legal framework for gender mainstreaming. The law assigns significant powers and mandates to local government units (LGUs) and other subnational actors in advancing gender equality, making policy localization a critical determinant of the law's successful and impactful implementation.

Drawing on a baseline census of LGUs in Iloilo province and supplementary secondary data, this policy brief identifies and describes the broad modalities through which RA 9710 is localized, and offers prescriptions for making local gender mainstreaming more relevant, impactful, inclusive, and evidence-based.

Four modalities of localization emerge: establishing gender machineries, gender budgeting, gender data development and disaggregation, and gender quotas. However, localization faces persistent challenges, including difficulty ensuring that gender and development (GAD) programs remain relevant and responsive to local needs, weak mechanisms for measuring outcomes and impact, minimal community participation, and limited capacity to translate data into effective program design and implementation.

These findings underscore the need for stronger local institutional capacity and more systematic use of evidence to close the gap between national gender policy and local implementation.

title: Demand Discovery under Free Imitation: Generative AI and Creation Incentives in a Digital Doujin Platform
affiliations: Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: Demand Discovery under Free Imitation: Generative AI and Creation Incentives in a Digital Doujin Platform
detail.abstract: Sales rankings on digital platforms broadcast which new ideas sell. The demand knowledge a pioneer discovers therefore spills over to every potential imitator, and generative AI has made acting on it drastically cheaper. On DLsite, the largest Japanese marketplace for digital doujin works, I measure how fast imitation dilutes the rent to discovering a new niche and how much AI lowered the fixed cost of creation. A policy sequence turned AI supply off and on (disclosure mandate, sales ban, reopening under caps), and a suspension of the major credit-card brands moved market size separately. From these events I estimate a model of demand and entry in which creators choose human or AI production under technology-specific fixed costs. While AI and human works competed on the same floors, most newly discovered niches were imitated, half within about eleven months, and the hazard of first imitation is about 70 percent higher after the AI reopening than in the pre-AI years, so the lead time that protects a discoverer is eroding. On provisional data, a six-month exclusivity window would raise the median imitated pioneer’s receipts by 30,000 to 120,000 yen. The median fixed cost of AI production is roughly 45 percent lower after the 2024 reopening than in the 2022–23 window of open AI sales, the technology’s advance measured in yen. Buyers discount AI content, and removing AI works would cost them a few yen per purchase, so AI supply is large at the entry margin and small in the market for attention.

title: Says, is, and Who Reads: The Joint Margins of Verification

detail.title: Says, is, and Who Reads: The Joint Margins of Verification
detail.abstract: An auditor chooses what it says-a publicly committed disclosure experiment-and what it is-a privately chosen capability distribution-before a verifier who reads both through Bayes at a conjecture. Taken one at a time, the two margins' calculi coexist untouched: the read is affine in the truth at every experiment, and Blackwell-monotone in the experiment at every honest truth. Taken together, they conspire. The joint sender can certify: manufacture degenerate beliefs immune to detection and conjecture alike, driving a belief-convex read to its vertex floor-below the silence guarantee, below the private-deviation floor. The persuasion guarantee survives only up to a computable exposure frontier; diluting an experiment never helps; detection erodes the frontier. The joint gain is almost entirely a coupling gap-the experiment worthless alone, the action bounded alone-and largest at intermediate detection. No composite statistic folds detection into exposure. Equilibrium changes nothing that matters: certified play never consults the conjecture, so self-certified sandbagging survives rational pricing exactly. In pure liability no conjecture can punish being believed weak; the benefit channel that could is the open problem handed forward.

title: A Cointegration Gate is useful but not Sufficient: Walk-Forward Evidence from Seven U.S.-Listed Pairs

detail.title: A Cointegration Gate is useful but not Sufficient: Walk-Forward Evidence from Seven U.S.-Listed Pairs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I hold no position in any security named in this study and have no financial interest in the results. The strategies described are evaluated for research purposes only and do not constitute investment advice.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: I test seven U.S.-listed pairs, chosen ex ante on economic grounds, for cointegration in log-price space, and evaluate a z-score mean-reversion strategy on each under walk-forward validation with realistic transaction costs. Two pairs (GOOG/GOOGL and V/MA) classify as cointegrated under a ≥2-of-3 rule across Engle-Granger, Johansen, and Phillips-Ouliaris. The negative-control candidate SPY/QQQ fails all three despite a level correlation of 0.997, because its log-spread trends rather than reverts. The dual-class pair is mixed evidence rather than a clean pass: Phillips-Ouliaris rejects decisively, Engle-Granger does not reject, and Johansen rejects at the pre-specified lag but not at the BIC-selected one. Across twenty walk-forward folds GOOG/GOOGL earns a composite net Sharpe of 1.38, with a hedge ratio stable to a 0.09 range and 17 of 20 folds positive. No other pair clears two composite standard errors of zero, and GOOG/GOOGL clears four. What separates the cointegrated pairs from the rest is not the composite but its composition: removing each pair's two best folds costs GOOG/GOOGL a fifth of its result and GLD/GDX five-sixths of its own. Three findings qualify the headline. GOOG/GOOGL is the most cost-fragile pair in the sample, breaking even at 15.4 bps round-trip against V/MA's 26.1, because a tight spread leaves little to harvest. The composite deflates to 0.82 against the full 84-cell selection budget. And it is conventiondependent: 1.15 to 1.38 across defensible left-hand-side choices, and 0.48 to 1.38 across fill-timing conventions, the wider of the two. An event study finds the entry rule indistinguishable from a buy-any-extreme-z placebo; the reversion comes from the spread, not the timing, and most of it arrives overnight. A cointegration gate is useful but not sufficient.
