detail.abstract: The artificial intelligence industry is executing the largest private infrastructure buildout in economic history: the five largest hyperscale operators spent approximately $381 billion on capital expenditure in 2025, with cumulative 2025 to 2026 outlays estimated above one trillion US dollars. This paper asks whether that trajectory is sustainable and evaluates the three classes of alternative most frequently proposed to escape it: quantum computing, orbital data centers, and non-von-Neumann architectures. Drawing on primary financial disclosures, peer-reviewed physics and computer architecture literature, and institutional energy data, the analysis reaches three findings. First, the buildout's financial character is dispersion rather than uniform strain: free cash flow has turned negative at two of the five operators, but investment intensity at strongly capitalized firms must be distinguished from credit strain, which concentrates in the most levered operator and a vendor-financed periphery, while the depreciation schedules governing reported earnings are demonstrably discretionary. Second, none of the proposed technological alternatives can substitute for conventional accelerated computing on any relevant timeline. The evidence against quantum computing for machine learning comes largely from within the quantum research community; orbital data centers face a thermal constraint that launch costs cannot shrink, only cheapen; and the commercializing fraction of photonic and neuromorphic computing has retreated from compute to interconnect and from replacement to augmentation. Third, the binding constraint on AI scaling is not semiconductor physics, which retains two to three orders of magnitude of headroom, but electricity delivery, where median generation interconnection now exceeds five years and large-load energization runs on multi-year timelines. The policy implication inverts the usual case for international coordination: the binding resource is geographically stranded, and the coordination object that survives export control is the power contract rather than the placement of compute. Cooperation precedents from big science and, more aptly, from cross-border electricity institutions are assessed, with export control identified as the principal legal obstacle.

title: Maximizing De Minimis
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis - School of Law

detail.title: Maximizing De Minimis
detail.abstract: The circuit split on the applicability of de minimis exceptions to digital sampling has stirred controversy for the last decade. An adequate resolution to this split ought to treat copyright interpretation as an institutional choice, incorporating economic concerns into statutory construction. This Comment analyzes the copyright system as an institutional allocation of rights under positive transaction costs. The choice between the Sixth Circuit’s interpretation in Bridgeport and the Ninth Circuit’s interpretation in Ciccone reflects fundamental alternatives between resource allocations under costly bargaining. Therefore, the institution of the de minimis doctrine within digital samples of copyrighted work should account for the same institutional difficulties that standard property and tort law have long considered. Three major economic problems arise: transaction costs, anticommons problems, and rent-seeking. High transaction costs prohibit bargaining over licensing, so the right to use the digital work must be assigned to the most productive party. Given the chilling effect on creative innovation that the Sixth Circuit’s interpretation would have, the applicability of de minimis exceptions is preferrable. The de minimis doctrine also mitigates the anticommons problems by allowing broader access to complementary goods, mirroring the fair use doctrine’s economic role. Finally, the de minimis doctrine limits rent-seeking behavior by copyright holders and prohibits such holders from obtaining rents on non-expressive aspects of a work. Ultimately, U.S. copyright law should be read to maximize the creative productivity of de minimis exceptions to prevent the high transaction costs of licensing from limiting creative interplay between artists’ works.

reference: Journal of Research in Business, volume 8, issue 1, 2023[10.54452/jrb.1027577]
title: Elections and Stock Market Returns: Evidence from Borsa Istanbul
affiliations: Işık University

detail.title: Elections and Stock Market Returns: Evidence from Borsa Istanbul

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Research in Business, volume 8, issue 1, 2023[10.54452/jrb.1027577]

detail.abstract: Stock prices may display predictable patterns around major political events, particularly in emerging market economies where political risk is a key component of asset risk premiums. One distinct event that would be expected to result in an abrupt increase in political risk is elections. Motivated by this notion, we study the returns for a set of indicator and sectoral indices of Borsa Istanbul stocks and the U.S. Dollar-Turkish Lira exchange rate around political elections held in Turkey over 2001-2020. Our tests reveal an accumulation of economically and statistically significant positive abnormal returns for all Borsa Istanbul stock i ndices and negative abnormal returns for the U.S. Dollar-Turkish Lira exchange rate over a window that starts as early as a month before the election date and extends for two weeks into the post-election period, with the effect being particularly strong in the week that immediately follows the election. Consistent with a political risk-based story, volatility of index returns starts increasing over the same period and plateaus out at a level that is roughly one-and-a-half to two-folds greater than its pre-election period average.

title: Equality on whose Time? Women's Labour, Care, and the Cost Allocation of Relational Life: A View from the Reality Paradigm
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Equality on whose Time? Women's Labour, Care, and the Cost Allocation of Relational Life: A View from the Reality Paradigm
detail.abstract:
This article argues that discussing equality between women and men solely in terms of legal status, participation
in paid work and equal treatment leaves out the life in which equality is to be realised. The problem is not
women’s participation in working life. The problem is that a worker model presumed to be free of care burdens,
undisturbed by bodily interruption and permanently available is applied to all human beings as though it were a
neutral norm. Where the mismatch between paid work and social reproduction is left unresolved, women are
included in employment while the sphere of care left upon them remains unreorganised. Participation rises while
the burden does not fall; two separate obligations converge upon the same body and the same time.
The article analyses this structure through four propositions: the allocation of public necessity to the private
sphere; the gendered privatisation of the costs of social reproduction; the state’s constitutive role in the
distribution of these costs; and the operation of non-intervention as an instrument of allocation. Nurseries,
kindergartens, pre-school education and care homes are examined within this framework — without denying
their existence or their benefits — in terms of the conditions under which they cease to be free options and
become compulsory institutions that preserve the continuity of working time. The same mechanism’s removal of
family, kinship, friendship and belonging from everyday life, and their compression into annual leave and the
category of “holiday”, is addressed through the concepts of relational reproduction, the condensation of needs
into leave time, and relational buy-back. Remote work, in turn, is passed through the same apparatus as the
strongest apparent counter-example to the thesis; through the concepts of the parallelisation assumption, the
allocation of workplace costs to the household and reverse evacuation, it is argued that the allocation of costs
does not change even when space is inverted — an invariance formulated as a testable hypothesis that the constitutive variable is time, not space. The claim of this article is not to have discovered care labour; it is to bind
the mechanisms shown piecemeal across the literatures of care, work and relational time into a single
explanatory architecture under the sequence of preconditioning–classification–foreclosure–write-back–feedback.
Through the lens of the Reality Paradigm, the fundamental question is not the concepts with which the state
declares equality, but the conditions under which it constructs, in advance, the space in which equality is to be
lived — and to whom it allocates the costs of those conditions. The combined effect of working hours, leave,
wage dependency, social security, care services, school hours, housing, transport and workplace performance
norms is conceptualised here as temporal and reproductive infrastructure. The article shows that this
infrastructure can constitute a reality circuit which first narrows women’s options and then writes the outcome it
has produced back onto them as their nature or their free choice. It further discusses, through macroeconomic
blindness and the vital return deficit, how aggregate indicators of production and consumption render invisible
the costs of unpaid care, time poverty, and the failure of produced value to return to human life.
The first empirical ground of this text is the life its author has lived and, because of the organisation of work, has
been unable to live. This situated testimony may be multiplied as readers recognise the same interruptions in
their own lives; yet experiential recognition is not substituted for causal or comparative judgement. Türkiye, the
United States and Europe are compared not on a single scale of development but as regimes that allocate the
costs of care in differing measures to the family, the market or the public; a worked example of the analytical
apparatus is presented on Turkish data. The constitutive question of the article is this: who pays for the life that
produces the continuity of the state and of society?

title: Temporal Dimensions and Chronological Robustness [Series Paper #2]: The Super-Invention Taxonomy and Direction of Humankind
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Temporal Dimensions and Chronological Robustness [Series Paper #2]: The Super-Invention Taxonomy and Direction of Humankind

declarations.ethicsApproval: This strudy does not include patients/participants.
declarations.funderStatement: Nobody funded this research.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a quantitative methodology for analyzing the long-term developmental trajectory of humankind through the lens of Super-Inventions (SIs). Shifting away from localized historical studies, we examine humankind as a single, unified entity spanning the Homo sapiens period from 50,200 BCE to 2026 CE. 
      By establishing unified selection criteria and tracking four chronological temporal markers (Emergence Date and three System Integration Dates), we construct a stable framework for evaluating civilizational complexity. Utilizing a segmental analysis across seven distinct eras, combined with Monte Carlo Sensitivity Analysis (MCSA) and random data ablation stress tests, we demonstrate that the proposed integration sequence (specifically utilizing the terminal integration marker SID123) is exceptionally resilient to both localized dating uncertainties and dataset attrition. 
     The findings confirm that deep-level history can be studied as an invariant, quantitative property of humankind as a complex system, offering a solid foundation for future macro-historical research.

title: The Name-Reality Gap: A Diagnostic Framework for Understanding UN Reform Stagnation

detail.title: The Name-Reality Gap: A Diagnostic Framework for Understanding UN Reform Stagnation
detail.abstract: Over the past three decades, proposals for UN reform have proliferated while substantive progress has remained strikingly limited. This article argues that the impasse stems not from a shortage of reform proposals or from great-power politics alone, but from a systematic blind spot in how the reform problem has been framed. Reform debates have persistently focused on adjusting the UN's nominal structure-seat distribution, institutional architecture, Charter amendment-while neglecting the hollowing out of its operational capacity. This article introduces the concept of the "Name-Reality Gap" as a diagnostic tool: the nominal authority of the UN has continuously expanded while its operational capacity has failed to keep pace, producing a structural disjuncture that is not a transient performance deficit but a self-reproducing feature of the UN system. The article provides an operationalizable definition of the Name-Reality Gap, distinguishes its three manifestations, traces its three structural sources, and conducts a preliminary plausibility probe across the security, development, and health governance domains. The framework offers an alternative diagnostic lens for UN reform scholarship.

title:
Optimal Allocation of Investigative Authority under Incomplete Contracts 
A Contract-Theoretic Model of Police-Prosecutorial Separation and Supplementary Investigation Rights
affiliations: Inha University in Tashkent

detail.title:
Optimal Allocation of Investigative Authority under Incomplete Contracts 
A Contract-Theoretic Model of Police-Prosecutorial Separation and Supplementary Investigation Rights
detail.abstract: This paper models investigative authority as a residual-control-right problem in a public organization. A police agency produces the first investigation; a prosecutorial or charging agency can be given an intensity 𝑅 ∈ [0,1] of supplementary investigative authority. More authority can generate independent information, correct first-stage error, and discipline the initial investigator. It can also induce errors in the opposite direction, expose cases to political use of the charging institution, duplicate effort, delay disposition, and dilute responsibility for first-record quality. The optimum equates the marginal value of verification and correction to the marginal losses from governance risk, duplication, and interagency holdup. Bounded overlap strictly dominates both complete separation and plenary integration when the endpoint marginal conditions have opposite signs. Optimal authority rises with the social loss from surviving first-stage error and from unchecked capture of the initial agency, but falls with the loss from political use of the charging institution. A fixed implementation cost creates a separate extensive margin and can make the global choice discontinuous. Police effort may rise or fall with overlap, depending on whether accountability dominates responsibility dilution. Costless pointwise contingency weakly dominates a uniform grant; with imperfect and costly screening, that result becomes conditional on classification value and precision. The paper maps these results to South Korea's 2021-2026 reallocation of investigative authority and develops an empirical design using linked case records, predetermined reform exposure, and treatment-timing-robust event studies. The relevant design question is not simply separation or integration, but who may correct which error, under what verifiable trigger, with what recorded reason, and at whose cost.

title: Independent Information and Social Reproduction in Financial Markets Tail Shape, Identification, and Empirical Stress Tests

detail.title: Independent Information and Social Reproduction in Financial Markets Tail Shape, Identification, and Empirical Stress Tests
detail.abstract: An expansion of information has no single effect on financial-market tails. It may add independent judgments or reproduce existing ones. This paper separates these channels in a Poisson branching model. The independent seed rate controls the number of separately rooted cascades. The social reproduction number controls dependence within each cascade. More independent seeds lower standardized excess kurtosis, whereas stronger reproduction raises it. When reach and acceptance increase both channels, excess kurtosis has an exact U-shaped response. Even if both composite rates are known, reach and acceptance remain separately unidentified. Tests across twenty equity markets show that the mechanism matches dynamic dependence better than GJR-GARCH-𝑡 but matches tails and cross-market variation worse. Overall holdout loss is nearly identical. An event study of 376 after-hours earnings filings shows that absolute price and volume responses peak on the first tradable day. Later excess volume disappears relative to the already elevated pre-filing day. The theory states both an observable signature and a firm limit. Aggregate market data can test its distributional implications, but they cannot recover the underlying social process.

title: Corporate Disclosure on LinkedIn around Earnings Announcements
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, National University of Singapore - NUS Business School,  and National University of Singapore

detail.title: Corporate Disclosure on LinkedIn around Earnings Announcements
detail.abstract: We examine how firms disclose on LinkedIn, a professional networking platform widely used by labor market participants, around earnings announcements. We find that firms issue more LinkedIn posts during earnings announcement weeks, and that this effect is stronger for firms with negative earnings news. Moreover, the effect of negative earnings news on LinkedIn posting frequency is more pronounced when firms are more concerned about human capital attraction and retention and when more of their current and potential employees are on LinkedIn. To examine the content of LinkedIn disclosure, we compare the topics and tone of LinkedIn posts during earnings announcement weeks with those of concurrent earnings conference calls, an investor-oriented disclosure channel covering the same underlying earnings news. We find that when firms have negative earnings news, their LinkedIn posts share fewer overlapping topics with conference calls and adopt a more positive tone. Finally, we find that LinkedIn disclosure during earnings announcement weeks is associated with attenuated unfavorable labor market responses following negative earnings news. Overall, our findings are consistent with the conjecture that firms disclose on LinkedIn to mitigate the adverse labor market consequences of their weak fundamental performance.

title: Algorithmic Microfinance 2.0: From Lending to Investing for a Sustainable Economy through Mass Investment Participation and Financial Literacy for All.

detail.title: Algorithmic Microfinance 2.0: From Lending to Investing for a Sustainable Economy through Mass Investment Participation and Financial Literacy for All.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All work was conducted independently by the author without institutional, governmental, or private financial support.

keywords: Local Cluster Development Micro- Finance Pool

detail.abstract:
Everyone can be an investor. Investment participation is a basic financial right. This paper specifies a constitutional micro-escrow architecture that makes this right operational. One absolute rule governs entry: the maximum value of any investment unit in any pool is $1 USD or equivalent, enforced by the smart wallet, with no minimum investment limit of any kind. Any person holding a verified national identity and a mobile wallet may therefore invest at any amount — from a student's pocket money upward — on constitutionally identical terms to any larger investor. Wealth determines quantity of participation, not quality of participation.

Two pool products share one constitutional architecture. Pool 1, the General Startup Micro-Finance Pool, funds new products or services with social or environmental value through full digital smart contract infrastructure exclusively. Pool 2, the Local Cluster Development Micro-Finance Pool (LCDMFP), funds geographically-anchored production clusters — GI-registered or GI-eligible agro products, traditional handicrafts, area-specific processed goods, and localised manufacturing or fabrication hubs — through full digital or semi-digital infrastructure as cluster conditions determine. General retail trading is outside scope for both pools.

The architecture eliminates founder custody of pooled capital by construction. The Digital Startups Pool Regulatory Authority (DSPRA) verifies KYC, KYB, and expertise before issuing Pool Build Permission. A Combined Governing Board (CGB) — 50% Founder Committee, 50% Investor Governance Committee (IGC) — is constituted before any business operation begins; all pre-CGB formation costs are non-refundable founding costs borne by the founder, and investor capital remains untouched until the CGB exists. The CGB writes and locks all smart contract parameters. Every fund release is step-locked and paid directly to a verified third-party beneficiary — never to the founder — with a Veto Officer elected from the IGC holding delegated co-signature authority, and no cash transaction permitted after CGB formation. Micro-tokens transfer freely between KYC-verified investors. Fraud triggers automatic wallet freeze, on-chain evidence preservation, and regulatory referral. Pool 2 adds a minimum 30% producer carve-out within the IGC allocation, a mandatory certified professional in the Founder Committee, a Production Advance Facility, member producer purchase priority, and zero financial loss exposure for non-member producers.

title: He Is Looking Down on Me: Anticipated Contempt, Status-protective Devaluation, and Status-sensitive Aggression in the Workplace
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: He Is Looking Down on Me: Anticipated Contempt, Status-protective Devaluation, and Status-sensitive Aggression in the Workplace
detail.abstract:
This paper theorizes how the recurrent phrase “He is looking down on me” may transform perceived social devaluation into a persistent interpersonal pattern. The study begins with two male skilled workers observed in different workplaces. Although they differed in actual competence and career history, both placed substantial value on technical skills and credentials, engaged frequently in social comparison, and repeatedly used nearly identical expressions of perceived contempt toward multiple different people.

The paper defines Anticipated Contempt as the tendency to perceive that others regard the self as inferior, incompetent, ridiculous, or of lower value before clear evidence of contempt is established. It further introduces Recurrent-Phrase Framing, a process through which repeated expressions compress ambiguous interpersonal events into a stable relational narrative: the other becomes “the person who looks down on me,” while the self becomes “the person who is unfairly underestimated.”

The central argument is that recurrent phrases do not merely express pre-existing emotions. Through repeated verbalization, they may repeatedly reactivate attention, memory, shame, anger, vigilance, facial expression, tone of voice, and interpersonal behavior in the same direction. This Self-Formative Effect can gradually produce a defensive and hostile interpersonal style. Others may then withdraw, and that withdrawal can be reinterpreted as further evidence of contempt, creating a self-fulfilling loop between expectation, language, behavior, and social response.

The paper also argues that the desire not to be looked down upon is not inherently maladaptive. Earlier in life, it may be converted into effort, credential acquisition, skill development, and achievement. However, when the same comparison-based strategy persists after occupational and relational demands change, its function may reverse. The motivation to “prove them wrong” can shift toward the easier strategy of lowering others, producing Status-Protective Devaluation, incivility, and aggression.

By integrating research on social comparison, rejection sensitivity, hostile attribution, contingent self-worth, shame, rumination, framing, self-verification, self-fulfilling interaction, and workplace incivility, this paper proposes a middle-range model of how repeated language can help shape both the speaker and the social world the speaker repeatedly encounters.

title: The Carbon Handshake Architecture: From Verified Carbon to Settled Farmer Income — A Conceptual Design-Science Framework for Smallholder Carbon Finance in India: Institutional Coordination, Digital MRV, Blended Finance, Benefit Sharing and Settlement

detail.title: The Carbon Handshake Architecture: From Verified Carbon to Settled Farmer Income — A Conceptual Design-Science Framework for Smallholder Carbon Finance in India: Institutional Coordination, Digital MRV, Blended Finance, Benefit Sharing and Settlement

The author declares no other competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the research, analysis or conclusions presented in this paper

It did not involve human participants, interviews, surveys, experiments, patient data, personal data collection or animal research. No primary empirical data were collected; therefore, institutional ethics approval and informed consent were not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was prepared independently and received no external funding, research grant, sponsorship or financial support.

detail.abstract:
Smallholder carbon finance in India is constrained not only by methodology or market access, but by fragmentation across farmer enrolment, evidence generation, verification, transition finance, aggregation, registry operations, benefit sharing and payment settlement. This paper formalises the Carbon Handshake Architecture as an integrated institutional design for converting verified climate-positive agricultural activity into transparent and timely farmer income. It uses a conceptual design-science approach derived from the published practitioner work The Carbon Handshake: The Golden Suture.

The end-to-end smallholder carbon-finance transaction—beginning with consent and plot enrolment and ending with value allocation, beneficiary payment, reconciliation, grievance handling and reversal control—is treated as the unit of analysis. Four linked constructs are formalised. The Golden Suture specifies institutional interface governance; the Digital Spine specifies hybrid digital monitoring, reporting and verification and interoperable evidence; the 1:10 Multiplier specifies conditional catalytic-risk allocation and commercial-finance mobilisation; and the 80:20 Rule specifies ex-ante distributive governance and a farmer-value floor. The Interoperable Ledger, Farmer Producer Organisation aggregation, direct settlement, a defined payout service-level agreement, safeguards and stage-gated regional pilots operate as supporting mechanisms.

The paper defines the 72-hour payout clock as the interval from confirmed sale settlement to beneficiary credit and adopts 80 per cent of realised gross sale value as the proposed minimum farmer allocation, with the remaining 20 per cent constituting the complete enabling-cost and buffer envelope. These are transparent design normalisations, not existing legal mandates. The paper presents a conceptual implementation architecture rather than an empirically validated impact model. Ratios, costs, prices and programme scales remain illustrative unless independently verified. Its contribution is a falsifiable architecture for testing transaction cost, evidence quality, blended-finance additionality, benefit sharing, settlement reliability and institutional coordination in India and other smallholder economies.

title: A Recursive Institutional Architecture for Structuring National Innovation-Policy Problems: Introducing RIPSA

title: Anchored at the Floor: Pass-Through of Formula-Pinned Pay Floors to Above-Floor Pay in New York City's High-Volume For-Hire Sector

detail.title: Anchored at the Floor: Pass-Through of Formula-Pinned Pay Floors to Above-Floor Pay in New York City's High-Volume For-Hire Sector
detail.abstract: New York City indexes its per-trip minimum pay floor for high-volume for-hire services to the regional CPI-W each March. Where the floor binds, pass-through of an indexation is one by accounting; the open question is what happens to the cushion drivers were already paid above the formula. Using the full universe of published TLC trip records—505.0 million trips over 26 months, 413.0 million in the analysis sample—I find that at the March 2026 event Uber passed only 0.79 of the mandated increase through to above-floor pay (t against one = −4.4) while Lyft passed it through fully. Uber’s shortfall is dose-proportional: cells mandated a larger increase had more cushion clawed back, and roughly a fifth of the indexation was financed out of pay the platform had previously been offering above the formula. The result is below one in all 36 specifications of a specification curve and strengthens as cells are refined. I also show that the obvious way to state such a result—comparing above-floor cells to an estimated coefficient on cells at the floor—is contaminated by endogenous stratification (Abadie et al., 2018): classifying cells on a finite-sample estimate of their own cushion induces dose-proportional regression to the mean that drives the at-the-floor coefficient to 1.26 against a value accounting fixes at one. Out-of-sample classification removes it. Under this regime the formula has become an anchor as well as a floor, so mandated raises are partly self-financed out of above-floor pay.

title: Status Seeking and Sustainability: The Moderating Role of Income Inequality in the Status Values-Environmental Values and Behavior Nexus and the Green Gap

detail.title: Status Seeking and Sustainability: The Moderating Role of Income Inequality in the Status Values-Environmental Values and Behavior Nexus and the Green Gap

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a secondary analysis of publicly available, anonymized datasets from the European Values Study, World Values Survey, Standardized World Income Inequality Database (SWIID), and the World Bank. Ethical approval was obtained by the original data collectors, and no additional ethical approval was required for this secondary analysis.

detail.abstract: Income inequality shapes consumption patterns through status competition and social comparison, while environmental values and behaviors depend on both individual orientations and the social conditions that enable their translation into action. While previous research has examined these relationships separately, less is known about how inequality shapes the link between status values, environmental values, and behavior. Using the joint European Values Study-World Values Survey dataset combined with country-level income inequality data, this study employs multilevel mixed-effects regression models with country-level random effects. The analysis covers 84 countries, four income groups, and three time periods spanning 1980-2024. The findings show no universal trade-off between status values and environmental values. While status values are negatively associated with environmental values in some high-income contexts, these relationships weaken over time and are often positive in middleand low-income contexts. However, a trade-off pattern is found for the relationship between status values and environmental behavior, which is generally weak and either significantly negative or statistically insignificant. Furthermore, income inequality does not systematically reinforce a status-environment tradeoff. Instead, higher inequality often strengthens positive associations between status values and environmental values, consistent with mechanisms such as green status signaling. Nevertheless, income inequality consistently weakens the translation of environmental values into environmental behavior, thereby widening the green gap. These findings challenge the assumption that status values are inherently incompatible with environmentalism and identify income inequality as a structural factor that reinforces the alignment between status values and environmental values while simultaneously widening the environmental value-behavior gap.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Partial Homogeneity in Staggered Difference-in-Difference
affiliations: Ashoka University - Department of Economics and Ashoka University

detail.title: A Bayesian Approach to Partial Homogeneity in Staggered Difference-in-Difference
detail.abstract: In staggered difference-indifferences (DiD) designs, units enter treatment at different calendar times, so the treatment effect is not a single number but a set of Cohort-Average Treatment effects on the Treated (CATTs), one per cohort-time cell. Estimating every CATT as its own parameter, as the standard fully flexible estimator does, is unbiased but inefficient when some of these effects are in fact equal, whereas pooling them all into a single two-way fixed effects (TWFE) coefficient is efficient but biased whenever the heterogeneity is genuine. We frame the choice between these extremes as a partition-selection problem on the cohort-time cells and address it with a Dirichlet Process (DP) mixture prior on the CATTs. The model favors parsimonious groupings without fixing their number, and a collapsed Gibbs sampler delivers point estimates, credible intervals that marginalize the unknown partition, and co-clustering probabilities for every pair of CATTs. With the error variance held fixed, the model's maximum a posteriori (MAP) partition reduces to an ℓ 0-penalized regression, connecting the Bayesian formulation to the homogeneity-pursuit literature. In a calibrated simulation, the model cuts the sampling variance of the cohort-time effects by 26-52% relative to the fully flexible estimator, without the pooled estimator's bias, provided the distinct effects are separated enough to be recovered, and the posterior delivers near-nominal confidence-interval coverage by averaging over the unknown partition. In two applications the method recovers a precision-improving partial-homogeneity structure in one, where the cohort-time effects are genuinely heterogeneous, and reports that full pooling is adequate in the other, where they are not.

title: Catastrophic in Level, Progressive in Rate: The Distributional Incidence of Nigeria's 2023 Petrol Subsidy Removal and the Failure of Compensation

detail.title: Catastrophic in Level, Progressive in Rate: The Distributional Incidence of Nigeria's 2023 Petrol Subsidy Removal and the Failure of Compensation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper uses publicly available, anonymized secondary survey data including, the Nigeria General Household Survey Panel, Waves 4 and 5. No new data involving human participants were collected, so ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or NGO.

detail.abstract: On the 29th of May 2023, Nigeria removed its petrol subsidy with flotation of the Naira alongside, the spillover effect was a tripling pump prices for a population exceeding 217 million. Using the General Household Survey Panel (2023-2024, Wave 5) linked to Wave 4 (2018-2019), this paper provides the first ex-post distributional assessment of the reform from post-reform household microdata. Because no Wave 5 consumption aggregate was published, this paper constructs one by replicating the official Deaton-Zaidi methodology and deflate it with a survey-based price index by using a household spatial Paasche index combined with a temporal food deflator (2.47×) estimated from common item unit values across the two waves, instead of a single national CPI scalar. The construction reproduces the published Wave 4 aggregate closely (ratio 1.000, logcorrelation 0.964) and yields a 2018-2019 poverty headcount of 37.7%, just 2.4% points below the official NLSS published rate of 40.1%. Real median per capita consumption fell by 37.1% between 2018-2019 and 2023-2024. The poverty headcount rose from 37.7% to 64.2%, with the poverty gap and severity rising in step, while inequality rose gradually (Gini 0.366 to 0.402). Formal progressivity statistics sharpen the picture because the concentration index of petrol spending was 0.52 and it remained roughly stable at 0.55, while the Kakwani index shifted only from +0.156 to +0.149, so the prereform subsidy was highly pro-rich and petrol exposure remained pro-rich throughout the reform. Compensation failed the most exposed because only 3.9% of households received any assistance, coverage was flat across the distribution, and a weighted logit gives a small, statistically insignificant consumption gradient. The programme's failure is one of near-absolute absence, not regressive tilt. The reform was progressive in the benefit it withdrew yet catastrophic in its absolute effect on the poor, who were left majorly uncompensated. The binding policy failure is the compensation architecture, not the price change.

title: Marginal Tax Rates and Individual Income Tax Compliance
affiliations: , Indiana University Bloomington - School of Public & Environmental Affairs (SPEA) and U.S. Department of the Treasury, Office of Tax Analysis (OTA)

detail.title: Marginal Tax Rates and Individual Income Tax Compliance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No authors have any interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: The study was not funded.

detail.abstract: We study how marginal tax rates affect the amount of income tax underreporting by individual income taxpayers in the U.S. This is an interesting and open question, as theoretical models suggest an ambiguous effect (see Allingham and Sandmo (1972)), and previous empirical studies are generally dated and do not account for the endogeneity of marginal tax rates to reported income. Our study uses new methods and more recent data to identify the causal effect of marginal tax rates on income reporting in the United States. Utilizing administrative tax audit data from the National Research Program that span 2006-2017, we estimate the responsiveness of noncompliance as measured by audit adjustments to marginal tax rates using three approaches: pooled cross-section regression, difference-indifferences estimation of the Kansas state tax reform, and examining differences in bunching at kinks in marginal tax rate schedules in pre-and post-audit income. Across all three approaches, results consistently show that higher marginal tax rates lead to greater amounts of non-compliance, with elasticities ranging from 0.03 to 0.26, and with larger elasticities for taxpayers with Schedule C or E income and in response to larger tax rate changes.

title: Forex Guard: A Privacy-Preserving Local-First Framework for Dual-Currency Budget Management and Exchange-Rate Risk Mitigation for Indian Students in Japan.

detail.title: Forex Guard: A Privacy-Preserving Local-First Framework for Dual-Currency Budget Management and Exchange-Rate Risk Mitigation for Indian Students in Japan.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial interests, personal relationships, or competing interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual research paper and did not involve human participants, personal data, animal subjects, or clinical experiments. Therefore, ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
International students studying in Japan often receive financial support from InIdia in Indian Rupees (INR) while managing their daily expenses in Japanese Yen (JPY). Although their monthly living expenses may remain relatively stable, fluctuations in the JPY–INR exchange rate continuously alter the purchasing power of remitted funds, making long-term financial planning difficult. Existing budgeting applications primarily focus on single-currency expense management, whereas foreign exchange platforms concentrate on currency conversion and remittance services. Current solutions rarely integrate exchange-rate volatility, behavioral budgeting principles, and student-specific financial constraints into a unified budgeting system.

This paper proposes Forex Guard, a privacy-first dual-currency budget monitoring framework designed specifically for Indian students residing in Japan. The proposed system combines lightweight statistical forecasting, historical exchange-rate variance, local spending velocity, and behavioral finance principles to provide dynamic budgeting guidance while preserving user privacy through a local-first architecture. Rather than attempting to predict exact exchange rates, Forex Guard estimates practical risk buffers using rolling statistical measures to improve financial resilience under currency uncertainty. The framework also incorporates student-oriented features, including dual-currency purchasing power visualization, categorized expense tracking, part-time work-hour awareness, and offline-first data management.

As a software engineering research proposal, this paper presents the conceptual system architecture, technical justification, implementation strategy, evaluation methodology, and acknowledged limitations of the proposed framework. The proposed evaluation employs forecasting accuracy metrics, the System Usability Scale (SUS), the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), and budget variance analysis to assess the system's potential effectiveness in improving budgeting accuracy, reducing cognitive workload, and supporting financially informed decision-making for Indian students studying in Japan.

detail.abstract: Moral judgment is often treated as an external alignment constraint in AI systems. This paper argues that moral judgment should instead be understood as an intellectual capability that guides decision-making under normative uncertainty. Framed this way, ethics becomes a designable system component rather than an after-the-fact restriction.

title: Quantifying the Cost of Oil Shocks: The Case of the Transportation Sector
affiliations: Banque de France

detail.title: Quantifying the Cost of Oil Shocks: The Case of the Transportation Sector
detail.abstract: I study the impact of oil shocks on key financial ratios of transportation firms over the past two decades, both during and outside periods of energy crisis. I investigate heterogeneous effects across transportation modes, shock signs, and firm sizes. I also discuss the trade-off between the cost related to oil shocks and the cost of financing the low-carbon transition. Using firm-level data, I show that exposure to oil shocks significantly influences real outcomes but in an asymmetric manner: following oil price increases, profit margins decline, labor share and debt increases, whereas oil price decreases generate no effects. I show that the transmission of oil price increases operates through rigidities on the labor side. These effects vanish in the medium term. Quantitatively, one-standard deviation higher weighted-oil price increase leads to a 8.2% decrease in profit margin. However, even if the magnitude is economically significant, I show that these effects are modest when compared with an investment option hedging against these shocks. I extend the analysis to the 2022 energy crisis and show that public support largely offset the adverse effect of price increases. All in all, I show that oil shock did not provide incentives to finance the low-carbon transition over 2000-2022. Finally, I assess the external validity over two major European countries. This paper has implications for financial stability and climate transition regardless of the origin of energy price shocks (climate risks, carbon taxation, geopolitical events). I also provide quantitative evidence on the financial challenge posed by the low-carbon transition.

title: Counterexamples and Sufficient Conditions: Comments on "Optimally-Transported Generalized Method of Moments"
affiliations: Mizuho-DL Financial Technology Co., Ltd.

detail.title: Counterexamples and Sufficient Conditions: Comments on "Optimally-Transported Generalized Method of Moments"
detail.abstract: We comment on the optimally-transported generalized method of moments (OT-GMM) estimator proposed by Schennach & Starck (2026a) and give counterexamples to Theorems 2-6 under their stated assumptions. First, the assumptions used in the small-error analysis are insufficient for consistency in Theorem 2 and asymptotic normality in Theorem 3. Next, we consider the large-error analysis, in which Theorem 4 states that the OTGMM estimator is equivalent to a GMM estimator with modified moments. We show that in a scalar model, Theorem 4 selects a value that differs from the unique OTGMM minimizer and violates the OTGMM sample moment restriction. In an overidentified model satisfying the assumptions used in Theorems 5 and 6, the first component of the Lagrange multiplier has different probability limits under the OTGMM estimator and the GMM estimator with modified moments. Under misspecification, the population value selected by OTGMM depends on the transport metric and on which variables may be adjusted. We give a sufficient condition under which solutions of the modified moment equations also solve the original constrained problem at a given parameter value, and separate conditions for consistency and asymptotic normality of the OTGMM estimator. We also show that Assumption 16 does not imply the matrix bound used in the supplemental proofs and replace Assumption 16 with a matrix condition that yields the bound.

title: The Enclosure of the Social Brain: Model Autophagy Disorder, Cognitive Wealth, and a Sociotechnical Design Framework for AI-resilient Information Systems

detail.title: The Enclosure of the Social Brain: Model Autophagy Disorder, Cognitive Wealth, and a Sociotechnical Design Framework for AI-resilient Information Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interests
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

detail.abstract:
The rapid deployment of generative artificial intelligence (AI) within organ-
izational and educational information systems (IS) presents structural chal-
lenges that conventional AI governance frameworks are not equipped to ad-
dress. This paper argues that contemporary AI systems are executing a
digital enclosure of humanity's collective cognitive commons - what we term
Cognitive Wealth - by commodifying the accumulated intellectual heritage
of the social brain into private, subscription-based reasoning engines. This
enclosure is accelerated by two interlocking crises with direct implications
for IS design. First, the recursive ingestion of synthetic training data drives
Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD), a statistically formalizable degeneration
in which AI models progressively drift from the ground-truth distribution of
human knowledge. Second, the uncalibrated offloading of cognitive pro-
cesses onto AI interfaces induces two distinct behavioral pathways: cogni-
tive atrophy in adult professionals and cognitive foreclosure in novice learn-
ers. We advance three contributions. First, we synthesize the IS, cognitive
science, and AI ethics literatures to formalize Cognitive Wealth as an ana-
lytically tractable design concern for information systems researchers. Sec-
ond, we present a mathematical treatment of MAD, grounding it in Kullback-
Leibler divergence theory, and demonstrate through formal proof that au-
tophagous training loops produce strictly non-decreasing divergence from
the true human data distribution. Third, drawing on design-science research
methodology, we propose a Sociotechnical Design Framework for Cognitive
Wealth Preservation comprising three artifact-level components: a Socratic
Interface, an Adaptive Epistemic Escalation Layer, and an Open Cognitive
Commons governance model. We subject each component to adversarial di-
alectical critique, surfacing the tensions between system efficiency, human
cognitive sovereignty, and the political economy of data enclosure. We con-
clude with a structured agenda for future IS and AI research.

title: Church Diplomacy of the Russian Orthodox Church as a Non-State Actor in the Digital Era: Instruments, Functions, and International Presence
affiliations: MGIMO University

detail.title: Church Diplomacy of the Russian Orthodox Church as a Non-State Actor in the Digital Era: Instruments, Functions, and International Presence
detail.abstract: The growing salience of non-state actors in contemporary international relations has brought religious institutions to the centre of scholarly attention. This paper examines the church diplomacy of the Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) as a distinctive form of non-state diplomatic activity operating at the intersection of religious mission, public diplomacy, and value-normative communication. Drawing on social constructivist theory and a systematic analysis of the ROC's institutional structures, official documents, and external communication practices, the paper identifies the core functions, subjects, instruments, and strategic logic of ROC church diplomacy in the digital era. The paper argues that the ROC's international presence is grounded not in material coercion but in moral authority, symbolic capital, and transnational ecclesiastical networksresources that are increasingly projected through digital channels. The digitalization of inter-church communication, multilingual online platforms, and social media has fundamentally reconfigured the ROC's capacity to engage global audiences, promote its value agenda, and exercise normative influence in world politics. The paper further situates ROC church diplomacy within the broader phenomenon of religious soft power and its relationship to Russian foreign policy, arguing for an analytically nuanced understanding that resists both the reduction of church diplomacy to state instrumentality and its mischaracterisation as purely spiritual activity.

title: Revisiting Earnings Management with a Focus on The Impact of Sox and Auditing
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Paul Merage School of Business and UC Irvine/The Paul Merage School of Business

detail.title: Revisiting Earnings Management with a Focus on The Impact of Sox and Auditing
detail.abstract: We revisit the issue of earnings management (EM) more than 35 years after Schipper’s (1989) influential commentary on the subject. Revisiting is timely as important legislative, regulatory, and other events have occurred since 1989, including accounting fraud scandals, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and increased regulation of auditing, and the EM literature’s recognition managers can use real activities in addition to accounting-based EM tools to manage earnings. We discuss some key findings of EM research and focus on the likely impact of SOX and auditing on EM. Recent research supports the following: continuation of early findings showing a decline in accounting-based EM post-SOX; volatility in real EM and a lessening of the substitution between accounting-based and real EM post-SOX; and evidence suggesting external auditors constrain EM in settings of heightened pressures to manage earnings.

title: To Share or Not to Share? The Role of Visible Share Counts in Driving Sharing Behavior: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, , Hefei University of Technology and University of Delaware

detail.title: To Share or Not to Share? The Role of Visible Share Counts in Driving Sharing Behavior: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
detail.abstract: User-generated content (UGC) sharing is an inherent feature of social media platforms, driving both user engagement and content diffusion. Despite its central role, platforms differ in whether they publicly display share counts, reflecting mixed understanding of how visible share counts affect user behavior. This study investigates the effect of publicly visible share counts on subsequent user sharing. Under an overarching self-presentation framework, share counts may influence subsequent user sharing through two opposing mechanisms: a quality-signaling mechanism that encourages sharing and a uniqueness-signaling mechanism that discourages it. In collaboration with a music-based social media platform, we conduct a blocked randomized field experiment that exogenously increases the displayed share counts of useruploaded singing recordings. Analyzing 73,665 recordings posted over a two-month period, we find that increasing publicly visible share counts significantly reduces subsequent sharing. This negative net effect is consistent with uniqueness-signaling considerations outweighing quality-signaling considerations on average in this setting. Theory-guided subgroup patterns are directionally consistent with this interpretation, although the corresponding interaction tests are not statistically significant and are therefore treated as suggestive. We discuss the theoretical and practical implications for platform design and creator equity.

title: Foreign Participation Under Nigeria's Local Content Act and the Limits of Nigerian Corporate Law
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Foreign Participation Under Nigeria's Local Content Act and the Limits of Nigerian Corporate Law

keywords: Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development Act

detail.abstract:
Nigeria's general investment regime permits foreign investors to own up to 100 per cent of the equity in a Nigerian company. The Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development Act 2010 (“Local Content Act” or “Act”), however, adopts a markedly different approach. While it does not prohibit foreign ownership, it reserves many of the industry's most significant commercial advantages, including first and exclusive consideration in the award of oil blocks, licences and contracts, together with preferential treatment in bid evaluation, for "Nigerian companies" and "Nigerian indigenous companies" that satisfy statutory ownership thresholds and demonstrate meaningful local capacity. A foreign investor may therefore lawfully establish and wholly own a Nigerian subsidiary yet remain ineligible for the regulatory preferences that often determine commercial competitiveness. This article argues that corporate nationality should not be conflated with Nigerian content. The central inquiry under the Local Content Act is not simply whether a company is incorporated in Nigeria, but whether its ownership, governance, operational capacity and commercial activities genuinely advance the Act's local content objectives.

The article traces the evolution of Nigeria's local participation policy from the indigenisation programme of the 1970s to the enactment of the Act in 2010 before examining the legislation's principal regulatory mechanisms, including the Nigerian Content Plan (“NCP”), the Schedule's minimum Nigerian content thresholds, the margin of preference, the US$1 million contract review regime, expatriate employment restrictions, and the Nigerian Content Development Fund (the “Fund”). It then demonstrates that six distinct concepts, namely incorporation, ownership, control, operational capacity, technical capability and activity-specific Nigerian content obligations, have too often been collapsed into the single question of corporate registration, notwithstanding that the Local Content Act treats each as serving a different regulatory function.

Applying this analytical framework to the principal models of foreign participation, including wholly owned subsidiaries, equity joint ventures, contractual alliances and technology transfer arrangements, the article identifies the boundary between legitimate corporate structuring and impermissible "fronting", whereby nominal Nigerian ownership is used to obtain statutory advantages intended for genuine local participation. It concludes that compliance with the Local Content Act ultimately depends upon substance rather than form. A structure achieves lasting legal and commercial legitimacy only where Nigerian equity represents genuine ownership, bears real commercial risk and reward, and is supported by demonstrable Nigerian capacity to perform the relevant work. In the local content regime, incorporation opens the door but substance determines whether the company may lawfully remain in the room.

title: The Conditions of Dynamic Aggregation: Coordinates, Measurement, and Contested Institutions

detail.title: The Conditions of Dynamic Aggregation: Coordinates, Measurement, and Contested Institutions
detail.abstract: Accounting consistency and predictive sufficiency are different properties. An official aggregate can continue to measure exactly what it was designed to count while ceasing to contain the state needed to predict subsequent dynamics. This paper develops a framework for identifying that failure. Economic interaction has three distinct effects: dispersion erases hidden variation, common exposure aligns agents through shared inputs, and strategic complementarity amplifies alignment through endogenous feedback. Their balance determines whether a selected macro state closes dynamically, whether distributions, networks, or histories must be added, or whether low-dimensional closure survives in new coordinates. The paper turns this distinction into a diagnostic protocol for applied work: a placebo-calibrated pre-estimation sufficiency check, a horizon-specific closure profile with joint inference, a matched-complexity replacement test that distinguishes missing state variables from obsolete coordinates, and regime-conditional state selection. An exact hidden-state elimination shows how omitted state generates transients and memory. Institutions alter adjustment speeds, feedback channels, common exposures, and measurement perimeters while agents adapt around them. Proposition 1 derives a perimeter-leakage result. When a regulated actor can satisfy a measured reduction through genuine reduction or off-perimeter relocation, convex adjustment costs imply that relocation rises with the relative cost of genuine reduction. If relocated interaction remains systemically effective, the proxy improves faster than the latent object; when 𝜂 < 0, the proxy improves while effective coupling worsens. Financial regulation and national accounting illustrate the framework, and delegated cognition supplies a prospective coordinate-replacement application. The paper is conceptual and analytical. It specifies diagnostics and empirical designs rather than reporting estimates.

title: Global Review of Emergency Management Systems Supporting Early Warning, Alert, and Response
affiliations: Resolve to Save Lives, Government of the United States of America - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Resolve to Save Lives and

detail.title: Global Review of Emergency Management Systems Supporting Early Warning, Alert, and Response

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Several authors are affiliated with Resolve to Save Lives or the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which have supported the development or implementation of emergency management systems (i.e., EAMS, Africa CDC EMS, ZEBRA) included in this assessment. These systems were evaluated using the same framework and criteria applied to all platforms included in the study. The authors declare no other competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: Gates Foundation and US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

detail.abstract:
Background: Early warning, alert, and response (EWAR) capacity is required to detect and respond to public health emergencies. Various digital systems exist to support public health emergency management but are not well documented in the literature. We reviewed existing systems to identify and characterize those used to manage EWAR data and activities, assess their value to users, and highlight best practices, design elements, implementation strategies, and enabling environments that contribute to successful use.

Methods: We conducted a mixed-methods landscape assessment to identify and characterize systems used to support EWAR workflows. Systems were identified through literature review and expert consultation and screened using predefined functional criteria. We assessed eligible systems through technical document review, system demonstrations, and key informant interviews, and analyzed qualitative data using thematic analysis.

Findings: Of 18 systems identified for review, 10 were eligible for assessment and implemented in 39 countries across five World Health Organization regions. Eight of the ten systems supported early warning functions and data visualization and fewer integrated multiple data sources or addressed a majority of response functions. Themes identified from key informant interviews included system value and challenges to sustainability.

Interpretation: Digital systems increasingly serve as centralized coordination platforms for epidemic intelligence, enabling shared situational awareness and improved response coordination even with siloed surveillance systems. However, limited data and process integration, inadequate governance and partner coordination, and sustainability constraints often prevent these systems from achieving full potential. Addressing these challenges will strengthen their effectiveness in supporting end-to-end emergency management.

title: The Case for Statutory Regulation as the Preferred Governance Model for Social Media Platforms
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: The Case for Statutory Regulation as the Preferred Governance Model for Social Media Platforms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors did not receive any funding for this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper aims to make the normative and objective case for statutory regulation, as the overall preferred way to govern social media platforms. It introduces the topic, summarizes relevant literature on it, and provides unique arguments for why statutory regulation is an overall better system. It argues that statutory regulation is best fit with the economic realities of a free market, argues that it prevents unlawful censorship, and creates a unified framework of regulation. Finally, it recommends policy measures and principles for best practice in designing policies. It recommends that intergovernmental institutions and international law play a strong role in regulating social media platforms, recommends the creation of an international court of arbitration and digital rights statutory court to solve disputes between users, platforms, and governments, condemns blanket bans on social media and extremely strong regulation of these platforms, and more.

title: Why Balochistan Has Not Converted Assets into Prosperity, and the Way Forward

detail.title: Why Balochistan Has Not Converted Assets into Prosperity, and the Way Forward

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Disclosure Statement: The views, analysis, and conclusions presented in this paper are solely those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views, policies, or positions of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the United Nations, or any other organization with which the author is affiliated. The author declares no financial, commercial, or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the preparation or conclusions of this paper.

detail.abstract:
Balochistan is Pakistan's largest province by area and possesses substantial natural resource wealth, including mineral reserves, energy resources, and the strategic Gwadar Port. Despite significant public investment through federal and provincial Public Sector Development Programmes (PSDPs), the province continues to record the highest poverty rates in the country. This paper draws on secondary data, government reports, and published literature to examine the factors contributing to the disconnect between resource endowments, public spending, and socioeconomic outcomes in Balochistan.

The analysis identifies several interrelated constraints, including low development fund utilization, institutional capacity gaps, limited local benefit-sharing from major investments, human capital deficits, and weak monitoring and accountability mechanisms. The paper argues that the primary challenge is not the availability of resources or development financing, but the limited institutional capacity to convert these assets and investments into measurable and sustainable development outcomes.

Building on principles of Results-Based Management (RBM), public sector performance management, and evidence-based planning, the paper proposes a governance-focused reform agenda that includes strengthening monitoring and evaluation systems, institutionalizing results frameworks, deploying digital performance dashboards, enhancing transparency in public investment management, and improving local benefit-sharing from major infrastructure and extractive projects. The paper concludes that sustainable poverty reduction in Balochistan will depend less on increasing development allocations and more on improving the effectiveness, accountability, and outcome orientation of institutions responsible for planning, implementing, and monitoring development investments.

title: Digital Innovation for Circular Economy Transformation: The DICE Mechanism Architecture
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Eindhoven University of Technology and University of Exeter

detail.title: Digital Innovation for Circular Economy Transformation: The DICE Mechanism Architecture
detail.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly mobilized to support circular economy (CE) transitions, yet innovation management research lacks a clear explanation of how digital innovation (DI) is organized to enable, coordinate, reconfigure, and stabilize circular systems. Existing studies are dominated by technology-centric and performance-focused perspectives, focusing primarily on individual technologies and their CE outcomes while offering limited understanding of the generative mechanisms through which DI is configured and managed to enable circular transformation. This study addresses this gap by developing the DICE configurational mechanism architecture through a two-tiered research design combining grounded theory-informed meta-synthesis and empirical elaboration. Synthesizing evidence from 107 studies, the first tier theorizes how DI shapes circular systems through six interdependent mechanisms: lifecycle datafication and traceability; digital matching and coordination; circular flow reconfiguration; circular value architecture reconfiguration; digital accountability and compliance; and digital participation and behavioral intervention. The second tier examines how these mechanisms are activated and combined into distinct configurations across empirical contexts, drawing on an analysis of 36 DICE initiatives. The findings show that digitally enabled circularity does not emerge from technologies themselves or from universally integrated transformation models, but from contingent configurations of mechanisms spanning informational, relational, operational, economic, institutional and behavioral domains. The study contributes to innovation management by conceptualizing digital circular innovation as a configurational challenge and by demonstrating how distinct combinations of DI mechanisms support alternative pathways to circular transformation. The resulting DICE architecture provides an integrative lens for understanding and guiding digitally enabled circular transformation across diverse organizational and ecosystem contexts.

title: Rebuilding Startups: An Empirical Study on Remote Work and Skill Complementarity
affiliations: , University of Texas at Austin, University of Pittsburgh and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Information, Risk and Operations Management

detail.title: Rebuilding Startups: An Empirical Study on Remote Work and Skill Complementarity
detail.abstract: Remote work has become a central managerial choice in the future of work, yet its implications for firms' talent composition and organizational structure remain underexplored. This question is especially important for startups, which often operate with small teams and limited resources while facing strong constraints in accessing talent through local labor markets. We focus on skill complementarity, a dimension of talent composition that is particularly critical to startups' early-stage development. By integrating LinkedIn job postings, worker skills, and worker mobility data, we study the impact of remote work on skill complementarity in startups. We find that higher remote work intensity increases firm-level skill complementarity, primarily by helping startups recruit new workers whose skills better match the firms' hiring needs and diversify the skill sets of existing employees. We further show that this shift in workforce composition carries important organizational consequences: remote work is associated with greater organizational hierarchy through increased skill complementarity. These findings suggest that, for startups, remote work is not merely a flexibility policy but a strategic hiring mechanism that helps young firms assemble complementary talent despite resource constraints. At the same time, this may push startups toward more hierarchical structures, which serve as formalized coordination mechanisms to effectively achieve the value of a more complementary workforce.

title: Shareholder Activism as an M&A Catalyst in Japan

detail.title: Shareholder Activism as an M&A Catalyst in Japan
detail.abstract: This note raises the question of whether shareholder activism has led to increased value or diminished value for Japanese private equity's rapidly developing "take private" market. According to M&A data, Japanese related M&A volume was $385.9 billion in 2025, representing a year over year increase of 33%. Additionally, the number of public shareholder activist campaigns has increased nearly 90% and is estimated to be around 85 campaigns, making Japan the second largest country in terms of shareholder activism markets, after the U.S. To assess the impact of shareholder activism on the valuation of public companies, analysed four precedent transactions: Toshiba, Fuji Soft, Topcon and Makino. Based on this analysis we applied an anchoring strategy to determine what real market prices would be. Shareholder activists are a legitimate catalyst for M&A activity in Japan providing both motivations to produce transactions and discipline by especially sensitive nature of the "headline" business being acquired as seen within our benchmarking. The last example illustrates that while shareholder activists can play an important role as a catalyst for M&A activity in Japan, it is still unknown how much realized value has been produced from shareholder activist involvement. There are at least two equally important determinants influencing the realization of value from shareholder activist participation-one being pricing discipline and the other being the regulatory execution risk associated with M&A transactions.

title: Can GAID Guide New Sales Hires to Stay? The Effects of a Generative AI Digital-Human Coach on Early-Stage Turnover at a Leading Beverage Company
affiliations: , Renmin University of China,  and University of Miami - Business Technology

detail.title: Can GAID Guide New Sales Hires to Stay? The Effects of a Generative AI Digital-Human Coach on Early-Stage Turnover at a Leading Beverage Company
detail.abstract: Early-stage turnover among new sales hires is a persistent challenge for firms, yet traditional training and human mentoring often struggle to provide continuous, personalized, and contextualized sales support. This study examines whether access to a generative AI digital-human coaching system reduces turnover risk during new hires' first six months. The system translates selected experience patterns from prior sales practices into repeatable training resources through simulated customer interactions and immediate feedback; at the same time, it may also impose additional learning and information-processing demands as employees learn to use the system and interpret its feedback. Drawing on job demands-resources theory, we use employee-month panel data from a large beverage company affiliated with a Fortune Global 500 enterprise from January 2024 to February 2026 and employ an employee-month difference-indifferences design to identify the effect of generative AI digital-human coaching system access on turnover among new sales hires. The results show that access to the generative AI digital-human coaching system significantly reduces early-stage turnover risk among new sales hires; staggered difference-indifferences estimates, event-study evidence, instrumental variable analysis, and a series of robustness checks support this finding. Mechanism and process evidence is consistent with a resource-dominant interpretation: the reduction is concentrated in voluntary exits related to performance pressure, insufficient sales skills, and training difficulties, and greater improvements in sales capabilities are associated with lower subsequent turnover. Heterogeneity analyses show that AI training is more effective for new hires with limited prior work experience, higher educational attainment, and access granted during the early-to-middle onboarding stage. Additional analyses show that AI does not generate uniformly positive effects across employee groups: broader access to the system among new hires is associated with increased voluntary turnover among senior employees. This study extends research on workplace generative AI from productivity and task performance to early-stage new-hire retention and conceptualizes a generative AI digital-human coaching system as an enterprise application technology that simultaneously creates job resources and job demands.
